uni-ece-analog-communication.title: Analog Communication
uni-ece-analog-communication.description: Full B.Tech Analog Communication syllabus: Communication systems and noise; Amplitude modulation; Angle modulation (FM and PM); Radio receivers and noise performance; Pulse analog modulation and multiplexing; Revision, practicals & exam. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.Tech programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Communication systems and noise
courses.summary: Block diagram of communication systems, need for modulation, bandwidth, decibels, thermal noise, SNR, noise figure and noise temperature, cascaded stages.
outcomes: Explain why modulation is needed
Compute thermal noise power and voltage
Compute SNR, noise figure and equivalent temperature
Use Friis formula for cascades and find receiver sensitivity

lessons.title: The communication chain and why we modulate

scenes.text: Speech occupies 300 Hz–3.4 kHz. A quarter-wave antenna for 3 kHz would be 25 km long, and every speaker would interfere with every other.
Modulation shifts the message to a high carrier frequency, solving both problems.

steps.title: Block diagram
steps.body: Information source → input transducer → **transmitter** (modulator, amplifier, antenna) → **channel** (wire, free space, fibre; adds noise, attenuation, distortion) → **receiver** (RF amplifier, demodulator, filter) → output transducer. Baseband signal: the original message; passband: after modulation. Bandwidth B (Hz) is the spectrum occupied.

steps.title: Reasons for modulation
steps.body: 1) Practical antenna size ≈ λ/4 = c/4f. 2) Frequency-division multiplexing: many users share one medium. 3) Noise/interference reduction (e.g. FM). 4) Matching to channel properties. 5) Allows frequency allocation.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: Baseband 3 kHz: λ/4 = 3×10⁸/(4×3000) = **25 km**. Carrier 1 MHz: λ/4 = 75 m. Carrier 100 MHz: 0.75 m.

steps.title: Example 2 — decibels
steps.body: Power ratio 1000 = 30 dB; voltage ratio 10 = 20 dB. Gain 40 dB = ×10⁴ in power. 0 dBm = 1 mW; 30 dBm = 1 W; −30 dBm = 1 µW.

steps.title: Example 3 — bands
steps.body: AM broadcast: 535–1605 kHz (MF); FM: 88–108 MHz (VHF); TV, mobile: UHF; satellite: GHz.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Confusing power dB (10 log) with voltage dB (20 log).

activity.prompt: Quarter-wave antenna length (m) for a 1 MHz carrier.

scenes.text: Tune a radio between stations and hear the hiss. Part of it is the random thermal motion of electrons in the receiver's first resistor.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Noise sources
steps.body:
- **Thermal (Johnson):** open-circuit mean-square voltage **v_n² = 4kTRB**; available power **P_n = kTB** (independent of R). k = 1.38×10⁻²³ J/K; T = 290 K (reference) → kT = 4×10⁻²¹ W/Hz = −174 dBm/Hz.
- **Shot noise:** i_n² = 2qI_DCB (q = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C).
- **Flicker (1/f)**, partition noise, atmospheric/man-made noise.
White noise has flat PSD N0/2 (two-sided). **SNR = P_signal/P_noise**; SNR(dB) = 10 log.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting the 4 in 4kTRB (open-circuit voltage) versus kTB (power into a matched load).

activity.prompt: Thermal noise voltage (µV rms) of 10 kΩ over 1 MHz at 290 K.

lessons.title: Noise figure, equivalent temperature and cascades

story.title: Why the dish has a tiny amplifier on the front

scenes.text: A satellite dish places a low-noise block (LNB) right at the feed. Noise added in the first stage dominates the whole receiver.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **Noise figure F = SNR_in/SNR_out** (at T0 = 290 K); NF = 10 log F ≥ 0 dB. Equivalent noise temperature **T_e = (F − 1)T0**. For an attenuator of loss L at temperature T0: F = L. **Friis cascade:** F = F1 + (F2−1)/G1 + (F3−1)/(G1G2) + …; T_e = T1 + T2/G1 + T3/(G1G2).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: LNA: NF = 3 dB (F = 2), G = 20 dB (100). Mixer: F2 = 10 (10 dB). F = 2 + 9/100 = **2.09** → 3.2 dB. Without LNA: 10 dB. Gain before the noisy stage matters.

steps.title: Example 3 — cable first
steps.body: Cable loss 3 dB (F1 = 2, G1 = 0.5) before LNA (F2 = 1.26, 1 dB NF): F = 2 + 0.26/0.5 = 2.52 → 4.0 dB — worse than LNA first (≈1 dB).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using dB values directly in the Friis formula — convert to linear ratios.

activity.prompt: Cascade F (linear): F1=2, G1=100, F2=10.

lessons.title: Lab: Receiver sensitivity and link SNR

story.title: How weak a station can I hear?

scenes.text: A receiver datasheet lists sensitivity; you can derive it from first principles.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Sensitivity
steps.body: **P_min (dBm) = −174 + 10 log B + NF + SNR_min(dB)**.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: B = 200 kHz (FM), NF = 6 dB, required SNR 10 dB: −174 + 53 + 6 + 10 = **−105 dBm**.

steps.title: Example 2 — audio SNR
steps.body: Input SNR 30 dB, NF 3 dB → output SNR 27 dB.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using the signal bandwidth for baseband audio SNR but IF bandwidth for the receiver noise.

activity.prompt: Sensitivity (dBm): B=200 kHz, NF=6 dB, SNR=10 dB.

questions.q: Thermal noise power for 1 MHz at 290 K (dBm)

courses.title: Unit 2 · Amplitude modulation
courses.summary: Conventional AM, DSB-SC, SSB and VSB: spectra, power, generation and detection, with envelope detector design and transmitter calculations.
outcomes: Compute modulation index, bandwidth, powers and efficiency
Describe DSB-SC, SSB and VSB generation and detection
Design an envelope detector
Solve AM transmitter problems

scenes.text: An AM broadcast at 1000 kHz carries a 5 kHz audio tone; the receiver sees a carrier and two sidebands at 995 and 1005 kHz.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: AM wave
steps.body:
s(t) = A_c[1 + μ cos(ω_m t)] cos(ω_c t), **μ = A_m/A_c** (modulation index). μ ≤ 1 for envelope detection (μ > 1: over-modulation, distortion). Expanding: A_c cos ω_ct + (μA_c/2)cos(ω_c+ω_m)t + (μA_c/2)cos(ω_c−ω_m)t. **Bandwidth B = 2f_m**.

Powers (into R): P_c = A_c²/2R; each sideband μ²P_c/4; **P_t = P_c(1 + μ²/2)**; efficiency **η = μ²/(2 + μ²)** → 33.3 % at μ = 1. Multi-tone: μ_t = √(μ1²+μ2²+…). Envelope: A_c(1+μcos ω_mt); μ = (V_max − V_min)/(V_max + V_min).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body: Envelope V_max = 12 V, V_min = 4 V: μ = 8/16 = **0.5**; A_c = 8 V, A_m = 4 V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using μ in percent in formulas.
- Forgetting that bandwidth depends on f_m (highest message frequency), not f_c.

activity.prompt: Total power (W) for P_c = 100 W and μ = 0.6.

quiz.q: Max efficiency of conventional AM (single tone)

lessons.title: Lab: AM numericals and trapezoidal pattern

scenes.text: A student connects the AM signal to the Y-plates and the modulating signal to the X-plates of an oscilloscope: a trapezoid appears; its shape reveals μ.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Trapezoid method
steps.body: With the message on X and AM wave on Y, a trapezoid forms. If its parallel sides are a (long) and b (short): **μ = (a − b)/(a + b)**. A triangle means μ = 1 (b = 0); a rectangle means no modulation (a = b); a tilted/looped figure indicates phase shift or distortion.

steps.title: Example 2 — transmitter
steps.body: Carrier current in antenna 8 A; with modulation 8.93 A: 8.93/8 = 1.116 → 1 + μ²/2 = 1.246 → **μ = 0.70**.

steps.title: Example 3 — carrier suppression
steps.body: Total power 150 W at μ=1: carrier 100 W; if the carrier is suppressed, 50 W remain for the two sidebands — 66.7 % power saved.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Reading μ from the carrier amplitude only — you need both V_max and V_min.

activity.prompt: μ from antenna currents 8 A (unmodulated) and 8.93 A (modulated).

story.title: Squeezing more calls into a band

scenes.text: Long-distance telephone trunks stacked 4 kHz voice channels using SSB, halving the bandwidth versus AM.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Variants
steps.body:
**DSB-SC:** s = m(t)cos ω_ct; BW = 2W; no carrier power. Generated by balanced modulator/ring modulator/product modulator; needs coherent detection. **SSB:** one sideband only, BW = W; generated by the filter method (sharp filter) or the phase-shift (Hartley) method s = ½[m cos ω_ct ∓ m̂ sin ω_ct] (m̂ is the Hilbert transform). **VSB:** one sideband plus a vestige of the other, BW ≈ W + f_v; used for the video signal in analogue TV (vestigial filter response with odd symmetry about f_c).

Synchronous detection: multiply by cos(ω_ct + φ) and low-pass: output ∝ m cos φ; with phase error φ = 90° the output is zero; with frequency error Δω the message is modulated by cos Δωt (beating).

steps.title: Example 1 — power saving
steps.body: AM μ = 1, P_c = 100 W, P_t = 150 W. SSB carries one sideband = 25 W. Saving = (150 − 25)/150 = **83.3 %**. DSB-SC (50 W) saves 66.7 %.

steps.title: Example 2 — bandwidth
steps.body: Voice 300–3400 Hz: AM/DSB uses 6.8 kHz, SSB 3.1 kHz. 12-channel FDM group with 4 kHz spacing = 48 kHz.

steps.title: Example 3 — phase error
steps.body: Sync detector with local phase error φ = 30°: output amplitude × cos30° = 0.866 (−1.25 dB).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Calling SSB detection by an envelope detector — it requires a locally generated carrier.

activity.prompt: Percentage power saved moving from AM (μ=1) to SSB.

lessons.title: Lab: Envelope detector design and generation methods

scenes.text: A diode, a capacitor and a resistor pull the audio from an AM signal — no battery needed. But the RC value is critical.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Detector conditions
steps.body:
For a diode envelope detector: **1/f_c ≪ RC ≤ √(1 − μ²)/(μ ω_m)**. Too large RC → **diagonal clipping**; too small → carrier ripple. **Negative-peak clipping** when the load R_ac differs from R_dc: need μ ≤ R_ac/R_dc.

Generation: low-level (square-law diode, transistor base/collector modulation) and high-level (collector modulation of a class-C amplifier) — high efficiency for broadcast. Switching modulator, balanced modulator for DSB-SC.

steps.title: Example 2 — clipping
steps.body: R_dc = 10 kΩ, R_ac = 5 kΩ: μ_max for no negative-peak clipping = 0.5; μ = 0.8 → clipping.

steps.title: Example 3 — square-law
steps.body: i = a v + b v²; v = A_c cos ω_ct + m(t): cross-term 2b m(t)A_c cos ω_ct produces AM after tuned filter (needs bandpass at f_c).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Choosing RC from f_c only; the upper limit is set by the fastest message frequency and μ.

activity.prompt: Maximum RC (µs) for μ = 0.5, f_m = 5 kHz.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — design an AM broadcast transmitter

scenes.text: A station licenses 10 kW carrier. The chief engineer needs total power, sideband power and the supply for 80 % modulation.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Design
steps.body: P_c = 10 kW, μ = 0.8: P_t = 10(1 + 0.32) = 13.2 kW. Sideband total = 3.2 kW (1.6 kW each). Useful (info) fraction η = 0.64/2.64 = 24.2 %. With class-C PA efficiency 70 %: DC input for carrier = 10/0.7 = 14.3 kW. Audio power needed from modulator = 3.2 kW/0.7 = 4.57 kW for collector modulation.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting that the carrier power is unchanged by modulation; only sideband power is added.

activity.prompt: Total radiated power (kW) at μ = 0.8 with P_c = 10 kW.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Angle modulation (FM and PM)
courses.summary: Frequency and phase modulation, instantaneous frequency, deviation and modulation index, Bessel spectrum, Carson's rule, generation (direct and Armstrong), demodulation, PLL, pre-emphasis.
outcomes: Compute deviation, β and bandwidth with Carson's rule
Use Bessel functions to find spectral lines
Design an Armstrong modulator multiplier chain
Explain demodulators, PLL and pre-emphasis

story.title: Why FM stays clear in thunderstorms

scenes.text: Lightning crackles on AM radio but barely on FM. Noise mostly changes amplitude; FM carries information in frequency, which noise barely alters.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
s(t) = A_c cos[ω_ct + φ(t)]. Instantaneous frequency f_i = f_c + (1/2π)dφ/dt.
- **PM:** φ(t) = k_p m(t).
- **FM:** f_i = f_c + k_f m(t); φ(t) = 2πk_f∫m dt.
For m = A_m cos ω_mt: **frequency deviation Δf = k_f A_m**; **modulation index β = Δf/f_m**. PM: β_p = k_pA_m (peak phase deviation, independent of f_m), Δf = β_p f_m.
**NBFM** if β ≪ 1 (≈ 0.3): s ≈ A_c cos ω_ct − A_cβ sin ω_mt sin ω_ct, bandwidth ≈ 2f_m. **WBFM** if β > 1. Amplitude constant, so power P = A_c²/2R regardless of modulation.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: k_f = 5 kHz/V, m = 3cos(2π·1000t): Δf = 15 kHz; β = 15; Carson BW = 2(15+1) = 32 kHz.

steps.title: Example 2 — PM
steps.body: k_p = 2 rad/V, same m: β_p = 6 rad; Δf = 6×1 kHz = 6 kHz. If f_m is doubled, PM Δf doubles (12 kHz); FM Δf unchanged.

steps.title: Example 3 — instantaneous freq
steps.body: s = 10cos(2π·10⁶t + 8 sin 2π·10³t): f_i = 10⁶ + 8×10³ cos(2π10³t); Δf = 8 kHz; β = 8.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing deviation with bandwidth.
- Forgetting that in FM Δf ∝ amplitude only, in PM Δf ∝ amplitude × frequency.

activity.prompt: β for s = 10cos(2π·10⁶t + 8 sin 2π·10³t).

lessons.title: Lab: Bessel spectrum and Carson's rule

story.title: Why FM stations are 200 kHz apart

scenes.text: A commercial FM station deviates ±75 kHz with audio to 15 kHz. How much spectrum does it need? Carson's rule answers.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Spectrum
steps.body:
Single-tone FM: s = A_cΣ J_n(β) cos[(ω_c + nω_m)t]. Lines spaced f_m, amplitudes A_cJ_n(β); J_{−n} = (−1)^nJ_n. Carrier amplitude A_cJ_0(β) vanishes at β = 2.405, 5.520, 8.654. Power: ΣJ_n² = 1. **Carson's rule: BW ≈ 2(Δf + f_m) = 2f_m(β + 1)**; contains ≥ 98 % of power.

J_n(5): J0 = −0.178, J1 = −0.328, J2 = 0.047, J3 = 0.365, J4 = 0.391, J5 = 0.261, J6 = 0.131, J7 = 0.053.

steps.title: Example 1 — broadcast FM
steps.body: Δf = 75 kHz, f_m = 15 kHz: β = 5 (deviation ratio); BW = 2(75+15) = **180 kHz** (within 200 kHz channel).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body: Δf = 10 kHz, f_m = 2 kHz: β = 5; BW = 24 kHz. If f_m rises to 4 kHz at the same amplitude: β = 2.5, BW = 28 kHz.

steps.title: Example 3 — power in lines
steps.body: A_c = 10 V, β = 2.405: carrier amplitude 0, J1 = 0.519: first side-lines 5.19 V each; power in a line = amplitude²/2 = 13.5 W (per 1 Ω); total power 50 W.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Believing FM bandwidth is 2f_m like AM; it is 2(Δf+f_m).

activity.prompt: Carson bandwidth (kHz) for Δf = 75 kHz and f_m = 15 kHz.

lessons.title: Lab: FM generation — direct VCO and Armstrong method

scenes.text: A crystal oscillator is very stable but hard to deviate. Armstrong's method creates tiny phase modulation on a crystal carrier, then multiplies it up.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body: **Direct:** varactor diode in an LC oscillator (or VCO); simple, large deviation, but poor stability → AFC/PLL stabilisation. **Indirect (Armstrong):** integrate message → phase-modulate a crystal carrier (NBFM, β ≈ 0.2–0.3) → frequency multipliers raise carrier and deviation by N; mixers shift frequency without changing deviation. Multiplier of N multiplies f_c, Δf and β by N.

steps.title: Example — design
steps.body: Target: f_c = 90 MHz, Δf = 75 kHz. NBFM at 200 kHz with Δf1 = 25 Hz → total multiplication N = 75000/25 = **3000**. Choose ×50: 10 MHz, 1.25 kHz; mixer with 8.5 MHz (take difference) → 1.5 MHz, Δf unchanged; then ×60 → 90 MHz, Δf = 75 kHz ✓. Total 50×60 = 3000.

steps.title: Example — check β
steps.body: At f_m = 100 Hz (lowest audio): β1 = 25/100 = 0.25 (NBFM OK). Distortion small since max β < 0.3.

steps.title: Example — varactor
steps.body: LC oscillator f = 1/(2π√(LC)); C changes by ΔC: Δf/f ≈ −ΔC/2C. For f = 10 MHz and 0.75 % deviation, ΔC/C = 1.5 %.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking the mixer changes deviation — it only translates the carrier.

activity.prompt: Total frequency multiplication needed for Δf1 = 25 Hz to reach 75 kHz.

lessons.title: Lab: FM demodulation, PLL and pre-emphasis

scenes.text: A tuned circuit has sloping response; an FM signal tuned on the slope becomes AM and a diode detects it. Better circuits balance two slopes.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Demodulators
steps.body:
1) **Slope detector** (simple, non-linear). 2) **Balanced slope / Foster–Seeley** discriminator (phase-shift, S-curve; responds to AM). 3) **Ratio detector** (immune to AM, no limiter). 4) **Quadrature detector**. 5) **PLL**: phase detector + loop filter + VCO; in lock the VCO control voltage ∝ message. Lock range, capture range. Limiter before discriminators removes amplitude noise.

**Pre-emphasis/de-emphasis:** high audio frequencies have weaker energy but FM noise rises with frequency (triangular PSD); transmitter boosts highs with time constant τ (50 µs or 75 µs depending on region), receiver cuts equally. Corner f = 1/(2πτ): 3.18 kHz (50 µs), 2.12 kHz (75 µs). SNR improvement ≈ 13 dB for 75 µs.

steps.title: Example 1 — PLL
steps.body: VCO gain K_v = 10 kHz/V; message produces VCO control ±3 V for Δf = ±30 kHz → recovered message = f deviation/K_v.

steps.title: Example 2 — de-emphasis RC
steps.body: τ = 75 µs: R = 7.5 kΩ, C = 10 nF. τ = 50 µs: R = 5 kΩ, C = 10 nF.

steps.title: Example 3 — S-curve
steps.body: A discriminator with sensitivity 20 mV/kHz gives, for Δf = 75 kHz, peak output 1.5 V.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Omitting a limiter before a Foster–Seeley discriminator makes it sensitive to AM noise.

activity.prompt: De-emphasis corner frequency (kHz) for τ = 75 µs.

questions.q: β for Δf=50 kHz, f_m=10 kHz
Carson BW for β=5, f_m=15 kHz

courses.title: Unit 4 · Radio receivers and noise performance
courses.summary: Superheterodyne receivers, IF, image rejection, tracking, AGC, receiver parameters, and noise performance of AM, DSB-SC and SSB demodulation.
outcomes: Choose IF and LO frequencies and compute the image frequency
Calculate image rejection and tuning-range ratios
Explain AGC, AFC, squelch
Compare output SNR across AM, DSB-SC, SSB and FM

story.title: Why every radio has an IF

scenes.text: Filtering one station out of hundreds is easier at one fixed frequency. The superheterodyne converts every station to the same intermediate frequency (IF) and amplifies it there.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Block diagram
steps.body:
Antenna → RF amplifier (selectivity, image rejection, NF) → mixer (with local oscillator) → **IF amplifier & filter** (most gain, selectivity) → detector → AF amplifier → loudspeaker; AGC feedback from detector to RF/IF.

High-side injection: **f_LO = f_s + f_IF**; image frequency **f_im = f_s + 2f_IF**. Standard IFs: AM broadcast 455 kHz; FM broadcast 10.7 MHz; TV picture IF 38.9 MHz (Europe) / 45.75 MHz (USA)... (national standards vary). Advantages over TRF: constant bandwidth and gain at every station, high selectivity. Disadvantages: image and IF-breakthrough responses.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: Station at 1000 kHz, IF = 455 kHz: f_LO = 1455 kHz; f_im = 1000 + 910 = **1910 kHz**.

steps.title: Example 2 — tuning range
steps.body: MW band 535–1605 kHz: LO = 990–2060 kHz; ratio 2.08; capacitance ratio = 2.08² = **4.33**.

steps.title: Example 3 — FM
steps.body: Station at 98 MHz, IF = 10.7 MHz: f_LO = 108.7 MHz; f_im = 119.4 MHz (outside the 88–108 MHz band, so easy to reject).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: The image is 2×IF above the signal for high-side injection (not 1×IF).

activity.prompt: Image frequency (kHz) for a 1000 kHz station with IF 455 kHz.

lessons.title: Lab: Image rejection, selectivity and tracking

scenes.text: A radio tuned to 1000 kHz also hears a strong 1910 kHz transmitter faintly. Its image rejection is the RF stage's ability to suppress that.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Single-tuned RF stage with loaded Q: **image rejection ratio α = √(1 + Q²ρ²)**, ρ = f_im/f_s − f_s/f_im. Selectivity: ability to reject adjacent channels (set by IF filter). Sensitivity: minimum input for a standard output SNR. Fidelity: uniform response over message band. **Tracking:** LO must stay f_IF above the tuned circuit across the band — padder and trimmer capacitors give three-point tracking.

steps.title: Example 2 — higher IF
steps.body: Raise IF to 1.6 MHz for 30 MHz shortwave: f_im = 33.2 MHz; ρ = 1.1067 − 0.9036 = 0.2031; Q = 100 → α = 20.3 (26 dB) only — so double conversion is used at HF.

steps.title: Example 3 — selectivity
steps.body: Two stations 10 kHz apart; IF filter with 6 dB BW of 6 kHz and 60 dB BW of 18 kHz has shape factor 3 — poor; a 455 kHz ceramic filter gets about 2.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using Q of the unloaded coil rather than loaded Q.

activity.prompt: Image rejection ratio (linear) for f_s=1000 kHz, f_im=1910 kHz, Q=100.

options: improve image rejection at high f

lessons.title: AGC, AFC, squelch and receiver characteristics

scenes.text: A car radio's volume stays steady as the signal varies by 60 dB. Automatic gain control is why.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Circuits
steps.body: **AGC:** DC proportional to carrier level (from the diode detector) controls gain of RF/IF stages; simple AGC, delayed AGC (acts only above a threshold), amplified AGC. **AFC** keeps LO on frequency (FM). **Squelch** mutes audio when no carrier. **Dynamic range** = range of input levels handled (e.g. 100 dB). **Double-spotting**: same station at two dial points.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: Input varies 60 dB, AGC holds output within 6 dB → AGC compression ratio 54 dB.

steps.title: Example 2 — dynamic range
steps.body: Sensitivity −110 dBm, 1-dB compression at −10 dBm → dynamic range ~ 100 dB.

steps.title: Example 3 — AGC voltage
steps.body: Detector output across 100 kΩ/1 µF filter: τ = 0.1 s (slow compared with audio, fast enough for fading).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: AGC time constant too short removes the audio modulation.

activity.prompt: Sort each circuit by its function.

lessons.title: Lab: Noise performance of AM, DSB-SC and SSB receivers

story.title: Which modulation gives the cleanest voice?

scenes.text: With the same transmitted power and noise density, we compare outputs after demodulation.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Results
steps.body:
Define channel SNR γ = P_T/(N0W) (P_T = transmitted power). Figure of merit FOM = SNR_o/γ:
- **DSB-SC (coherent):** FOM = 1.
- **SSB (coherent):** FOM = 1.
- **AM (envelope, tone modulation):** FOM = μ²/(2+μ²) ≤ 1/3.
- **FM (tone):** FOM = 1.5β².
Envelope detection has a **threshold effect**: for carrier-to-noise below ~ 10 dB output SNR collapses; coherent detectors have no threshold.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body: Input signal power 1 mW at the detector, N0 = 10⁻¹⁰ W/Hz, W = 5 kHz: DSB-SC γ = 10⁻³/(5×10⁻⁷) = 2000 → 33 dB.

steps.title: Example 3 — why AM still survives
steps.body: Cheap envelope detectors and receivers outweigh the 4.8 dB loss in broadcast services.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Mixing P_T (total transmitted power) and carrier power in FOM definitions.

activity.prompt: Output SNR (dB) for AM, μ=1, tone, channel SNR γ = 30 dB.

questions.q: f_im for f_s=600 kHz, IF 455 kHz
Why choose IF 10.7 MHz for FM

options: same station at two dial points

courses.title: Unit 5 · Pulse analog modulation and multiplexing
courses.summary: Sampling for communications, PAM, PWM, PPM, aperture effect, time- and frequency-division multiplexing, crosstalk and telemetry design.
outcomes: Generate and demodulate PAM, PWM and PPM
Compute TDM frame rates and minimum bandwidth
Plan an FDM channel stack with guard bands
Estimate crosstalk and synchronisation needs

story.title: Sharing one wire among four sensors

scenes.text: A factory has four temperature sensors but one cable. A switch visits each sensor in turn, sending narrow pulses whose heights equal the readings — pulse-amplitude modulation.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: PAM
steps.body: Sampling theorem: f_s ≥ 2f_m (practically 2.2–2.5f_m; telephony 8 kHz for 4 kHz voice). **Natural sampling** keeps the shape of the signal during the pulse; **flat-top (sample-and-hold)** holds the sample value for τ. Flat-top spectrum is multiplied by τ·sinc(fτ) → **aperture effect** (high-frequency droop) corrected by an equaliser 1/sinc(πfτ/…). Demodulation: low-pass filter (+ equaliser). Bandwidth required ≈ 1/(2τ).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: f_m = 4 kHz, f_s = 8 kHz, τ = 10 µs: aperture droop at f_m: sinc(f_mτ) = sin(π×0.04)/(π×0.04) = 0.1253/0.1257 = 0.9974 → −0.02 dB — negligible. For τ = 62.5 µs (50 % duty): sinc(0.25) = 0.9003 → −0.91 dB, equalisation needed.

steps.title: Example 2 — guard
steps.body: f_m = 3.4 kHz voice, f_s = 8 kHz: guard band = 8 − 6.8 = 1.2 kHz for the anti-alias filter transition.

steps.title: Example 3 — bandwidth
steps.body: Pulse width 5 µs: BW ≈ 1/(2×5 µs) = 100 kHz.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using ideal sampling at exactly 2f_m — real filters need guard bands.

activity.prompt: Aperture droop factor sinc(f_mτ) for f_m = 4 kHz, τ = 62.5 µs.

story.title: The servo motor and the RC receiver

scenes.text: A radio-control servo reads a 1–2 ms pulse every 20 ms; the pulse width is the commanded angle. This is pulse-width modulation.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Generation
steps.body: **PWM (PDM):** compare message with a sawtooth/triangle; output high while m(t) > ramp; pulse width ∝ amplitude. **PPM:** pulse position shifted ∝ amplitude; derived from PWM by triggering on the trailing edge. PPM needs the least average power, constant-amplitude pulses make them noise-robust (amplitude limiter). Demodulation of PWM: integrate/low-pass; PPM → convert to PWM with an SR flip-flop and then integrate. Bandwidth ∝ 1/rise time.

steps.title: Example 1 — servo
steps.body: Period 20 ms; pulse 1.0 ms = 0°, 1.5 ms = 90°, 2.0 ms = 180°. Duty cycle 5–10 %. For 135°: width = 1.75 ms.

steps.title: Example 2 — linearity
steps.body: Sawtooth 0–5 V, period 100 µs; m = 2 V gives width 40 µs (40 % duty), m = 4 V → 80 µs.

steps.title: Example 3 — power
steps.body: PPM pulse of 1 µs every 100 µs with 10 V into 50 Ω: peak power 2 W, average 20 mW.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Calling PWM digital: amplitude is binary but timing is analog.

activity.prompt: Pulse width (µs) for m = 2 V against a 0–5 V sawtooth of period 100 µs.

scenes.text: Before digital exchanges, 12 phone calls were stacked in frequency on one cable (a group); 60 calls made a supergroup.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: FDM
steps.body: Each channel modulates a different subcarrier (SSB); channels are stacked with guard bands. Standard: 12 voice channels × 4 kHz = **group 60–108 kHz**; 5 groups = **supergroup (60 channels) 312–552 kHz**. Need linear amplifiers (intermodulation → crosstalk). Used in broadcasting, cable TV, analogue cellular (AMPS).

steps.title: TDM
steps.body: Sample N channels in sequence; frame period T_s = 1/f_s; frame contains N pulses plus a sync pulse. Pulse rate = N f_s. Minimum channel bandwidth ≈ (N f_s)/2 (Nyquist for pulses). TDM requires synchronisation (a marker pulse); crosstalk arises from finite bandwidth causing pulse tails; guard time reduces it.

steps.title: Example 1 — TDM
steps.body: 8 channels, f_m = 4 kHz, f_s = 8 kHz: pulse rate 64 kHz; min BW = **32 kHz**; frame 125 µs; slot 15.6 µs.

steps.title: Example 2 — FDM
steps.body: 10 SSB channels of 4 kHz with 1 kHz guard bands: 10×4 + 9×1 = **49 kHz**.

steps.title: Example 3 — crosstalk
steps.body: Pulse tail e^{−t/τ} with τ = 1 µs; slot guard 3 µs → residue e^{−3} = 5 % (−26 dB); 10 µs guard → 4.5×10⁻⁵ (−87 dB).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting the frame-sync slot when counting channels.

activity.prompt: Minimum bandwidth (kHz) for 8-channel TDM with f_s = 8 kHz.

story.title: Six sensors on a wind turbine

scenes.text: A turbine nacelle has six sensors (temperature, vibration, speed...). One cable carries all to the base using TDM-PAM.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Design
steps.body: Sensor bandwidths: 4 channels of 100 Hz, 2 of 1 kHz. Use common f_s = 2.5×1 kHz = 2.5 kHz for all (simple commutator): pulse rate = (6+1 sync)×2.5k = 17.5 kS/s; min BW ≈ 8.75 kHz. A more efficient design samples slow channels at 250 Hz: 4×250 + 2×2500 + sync 2500 = 8.5 kS/s; BW = 4.25 kHz — but needs a sub-commutator.

steps.title: Frame timing
steps.body: With 7 slots at 2.5 kHz: frame 400 µs; slot = 57.1 µs; with τ = 20 µs pulse and guard 37 µs crosstalk is negligible.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Sampling every channel at the highest rate wastes bandwidth.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of a TDM-PAM system.
items: Band-limit each channel with an anti-alias filter
Commutator samples channels in sequence
Add a sync pulse to the frame
Transmit over the channel
Separate channels with a synchronised decommutator
Low-pass filter each channel to recover the message

quiz.q: Pulse rate for 7 slots at 2.5 kHz (kS/s)

questions.q: Frame time for 4 channels at 8 kHz

courses.title: Unit 6 · Revision, practicals & exam
courses.summary: Formula sheet, standard analog-communication lab experiments (AM, FM, mixer, PLL, PAM/PWM, TDM), viva questions, exam-style problems and a 20-question exam.
outcomes: Recall all key analog-communication formulas
Plan and record standard laboratory experiments
Answer viva questions
Solve exam-style problems

scenes.text: Analog communication is about a dozen formulas used again and again. Learn them as a family.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Noise and basics
steps.body:
- v_n² = 4kTRB; P_n = kTB = −174 dBm/Hz + 10log B.
- F = F1 + (F2−1)/G1 + …; T_e = (F−1)290 K.
- Sensitivity = −174 + 10log B + NF + SNR_min (dBm).

steps.title: AM family
steps.body:
- μ = (Vmax−Vmin)/(Vmax+Vmin); P_t = P_c(1+μ²/2); η = μ²/(2+μ²); BW = 2f_m.
- I_t = I_c√(1+μ²/2).
- DSB-SC BW 2W; SSB BW W; VSB W+f_v.
- Envelope detector: RC ≤ √(1−μ²)/(μω_m).
- FOM: DSB-SC = SSB = 1; AM = μ²/(2+μ²).

steps.title: FM
steps.body:
- Δf = k_fA_m; β = Δf/f_m; BW ≈ 2(Δf+f_m).
- FM FOM = 1.5β²; J0 zeros at β = 2.405, 5.52, 8.65.
- Armstrong: multiply Δf and f_c by N; mixing preserves Δf.
- Pre-emphasis corner 1/(2πτ).

steps.title: Receivers & pulses
steps.body:
- f_im = f_s + 2f_IF; α = √(1+Q²ρ²).
- TDM: pulse rate = N f_s; BW_min = Nf_s/2; FDM group 60–108 kHz.
- PAM aperture: sinc(fτ).

steps.title: Top slips
steps.body: 1) μ as % in formulas. 2) dB vs ratio in Friis. 3) β vs Δf. 4) IF vs image. 5) Mixing P_c and P_t. 6) Forgetting guard bands.

activity.prompt: Match modulation with bandwidth.

scenes.text: Generate AM with a transistor/IC modulator, measure μ using the envelope and the trapezoid, and demodulate with a diode detector.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Carrier 1 MHz, 1 V p-p; message 1 kHz. 2) Vary message amplitude; note V_max, V_min on CRO; compute μ. 3) Trapezoid: message on X, AM on Y. 4) Over-modulation observation (μ>1). 5) Envelope detector: R = 10 kΩ, C = 10 nF check RC = 100 µs against limit. 6) Spectrum: find side-frequencies 999 and 1001 kHz.

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body: Keep probe ground leads short; set the CRO trigger on the message; avoid saturating the modulator.

activity.prompt: μ for Vmax = 1.5 V and Vmin = 0.5 V.

quiz.q: RC = 100 µs for fm=1 kHz μ=0.5 limit 276 µs OK?

lessons.title: Lab: FM generation, PLL and mixer/superhet experiments

scenes.text: Use a VCO IC (e.g. a 555/566 style VCO) to produce FM, measure deviation and sensitivity, and demodulate with a PLL IC.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Apply DC control voltages 1–5 V to the VCO and record output frequency: sensitivity K_v = Δf/ΔV. 2) Apply 1 kHz message; measure deviation; compute β and Carson BW. 3) Spectrum analysis: carrier null at β = 2.405. 4) Demodulate with PLL: observe lock range. 5) Mixer: apply f_s and f_LO; verify f_IF = f_LO − f_s. 6) Image response by sweeping input to f_s + 2f_IF.

steps.title: Observation table
steps.body:
| Control (V) | f_out (kHz) |
|---|---|
| 2 | 40 |
| 3 | 50 |
| 4 | 60 |
K_v = 10 kHz/V. A 1 V p-p (±0.5 V) sine gives Δf = 5 kHz; with f_m = 1 kHz: β = 5; Carson BW = 12 kHz.

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body: Keep the control voltage in the linear region of the VCO.

activity.prompt: Carson bandwidth (kHz): Δf = 5 kHz, f_m = 1 kHz.

lessons.title: Lab: Sampling, PAM/PWM, TDM and viva

scenes.text: Sample a 1 kHz sine at 8 kHz, 2 kHz and 1.5 kHz; reconstruct with a low-pass filter and watch aliasing.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Use a sample-and-hold or analog switch; message 1 kHz. 2) f_s = 8 kHz → clean reconstruction. 3) f_s = 1.5 kHz → alias at |1.5 − 1| = 0.5 kHz. 4) PWM: comparator with 0–5 V triangle; plot width vs m. 5) TDM: 4:1 analog multiplexer, clock 32 kHz; demultiplex and filter.

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body: Anti-alias filter before the sampler; common ground.

steps.title: Viva
steps.body: Use the question list in the activity.

activity.prompt: Viva questions with answers.

items.q: Why is FM less noisy than AM?
items.a: Noise mostly alters amplitude; FM information is in frequency and a limiter removes amplitude variations; also bandwidth expansion gives SNR improvement 1.5β².

items.q: What is the capture effect?
items.a: The stronger of two co-channel FM signals suppresses the weaker.

items.q: Why is IF fixed?
items.a: Selective filters and high-gain amplifiers are optimised once for the fixed IF.

items.q: What is pre-emphasis?
items.a: Boosting high audio frequencies before FM modulation so that de-emphasis in the receiver reduces noise.

items.q: Why SSB over AM?
items.a: Half the bandwidth and up to 83% power saving at μ=1.

quiz.q: 1.5 kHz sampling of 1 kHz yields alias

TDM min BW for 10 channels at 8 kHz

uni-ece-core.description: ECE core subjects unit by unit: Signals and Systems, Analog Electronics and Digital Electronics — with solved problems, code labs, quizzes and unit exams.

courses.title: Signals & Systems · Unit 1 · Classification of signals and systems
courses.summary: Continuous- and discrete-time signals, even/odd, periodic, energy and power signals, elementary signals (step, impulse, ramp, exponentials, sinusoids), time shifting/scaling/reversal, and system properties: linearity, time-invariance, causality, memory, stability and invertibility.
outcomes: Classify signals as even/odd, periodic, energy or power
Use step, impulse and ramp functions and their relations
Apply time shifting, scaling and reversal in the correct order
Test systems for linearity, time-invariance, causality, memory and BIBO stability
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Types of signals

scenes.text: An ECG trace is a continuous-time signal; a thermometer logging every minute gives a discrete-time sequence.
Classifying signals tells us which tools apply.

steps.title: Classifications
steps.body:
- CT x(t) vs DT x[n]; analog vs digital (amplitude quantised).
- **Even** x(−t) = x(t); **odd** x(−t) = −x(t). Any signal = xₑ + xₒ with xₑ = [x(t) + x(−t)]/2, xₒ = [x(t) − x(−t)]/2.
- **Periodic:** x(t + T) = x(t). Sum of periodic signals is periodic if the ratio of periods is rational; fundamental period = LCM.
- DT sinusoid cos(Ω₀n) is periodic only if Ω₀/2π is rational: N = 2πm/Ω₀ (smallest integer).

steps.title: Energy and power
steps.body:
E = ∫|x(t)|²dt (Σ|x[n]|² for DT). P = lim (1/2T)∫₋ᵀᵀ|x|²dt.
Energy signal: 0 < E < ∞ (P = 0) — e.g. finite pulses, decaying exponentials. Power signal: 0 < P < ∞ (E = ∞) — periodic signals, step. A signal can be neither (e.g. t·u(t)).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x(t) = cos 4t + sin 6t: T₁ = π/2, T₂ = π/3 ⇒ T = π.

**Example 2.** x[n] = cos(πn/4): N = 8. x[n] = cos(n/4): Ω₀/2π = 1/(8π) irrational ⇒ not periodic.

**Example 3.** x(t) = e^(−2t)u(t): E = ∫₀^∞ e^(−4t)dt = 1/4 ⇒ energy signal.

**Example 4.** x(t) = 5 cos(10t): P = 25/2 = 12.5 ⇒ power signal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming every DT sinusoid is periodic.
- Using amplitude instead of amplitude² for power (A²/2 for a sinusoid).
- Calling the step an energy signal (E is infinite).

activity.prompt: Energy or power signal?

quiz.why: sin 3t has period 2π/3 and cos 2t has period π. The smallest common multiple is 2π (3 and 2 periods).
The even part of x(t) is [x(t) + x(−t)]/2. The odd part is [x(t) − x(−t)]/2.
The power of A cos ωt is A²/2. For A = 3, that is 9/2 = 4.5.
For DT, N = 2πm/Ω₀ must be an integer. With Ω₀ = 0.3π, N = 2m/0.3 = 20m/3, so the smallest integer is for m = 3: N = 20.

quiz.q: Energy of a unit-height pulse of width 2

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

lessons.title: Elementary signals

scenes.text: A switch closing at t = 0 is a step; a hammer tap on a structure is (almost) an impulse.
Complicated signals are built from these simple blocks.

steps.title: Definitions and relations
steps.body:
- Unit step u(t) = 1 for t ≥ 0, 0 for t < 0.
- Unit impulse δ(t): zero for t ≠ 0, ∫δ dt = 1. δ(t) = du/dt; u(t) = ∫₋∞ᵗ δ(τ)dτ.
- Ramp r(t) = t·u(t); dr/dt = u(t).
- **Sifting:** ∫x(t)δ(t − t₀)dt = x(t₀); x(t)δ(t − t₀) = x(t₀)δ(t − t₀).
- Scaling: δ(at) = δ(t)/|a|.
- DT: δ[n] = u[n] − u[n − 1]; u[n] = Σ_(k≤n) δ[k].
- Complex exponential e^(st), s = σ + jω: grows/decays with σ, oscillates with ω.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** ∫₋∞^∞ (t² + 3)δ(t − 2)dt = 7.

**Example 2.** ∫₋∞^∞ e^(−t)δ(2t − 4)dt = ½e^(−2) (since δ(2t − 4) = ½δ(t − 2)).

**Example 3.** A rectangular pulse of height 3 from t = 1 to 4: x(t) = 3[u(t − 1) − u(t − 4)].

**Example 4.** Triangle rising from 0 at t = 0 to 1 at t = 1 then falling to 0 at t = 2: x = r(t) − 2r(t − 1) + r(t − 2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 1/|a| in δ(at).
- Sifting when the impulse lies outside the integration limits (result is 0).
- Writing pulses as u(t − a) + u(t − b) instead of a difference.

activity.prompt: Evaluate ∫ from −∞ to ∞ of (t³ + 1)·δ(t − 2) dt

quiz.why: The derivative of the unit step is the unit impulse, du/dt = δ(t).
u(t) − u(t − 3) is 1 from 0 to 3. Multiplying by 2 gives a pulse of height 2.
δ[n] = u[n] − u[n − 1], the first difference of the unit step.

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

lessons.title: Operations on signals

scenes.text: A DJ reverses a clip, then plays it at double speed starting 2 s later.
Order matters: shift, scale and reverse must be applied carefully.

steps.title: Operations
steps.body:
- Time shift x(t − t₀): delay (right) if t₀ > 0.
- Time scaling x(at): compress if |a| > 1, expand if |a| < 1.
- Reversal x(−t): mirror about t = 0.
- y(t) = x(at + b): method 1 — shift first by b to get x(t + b), then scale by a; method 2 — write x(a(t + b/a)): scale then shift by b/a.
DT scaling x[2n] keeps every second sample (decimation) — information can be lost.

steps.title: Quick check
steps.body: To find where y(t) = x(at + b) lives, solve 'argument within the original support' — inequalities never get the order wrong.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shifting by b after scaling (should shift by b/a).
- Reversing the direction of a delay.
- Forgetting that inequalities flip when dividing by a negative a.

activity.prompt: x(t) is non-zero on 0 ≤ t ≤ 4. y(t) = x(t/2 − 1) is non-zero from t = 2 up to t = ?

quiz.why: x(t − 3) is x(t) delayed by 3, i.e. shifted right.
x(3t) runs 3 times faster, so it is compressed in time by a factor of 3.

quiz.q: Support of x(2t) if x lives on [0, 4]
quiz.why: x(2t) is x compressed by 2. A signal on [0, 4] now lives on [0, 2].
x(−t + 2) is non-zero when 0 ≤ 2 − t ≤ 2, i.e. 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. So it lives on [0, 2] (a reversed and shifted copy).
x[3n] picks every 3rd sample of x[n]. That is decimation by 3.

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

lessons.title: System properties

scenes.text: An audio amplifier distorts when overdriven — it stops being linear.
We test system properties with simple input–output reasoning.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Linear:** superposition — T{ax₁ + bx₂} = aT{x₁} + bT{x₂} (implies zero input → zero output).
- **Time-invariant:** shifting the input shifts the output by the same amount.
- **Causal:** output depends only on present/past inputs.
- **Memoryless (static):** output depends only on the present input.
- **BIBO stable:** every bounded input gives a bounded output.
- **Invertible:** distinct inputs give distinct outputs.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** y(t) = t·x(t): linear ✔; time-variant (coefficient t) ✘; causal ✔; memoryless ✔; unstable (x = 1 gives y = t, unbounded).

**Example 2.** y(t) = x(t) + 2: non-linear (zero input gives 2); TI ✔; causal ✔.

**Example 3.** y[n] = x[n + 1]: linear, TI, **non-causal** (future input).

**Example 4.** y(t) = x(2t): linear, time-variant, non-causal (y(1) needs x(2)).

**Example 5.** y(t) = ∫₋∞ᵗ x(τ)dτ: linear, TI, causal, with memory, unstable (u(t) → ramp).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling y = x + 2 linear (it is affine).
- Testing time-invariance by shifting only the input inside but forgetting to shift t elsewhere.
- Assuming time scaling is time-invariant.

quiz.why: Linear systems satisfy superposition: the response to a sum of inputs is the sum of the responses, and scaling carries through.
y[n] = x[n + 2] uses a future input sample, so the system is non-causal.
y(t) = 3x(t) multiplies by a constant gain. It depends only on the present input, and is linear and time-invariant.
An integrator turns a bounded step input into a ramp, which grows without bound. So it is not BIBO stable.
For y(t) = x(t) + 5, a zero input gives output 5, not 0. A linear system must give zero output for zero input, so it is not linear.

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

questions.why: The unit step has infinite energy but finite average power 1/2. So it is a power signal.
e^(j2πt/5) has angular frequency 2π/5, so its period is 2π/(2π/5) = 5.
y(t) = x(t/2) stretches time. Shifting the input by t₀ does not just shift the output by t₀, so it is time-variant.

questions.q: Assertion (A): cos(2n) (DT) is not periodic.  Reason (R): 2/(2π) = 1/π is irrational.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A DT sinusoid cos(Ω₀n) is periodic only if Ω₀/2π is rational. Here 2/(2π) = 1/π is irrational, so the reason explains why it is not periodic.
By the sifting property, ∫ f(t)δ(t − t₀) dt = f(t₀), so the integral equals cos(π/3) = 0.5.

questions.q: Fundamental period of x[n] = cos(πn/6) + sin(πn/4)
questions.why: cos(πn/6) has period 12, and sin(πn/4) has period 8. The fundamental period of the sum is LCM(12, 8) = 24.

questions.q: x(t) on [−1, 3]; y(t) = x(−2t + 1) is non-zero on
questions.why: y(t) = x(−2t + 1) is non-zero when −1 ≤ −2t + 1 ≤ 3. That gives −1 ≤ t ≤ 1.

questions.q: Case: A sensor model y(t) = x(t)·x(t − 1). It is
questions.why: y(t) = x(t)·x(t − 1) multiplies two values of the input, so it is non-linear. It is time-invariant, causal (only past and present), and has memory.
Power = 3² + 4²/2 = 9 + 8 = 17. The DC term gives its square and the cosine gives A²/2.
δ(3t − 6) = δ(3(t − 2)) = δ(t − 2)/3. So the integral is e^(−4)/3.
The accumulator is linear, time-invariant and causal. A bounded input such as a step gives an unbounded output, so it is unstable.
The odd part is [e^t − e^(−t)]/2 = sinh t.

courses.title: Signals & Systems · Unit 2 · LTI systems and convolution
courses.summary: Impulse response, convolution integral and convolution sum, graphical and analytical evaluation, properties of convolution, causality and stability from h(t)/h[n], and LTI systems described by differential and difference equations.
outcomes: Compute continuous and discrete convolution
Use commutative, associative and distributive properties
Determine causality and BIBO stability from the impulse response
Relate difference/differential equations to impulse responses
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Impulse response and the convolution sum

scenes.text: Clap once in a hall and record the echoes — that is its impulse response.
Any music played there = convolution of the music with that response.

steps.title: Convolution sum
steps.body:
Any x[n] = Σ x[k]δ[n − k]. For an LTI system with impulse response h[n]: y[n] = Σₖ x[k]h[n − k] = x[n] * h[n].
Length: if x has N₁ samples and h has N₂, y has N₁ + N₂ − 1 samples.

steps.title: Table (multiplication) method
steps.body: Write x across the top and h down the side, fill products, and sum along anti-diagonals — fast for short sequences.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong start index of y (start = start(x) + start(h)).
- Forgetting to flip h when using the graphical method.
- Length errors (N₁ + N₂ − 1).

activity.prompt: Compute the convolution of x = [1, 2, 1] and h = [1, -1] without numpy and print the result list.
activity.starter:
x = [1, 2, 1]
h = [1, -1]
y = [0] * (len(x) + len(h) - 1)
# fill y[n] = sum x[k]*h[n-k]

print(y)
activity.solution:
x = [1, 2, 1]
h = [1, -1]
y = [0] * (len(x) + len(h) - 1)
for i in range(len(x)):
    for j in range(len(h)):
        y[i + j] += x[i] * h[j]
print(y)
activity.hint: Nested loops: add x[i]*h[j] into y[i+j].

quiz.q: Output length for x of 4 samples and h of 3
quiz.why: The convolution of lengths 4 and 3 has length 4 + 3 − 1 = 6.
Convolving with a shifted impulse shifts the signal: x[n] * δ[n − 2] = x[n − 2].
The impulse response completely describes an LTI system, since the output is the input convolved with it. This does not hold for non-LTI systems.

quiz.q: y[0] for x = {2, 3}, h = {4, 5} (both start at 0)
quiz.why: y[0] = x[0]h[0] = 2 × 4 = 8, since both signals start at 0.

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

lessons.title: Convolution integral

scenes.text: An RC low-pass filter has h(t) = (1/RC)e^(−t/RC)u(t).
Its response to any input is the convolution integral.

steps.title: Definition and graphical method
steps.body: y(t) = ∫₋∞^∞ x(τ)h(t − τ)dτ. Steps: flip h(τ) → h(−τ); shift by t; multiply by x(τ); integrate the overlap; repeat over ranges of t.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x = u(t), h = e^(−at)u(t): y = ∫₀ᵗ e^(−a(t − τ))dτ = (1 − e^(−at))/a for t ≥ 0.

**Example 2.** Two unit pulses on [0, 1]: y(t) = triangle — t for 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, 2 − t for 1 ≤ t ≤ 2, 0 elsewhere.

**Example 3.** e^(−t)u(t) * e^(−2t)u(t) = (e^(−t) − e^(−2t))u(t).

steps.title: Useful results
steps.body:
- x(t) * δ(t − t₀) = x(t − t₀)
- x(t) * u(t) = ∫₋∞ᵗ x(τ)dτ
- Width of x * h = sum of widths; start = sum of starts.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong integration limits for each interval of t.
- Forgetting u(t) on the final answer.
- Flipping x instead of h then mixing variables.

activity.prompt: y = u(t) * e^(−2t)u(t). Value of y(t) as t → ∞?

quiz.q: Convolution of two rectangles of equal width gives
quiz.why: Convolving two equal rectangles gives a triangle: the overlap area grows then shrinks linearly.
Convolving with δ(t) leaves the signal unchanged, since δ is the identity: x(t) * δ(t) = x(t).
Convolving with the unit step integrates the signal up to the present time: a running integral.

quiz.q: Width of a 2 s pulse convolved with a 3 s pulse
quiz.why: The width of the convolution of two finite pulses is the sum of the widths: 2 + 3 = 5 s.
In the Laplace domain, 1/(s + 1) squared is 1/(s + 1)², whose inverse is t e^(−t)u(t). Repeated poles give a factor of t.

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

lessons.title: Properties, causality and stability

scenes.text: Two equaliser stages in series act like one filter.
Associativity: h_total = h₁ * h₂ — and order doesn't matter.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- Commutative x * h = h * x
- Associative (x * h₁) * h₂ = x * (h₁ * h₂) ⇒ cascade h = h₁ * h₂
- Distributive x * (h₁ + h₂) ⇒ parallel h = h₁ + h₂
- Causal LTI ⇔ h(t) = 0 for t < 0 (h[n] = 0 for n < 0)
- BIBO stable ⇔ ∫|h(t)|dt < ∞ (Σ|h[n]| < ∞)
- Memoryless ⇔ h = kδ

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** h[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n]: Σ|h| = 2 < ∞ ⇒ stable; causal.

**Example 2.** h(t) = e^(2t)u(t): ∫ diverges ⇒ unstable.

**Example 3.** h[n] = u[n + 3] − u[n − 2]: non-zero for n = −3…1 ⇒ non-causal, stable (finite sum = 5).

**Example 4.** Cascade h₁ = δ[n] − δ[n − 1] with h₂ = u[n]: h = δ[n] (they undo each other — difference and accumulator are inverses).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Judging stability by h being bounded (need absolute integrability).
- Thinking cascade order matters for LTI systems.
- Forgetting that h(t) = u(t) is unstable.

activity.prompt: Classify the LTI system

quiz.why: A causal system cannot respond before the input, so its impulse response must be zero for t < 0.
An LTI system is BIBO stable if and only if its impulse response is absolutely integrable, ∫|h| < ∞.
In a parallel connection, the outputs add, so the overall impulse response is h₁ + h₂.
Σ|h[n]| = Σ (1/3)ⁿ for n ≥ 0 = 1/(1 − 1/3) = 3/2 = 1.5. The sum is finite, so the system is BIBO stable.
A memoryless LTI system output depends only on the present input, so h(t) = kδ(t) for a constant gain k.

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

lessons.title: Differential and difference equations

scenes.text: Stock analysts smooth prices with a 3-day moving average.
That is a difference equation: y[n] = (x[n] + x[n − 1] + x[n − 2])/3.

steps.title: LTI descriptions
steps.body:
CT: Σ aₖ dᵏy/dtᵏ = Σ bₖ dᵏx/dtᵏ; DT: Σ aₖ y[n − k] = Σ bₖ x[n − k] (with initial rest ⇒ LTI and causal).
- **FIR:** depends only on inputs (finite h). **IIR:** feedback from past outputs (infinite h).
Impulse response of y[n] − ay[n − 1] = x[n]: h[n] = aⁿu[n]. Of y′ + ay = x: h(t) = e^(−at)u(t).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** y[n] = 0.5y[n − 1] + x[n], x = δ[n], y[−1] = 0: y[0] = 1, y[1] = 0.5, y[2] = 0.25 … h[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n].

**Example 2.** 3-point moving average h = {1/3, 1/3, 1/3} (FIR). Step response settles to 1 after 3 samples.

**Example 3.** Natural + forced response: y′ + 2y = 4u(t), y(0) = 0 ⇒ y = 2(1 − e^(−2t)).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting initial rest when claiming LTI.
- Calling a recursive equation FIR.
- Wrong sign of the feedback coefficient when iterating.

activity.prompt: Iterate y[n] = 0.5*y[n-1] + x[n] for x = impulse (length 5) and print the first 5 outputs.
activity.starter:
x = [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]
y = []
prev = 0.0
# compute each y[n]

print(y)
activity.solution:
x = [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]
y = []
prev = 0.0
for v in x:
    prev = 0.5 * prev + v
    y.append(prev)
print(y)
activity.hint: Keep the previous output in a variable and update it each step.

quiz.why: A finite impulse response (FIR) system has an impulse response that lasts a finite time. It has no feedback.
The recursion y[n] = 0.9y[n − 1] + x[n] with an impulse input gives h[n] = (0.9)ⁿ u[n].
For y′ + 3y = x, the impulse response is the decaying exponential e^(−3t)u(t).

quiz.q: Moving average of length M is
quiz.why: A moving average adds a finite number of past samples with no feedback, so it is an FIR filter.

quiz.q: LTI requires the system be at
quiz.why: LTI analysis assumes the system starts at initial rest (zero initial conditions). Otherwise the output has a part not caused by the input.

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

questions.why: Convolution with δ(t) returns the same signal. δ is the identity of convolution.
A causal system has h[n] = 0 for n < 0, so it does not respond before the input.
In a cascade, the impulse responses convolve: h = h₁ * h₂.
u(t) * u(t) = ∫₀ᵗ 1 dτ = t u(t), the ramp r(t).
Σ|h[n]| = Σ(0.5)ⁿ = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2, which is finite. So the system is stable.

questions.q: Assertion (A): h(t) = sin(t)u(t) gives a BIBO unstable system.  Reason (R): ∫₀^∞|sin t|dt diverges.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: ∫₀^∞ |sin t| dt grows without limit, so h is not absolutely integrable. So the system is BIBO unstable, and R explains A.
Convolving with δ(t − 3) shifts the signal right by 3: e^(−2(t − 3))u(t − 3).

questions.q: Step response s[n] of h[n] = (0.5)ⁿu[n] as n → ∞
questions.why: As n → ∞, the step response tends to Σh[n] = Σ(0.5)ⁿ = 2.

questions.q: Case: An echo channel h[n] = δ[n] + 0.6δ[n − 4]. Input x = {2, 1}. y[4]
questions.why: y[4] = x[4] + 0.6·x[0] = 0 + 0.6 × 2 = 1.2. The echo is the input delayed by 4 and scaled by 0.6.
In the Laplace domain: 1/((s + 1)(s + 3)) = ½[1/(s + 1) − 1/(s + 3)]. So the result is ½(e^(−t) − e^(−3t))u(t).

questions.q: Rectangle of height 2 on [0, 1] convolved with itself: peak value
questions.why: Convolving a width-1 rectangle with itself gives a triangle on [0, 2] that peaks at t = 1, where the pulses fully overlap. Peak = 2 × 2 × 1 = 4.
Σ n aⁿ = a/(1 − a)². With a = 0.5, that is 0.5/0.25 = 2, finite, so the system is stable.

questions.q: Inverse of the accumulator y[n] = Σx[k]
questions.why: The accumulator sums past inputs. Its inverse is the first difference, y[n] = x[n] − x[n − 1].

lessons.title: Continuous-time Fourier series

scenes.text: A spectrum analyser shows a square wave's spikes at f₀, 3f₀, 5f₀…
Those spikes are its Fourier series coefficients.

steps.title: Exponential form
steps.body:
x(t) = Σ cₖ e^(jkω₀t), ω₀ = 2π/T, cₖ = (1/T)∫_T x(t)e^(−jkω₀t)dt. For real x: c₋ₖ = cₖ*.
Trigonometric: a₀ + Σ(aₖ cos kω₀t + bₖ sin kω₀t) with aₖ = 2Re cₖ, bₖ = −2Im cₖ, a₀ = c₀ (average value).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x(t) = cos ω₀t: c₁ = c₋₁ = ½, others 0.

**Example 2.** x(t) = 1 + sin(2ω₀t): c₀ = 1, c₂ = 1/(2j), c₋₂ = −1/(2j).

**Example 3.** Periodic rectangular pulse train, height A, width τ, period T: cₖ = (Aτ/T) sinc(kτ/T) where sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx). For 50% duty cycle, even harmonics vanish.

steps.title: Properties and power
steps.body: Time shift: x(t − t₀) ↔ cₖe^(−jkω₀t₀). Parseval: P = (1/T)∫|x|² = Σ|cₖ|². Even real x ⇒ real cₖ; odd real x ⇒ imaginary cₖ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting 1/T in cₖ.
- Mixing the sinc conventions (sin x/x vs sin πx/πx).
- Counting only positive k in Parseval for complex coefficients.

activity.prompt: Signal → nonzero Fourier coefficients

quiz.why: c₀ is the k = 0 coefficient: the average (DC) value of the signal.
For a real signal, the Fourier coefficients are conjugate-symmetric: c₋ₖ = cₖ*.

quiz.q: Power of cos ω₀t via Parseval
quiz.why: cos ω₀t has coefficients ½ at ±1. By Parseval, power = 2 × (1/2)² = 1/2.

quiz.q: Even real signal has coefficients that are
quiz.why: A real, even signal has real coefficients, since the sine (imaginary) parts vanish.

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

lessons.title: Fourier transform and standard pairs

scenes.text: A radar sends one short pulse, not a repeating wave.
For aperiodic signals the line spectrum becomes a continuous spectrum: the Fourier transform.

steps.title: Definition and pairs
steps.body:
X(jω) = ∫x(t)e^(−jωt)dt; x(t) = (1/2π)∫X(jω)e^(jωt)dω.
- δ(t) ↔ 1
- 1 ↔ 2πδ(ω)
- e^(−at)u(t) ↔ 1/(a + jω), a > 0
- e^(−a|t|) ↔ 2a/(a² + ω²)
- rect(t/τ) (width τ) ↔ τ sinc(ωτ/2π) = τ sin(ωτ/2)/(ωτ/2)
- e^(jω₀t) ↔ 2πδ(ω − ω₀); cos ω₀t ↔ π[δ(ω − ω₀) + δ(ω + ω₀)]
- u(t) ↔ πδ(ω) + 1/(jω)

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x = e^(−3t)u(t): X = 1/(3 + jω); |X| = 1/√(9 + ω²); ∠X = −tan⁻¹(ω/3).

**Example 2.** Pulse of height 1, width 2 centred at 0: X = 2 sin ω/ω; first zeros at ω = ±π.

**Example 3.** x = e^(−2|t|): X = 4/(4 + ω²).

steps.title: Time–bandwidth trade-off
steps.body: Narrower pulses have wider spectra — the first zero of a width-τ pulse is at f = 1/τ. That is why short pulses need wide bandwidth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting a > 0 for e^(−at)u(t) to have a transform.
- Omitting the 2π factors between ω and f conventions.
- Writing the transform of a constant as 1 instead of 2πδ(ω).

activity.prompt: |X(jω)| at ω = 4 for x = e^(−3t)u(t)

quiz.why: The Fourier transform of δ(t) is 1, by the sifting property.
The transform of e^(−at)u(t) is 1/(a + jω), for a > 0.
A constant has all its energy at ω = 0. Its transform is an impulse, 2πδ(ω).

quiz.q: First spectral zero of a 1 ms pulse
quiz.why: A pulse of width τ has its first spectral zero at f = 1/τ. For τ = 1 ms, that is 1 kHz.
cos ω₀t = (e^(jω₀t) + e^(−jω₀t))/2, so its transform is two impulses: π[δ(ω − ω₀) + δ(ω + ω₀)].

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

lessons.title: Properties of the Fourier transform and Parseval

scenes.text: Multiplying a voice signal by a carrier shifts its spectrum up to the carrier frequency.
That is the modulation (frequency-shift) property.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- Linearity
- Time shift x(t − t₀) ↔ e^(−jωt₀)X(jω) (magnitude unchanged)
- Frequency shift e^(jω₀t)x(t) ↔ X(j(ω − ω₀)); modulation x cos ω₀t ↔ ½[X(ω − ω₀) + X(ω + ω₀)]
- Scaling x(at) ↔ (1/|a|)X(jω/a)
- Differentiation dx/dt ↔ jωX; integration ↔ X/(jω) + πX(0)δ(ω)
- Convolution x * h ↔ XH; multiplication xy ↔ (1/2π)X * Y
- Duality; conjugate symmetry for real x: |X| even, ∠X odd
- **Parseval:** ∫|x|²dt = (1/2π)∫|X|²dω

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** FT of e^(−2(t − 1))u(t − 1) = e^(−jω)/(2 + jω).

**Example 2.** FT of t e^(−at)u(t) = 1/(a + jω)² (differentiation in frequency).

**Example 3.** Energy of e^(−t)u(t): time domain ∫e^(−2t) = 1/2; frequency: (1/2π)∫dω/(1 + ω²) = (1/2π)π = 1/2 ✔

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Changing |X| when a signal is only delayed.
- Missing the 1/|a| factor in scaling.
- Forgetting the 1/2π in Parseval (ω convention).

statements.s: Delaying a signal changes its magnitude spectrum.
Compressing in time expands in frequency.
Convolution in time is multiplication in frequency.

quiz.why: By the time-shift property, x(t − 2) has transform e^(−j2ω)X(jω).
Differentiation in time corresponds to multiplying by jω in frequency.
Time scaling: x(at) has transform (1/|a|)X(jω/a). For a = 2, that is ½X(jω/2).

quiz.q: Modulation by cos ω₀t shifts spectrum to
quiz.why: Multiplying by cos ω₀t shifts the spectrum to ±ω₀, each copy with half the amplitude.
Energy = ∫e^(−2t) dt from 0 to ∞ = 1/2. Parseval gives the same.

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

lessons.title: Frequency response and the DTFT

scenes.text: Turning the bass knob changes how much each low frequency is passed.
An LTI system multiplies each frequency by H(jω).

steps.title: Frequency response
steps.body:
For LTI systems: y = x * h ⇒ Y = HX, H(jω) = FT of h. A sinusoid e^(jω₀t) in gives H(jω₀)e^(jω₀t) out — eigenfunction property. |H| = gain, ∠H = phase shift.
First-order low-pass RC: H = 1/(1 + jωRC); cut-off ω_c = 1/RC where |H| = 1/√2 (−3 dB). Ideal filters (LPF, HPF, BPF) are non-causal; practical filters approximate them.

steps.title: DTFT
steps.body:
X(e^(jΩ)) = Σ x[n]e^(−jΩn) — periodic in Ω with period 2π. Inverse: x[n] = (1/2π)∫_(2π) X e^(jΩn)dΩ.
- aⁿu[n] ↔ 1/(1 − ae^(−jΩ)), |a| < 1
- δ[n] ↔ 1
- Low frequencies near Ω = 0, highest near Ω = π.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** RC LPF with R = 1 kΩ, C = 1 µF: ω_c = 1000 rad/s (159 Hz). Input cos(1000t) ⇒ output (1/√2)cos(1000t − 45°).

**Example 2.** 2-point average h = {½, ½}: H(e^(jΩ)) = ½(1 + e^(−jΩ)) = e^(−jΩ/2)cos(Ω/2): passes Ω = 0 fully, blocks Ω = π (low-pass).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting the DTFT to be aperiodic.
- Forgetting the phase shift in sinusoidal steady state.
- Calling ideal brick-wall filters realisable.

activity.prompt: RC low-pass: R = 2 kΩ, C = 0.5 µF. Cut-off ω_c = 1/RC in rad/s?

quiz.why: Complex exponentials e^(jωt) are eigenfunctions of LTI systems: the output is the same exponential times a constant, H(jω).
At the cut-off frequency, a first-order low-pass filter's gain is 1/√2, i.e. −3 dB.
The DTFT is periodic with period 2π, since e^(−jΩn) repeats when Ω increases by 2π.
The highest frequency in discrete time is Ω = π, where the sequence alternates sign every sample.
An ideal low-pass filter has a sinc impulse response, which starts before t = 0. So it is non-causal and cannot be built.

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

questions.why: Fourier series represents periodic signals as sums of harmonics.
A delayed impulse δ(t − t₀) has transform e^(−jωt₀) by the shift property.
The DTFT is periodic with period 2π.
c₀ is the average value. For 4 + 2cos ω₀t, the average is 4.
The transform is 1/(4 + jω). At ω = 0 this is 1/4.
The two-sided exponential e^(−|t|) has transform 2/(1 + ω²).

questions.q: Assertion (A): A time-limited pulse has an infinitely wide spectrum.  Reason (R): Its transform is a sinc function that only decays, never ends.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A signal that is limited in time has a spectrum that is not limited in frequency. A pulse has a sinc spectrum, which decays but never ends, so R explains A.

questions.q: FT of rect pulse width 4 (height 1) at ω = 0
questions.why: X(0) equals the area under the pulse: 1 × 4 = 4.

questions.q: Output of H = 1/(1 + jω) to cos t
questions.why: At ω = 1, H = 1/(1 + j) has magnitude 1/√2 and phase −45°. So the output is (1/√2)cos(t − 45°).

questions.q: Case: An audio LPF has R = 10 kΩ, C = 10 nF. Cut-off frequency in Hz
questions.why: The RC low-pass cut-off is f = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 10⁴ × 10⁻⁸) = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴) ≈ 1.59 kHz.
Multiplying by t differentiates the transform: e^(−2t)u(t) has 1/(2 + jω), so t e^(−2t)u(t) has 1/(2 + jω)².

questions.q: Energy of x(t) whose X(jω) = 1 for |ω| < 1, 0 else

questions.why: The DTFT of aⁿu[n] is 1/(1 − ae^(−jΩ)). At Ω = 0 with a = 0.5, that is 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2.

questions.q: Fourier series cₖ of a 50% duty square wave between 0 and 1 for k = 2
questions.why: A 50% duty square wave is symmetric, and even harmonics vanish. So c₂ = 0.

courses.title: Signals & Systems · Unit 4 · Laplace transform, Z-transform and sampling
courses.summary: Bilateral and unilateral Laplace transform, region of convergence, poles and zeros, transfer functions, causality and stability in the s-plane; Z-transform, ROC, inverse Z-transform, DT transfer functions; sampling theorem, aliasing and reconstruction.
outcomes: Find Laplace transforms with ROC and use poles/zeros
Judge causality and stability from ROC and pole locations
Compute Z-transforms, ROCs and inverses
Apply the sampling theorem and explain aliasing
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Laplace transform and ROC

scenes.text: A growing signal like eᵗu(t) has no Fourier transform.
Laplace adds a decay factor e^(−σt): X(s) exists in a region of the s-plane — the ROC.

steps.title: Definition and ROC
steps.body:
X(s) = ∫x(t)e^(−st)dt, s = σ + jω. ROC = values of s where the integral converges.
- Right-sided signals: ROC is right of the rightmost pole.
- Left-sided: left of the leftmost pole.
- Two-sided: a strip.
- ROC never contains poles.
- e^(−at)u(t) ↔ 1/(s + a), Re s > −a; −e^(−at)u(−t) ↔ 1/(s + a), Re s < −a (same expression, different ROC!).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x = e^(−2t)u(t) + e^(−3t)u(t): X = 1/(s + 2) + 1/(s + 3), ROC Re s > −2.

**Example 2.** x = e^(−2t)u(t) + e^(3t)u(−t): X = 1/(s + 2) − 1/(s − 3), ROC −2 < Re s < 3.

**Example 3.** Inverse of 1/((s + 1)(s + 2)) with ROC Re s > −1: e^(−t) − e^(−2t) for t ≥ 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving X(s) without its ROC (the inverse is not unique).
- ROC including a pole.
- Treating the unilateral and bilateral transforms as identical for two-sided signals.

activity.prompt: ROC shape

quiz.why: e^(−5t)u(t) is right-sided, and its transform 1/(s + 5) converges for Re s > −5.
The ROC cannot contain poles, because X(s) is infinite there.
The Laplace transform of δ(t) is 1, for all s, by the sifting property.

quiz.q: Same X(s) with different ROC gives
quiz.why: The same X(s) with different ROCs belongs to different time signals (right- or left-sided). So the ROC is needed for uniqueness.
The Laplace transform of u(t) is 1/s with ROC Re s > 0.

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

lessons.title: Transfer functions, poles, zeros and stability

scenes.text: A drone's controller has a transfer function H(s).
Poles in the right half-plane mean growing oscillations — instability.

steps.title: Transfer function
steps.body:
H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) = L{h(t)}. From a differential equation with zero ICs: Σaₖsᵏ Y = Σbₖsᵏ X. Poles = roots of the denominator, zeros = roots of the numerator.
**Causal & stable** LTI: ROC right of rightmost pole and includes the jω-axis ⇒ all poles in the left half-plane (Re p < 0).
Frequency response H(jω) = H(s) on the jω-axis (if the axis is in the ROC).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** y″ + 3y′ + 2y = x: H = 1/(s² + 3s + 2), poles −1, −2 ⇒ causal stable; h = (e^(−t) − e^(−2t))u(t).

**Example 2.** H = (s + 1)/(s² − s − 6) = (s + 1)/((s − 3)(s + 2)): pole at +3 ⇒ a causal version is unstable; a stable version (ROC −2 < Re s < 3) is non-causal.

**Example 3.** Second-order H = ω_n²/(s² + 2ζω_ns + ω_n²): underdamped ζ < 1 (complex poles), critically damped ζ = 1, overdamped ζ > 1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a system unstable just because it has a zero in the RHP (zeros don't affect stability).
- Forgetting that poles on the jω-axis give marginal (BIBO unstable) systems.
- Using initial conditions in transfer-function derivations (TF assumes zero ICs).

activity.prompt: Pole location → behaviour of the natural response

quiz.q: Causal LTI system is stable if all poles have
quiz.why: A causal LTI system is stable if all poles lie in the left half-plane, i.e. have negative real parts.
Taking the Laplace transform of y′ + 5y = x gives (s + 5)Y = X, so H(s) = 1/(s + 5).

quiz.q: Zeros in the right half-plane affect
quiz.why: A zero in the right half-plane does not affect stability, which depends on the poles. It changes the phase and shape of the response (non-minimum phase).
ζ = 1 gives repeated real poles. That is critically damped.

sources: Standard Signals and Systems syllabus (ECE core)

lessons.title: Z-transform and inverse Z-transform

scenes.text: A DSP chip runs y[n] = x[n] + 0.9y[n − 1] millions of times a second.
The Z-transform turns that recursion into H(z) = 1/(1 − 0.9z⁻¹).

steps.title: Definition, pairs, ROC
steps.body:
X(z) = Σ x[n]z^(−n). ROC: annulus in the z-plane.
- δ[n] ↔ 1 (all z)
- aⁿu[n] ↔ 1/(1 − az⁻¹), |z| > |a|
- −aⁿu[−n − 1] ↔ 1/(1 − az⁻¹), |z| < |a|
- naⁿu[n] ↔ az⁻¹/(1 − az⁻¹)²
Properties: shift x[n − k] ↔ z^(−k)X(z); convolution ↔ product.
Causal & stable DT LTI ⇔ all poles inside the unit circle (ROC |z| > r_max includes |z| = 1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that the ROC decides the inverse.
- Doing partial fractions in z instead of z⁻¹ inconsistently.
- Stability test using the left half-plane (for DT it's the unit circle).

activity.prompt: Z-transform facts

lessons.title: Sampling theorem, aliasing and reconstruction

scenes.text: In films, fast-spinning wheels can seem to rotate backwards.
The camera samples too slowly — that is aliasing.

steps.title: Sampling theorem
steps.body:
A band-limited signal with maximum frequency f_m is uniquely recovered from samples taken at f_s > 2f_m (Nyquist rate = 2f_m). Ideal sampling multiplies by an impulse train; the spectrum repeats every f_s.
Reconstruction: ideal low-pass filter (cut-off f_s/2) ⇒ sinc interpolation. Practical systems use an anti-aliasing filter before sampling and oversample.

steps.title: Aliasing
steps.body:
If f_s < 2f_m, spectral copies overlap: a tone at f appears at |f − kf_s| (the alias within 0…f_s/2).
Example: CD audio samples at 44.1 kHz to cover up to ~20 kHz hearing range with room for a practical anti-alias filter.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** x(t) = cos(200πt) + sin(600πt): f_m = 300 Hz ⇒ Nyquist rate 600 Hz.

**Example 2.** A 7 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz appears at |7 − 10| = 3 kHz.

**Example 3.** Signal sinc²-type with bandwidth 5 kHz multiplied by a 20 kHz carrier — highest frequency 25 kHz ⇒ Nyquist rate 50 kHz (for low-pass sampling).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ω (rad/s) and f (Hz) interchangeably.
- Taking f_m as the carrier frequency instead of carrier + bandwidth.
- Thinking anti-aliasing filters go after the sampler (they must come before).

activity.prompt: A 9 kHz tone is sampled at 12 kHz. Apparent (aliased) frequency in kHz?

quiz.why: The Nyquist rate is twice the highest frequency: 2 × 4 kHz = 8 kHz.
An anti-aliasing filter band-limits the signal before the sampler, so frequencies above f_s/2 cannot alias.
An ideal reconstruction filter is a low-pass filter with cut-off f_s/2. It removes the spectral images.

quiz.q: Spectrum of an ideally sampled signal is
quiz.why: Sampling with an impulse train makes the spectrum repeat every f_s. So it is periodic in frequency with period f_s.
options: periodic in f with period f_s

quiz.why: cos(1000πt) has ω = 1000π, so f = 500 Hz. The Nyquist rate is 2 × 500 = 1000 Hz.

questions.why: The Laplace transform of e^(−at)u(t) is 1/(s + a).
Z{u[n]} = Σ z⁻ⁿ for n ≥ 0, a geometric series that sums to 1/(1 − z⁻¹) for |z| > 1.
The Nyquist rate is twice the highest frequency f_m: 2f_m.
The denominator factors as s² + 5s + 6 = (s + 2)(s + 3), so its roots, the poles, are −2 and −3. (The numerator's zero at −2 would cancel one of them if simplified.)
(0.5)ⁿu[n] has transform 1/(1 − 0.5z⁻¹), which has a pole at z = 0.5.

questions.q: Aliased frequency: 13 kHz sampled at 8 kHz
questions.why: With f_s = 8 kHz, frequencies fold around multiples of f_s. 13 kHz is 3 kHz away from 16 kHz, so it appears at 3 kHz.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A causal LTI system with a pole at s = +1 is unstable.  Reason (R): Its impulse response contains eᵗu(t), which is not absolutely integrable.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A pole at s = +1 in a causal system gives eᵗu(t), which grows and is not absolutely integrable. So the system is unstable, and R explains A.
The right-sided part (0.5)ⁿu[n] needs |z| > 0.5. The left-sided part needs |z| < 2. The ROC is the annulus between.
The ROC 0.5 < |z| < 2 includes the unit circle |z| = 1. So the system is stable, even though it is not causal.

questions.q: Case: A sensor signal has components up to 2.4 kHz and is sampled at 4 kHz. A 2.4 kHz component appears at
questions.why: Sampled at 4 kHz, a 2.4 kHz tone is above f_s/2 = 2 kHz, so it aliases to |2.4 − 4| = 1.6 kHz.
z⁻¹/(1 − 0.5z⁻¹) is the transform of (0.5)ⁿu[n] delayed by one sample: (0.5)^(n−1)u[n − 1].
Multiplying by t in time differentiates the transform. L{t e^(−2t)u(t)} = 1/(s + 2)², for Re s > −2.

questions.q: Minimum sampling rate for x(t) = sinc²(1000t), with sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx)
questions.why: sinc(1000t) has bandwidth 500 Hz; squaring doubles it to 1000 Hz ⇒ Nyquist 2000 Hz.

questions.q: Final value of y(t) for Y(s) = 5/(s(s + 2))
questions.why: By the final value theorem, y(∞) = lim s·Y(s) = 5/(0 + 2) = 2.5.

courses.title: Analog Electronics · Unit 1 · Diodes and their applications
courses.summary: PN junction, diode equation and models, half-wave, full-wave and bridge rectifiers with ripple and PIV, capacitor filters, Zener regulators, clippers, clampers and voltage multipliers.
outcomes: Use ideal, constant-drop and exponential diode models

Design a capacitor filter and a Zener shunt regulator
