courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Inside every adapter, diodes turn AC into DC.
They conduct one way — and the details of that 'one way' matter.

steps.title: Junction physics
steps.body: Diffusion of carriers creates a depletion region and barrier potential (~0.7 V Si, ~0.3 V Ge). Forward bias narrows it — current rises exponentially; reverse bias widens it — tiny saturation current I_s until breakdown (avalanche or Zener).

steps.title: Diode equation and models
steps.body:
I = I_s(e^(V/(ηV_T)) − 1), V_T = kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K, η = 1–2.
Models: ideal (short/open), constant drop (0.7 V), piecewise linear (0.7 V + r_f). Dynamic resistance r_d = ηV_T/I_D (≈ 26 mV/I_D). Current doubles for about every 18 mV (η = 1)… roughly ×10 per 60 mV.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 5 V source, 1 kΩ, Si diode (0.7 V): I = 4.3 mA.

**Example 2.** r_d at I_D = 2 mA (η = 1): 26/2 = 13 Ω.

**Example 3.** I_s = 10⁻¹⁴ A, V = 0.65 V, η = 1: I = 10⁻¹⁴·e^(25.1) ≈ 0.8 mA.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming the diode conducts when the anode is below the cathode by less than 0.7 V.
- Using the ideal model when the supply is only a few volts (error is large).
- Forgetting temperature: V_D falls ~2 mV/°C.

activity.prompt: 12 V supply, 1.13 kΩ resistor, Si diode (0.7 V drop). Current in mA?

quiz.why: The barrier (cut-in) potential of silicon is about 0.7 V (germanium about 0.3 V).
The thermal voltage V_T = kT/q ≈ 26 mV at 300 K.
The reverse saturation current is very small, since it comes from minority carriers.
The dynamic resistance is r_d = V_T/I = 26 mV/1 mA = 26 Ω.

quiz.q: Forward drop changes with temperature by
quiz.why: The forward voltage of a silicon diode drops by about 2 mV for each °C rise in temperature.

scenes.text: A hobbyist builds a 12 V DC supply from a transformer, diodes and a capacitor.
The capacitor smooths the bumps; ripple decides the capacitor size.

steps.title: Rectifier formulas (ideal diodes, resistive load, V_m peak)
steps.body:
- **Half-wave:** V_dc = V_m/π, I_rms = I_m/2, ripple factor 1.21, efficiency 40.6%, PIV = V_m, ripple at f.
- **Centre-tap full-wave:** V_dc = 2V_m/π, ripple factor 0.482, efficiency 81.2%, PIV = 2V_m, ripple at 2f.
- **Bridge:** V_dc = 2V_m/π, PIV = V_m, two diode drops per half-cycle, no centre tap needed.

steps.title: Capacitor filter
steps.body: Peak-to-peak ripple V_r ≈ I_dc/(fC) (half-wave) or I_dc/(2fC) (full-wave). V_dc ≈ V_m − V_r/2. Ripple factor ≈ 1/(4√3 fCR) for full-wave.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 230/12 V RMS transformer, bridge, ideal diodes: V_m = 16.97 V ⇒ V_dc = 10.8 V; with 0.7 V drops: V_m′ = 15.57 V.

**Example 2.** Full-wave with I_dc = 0.5 A, f = 50 Hz, ripple 1 V p-p: C = 0.5/(100 × 1) = 5000 µF.

**Example 3.** Half-wave, V_m = 20 V, R = 1 kΩ: V_dc = 6.37 V, I_dc = 6.37 mA, PIV = 20 V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using RMS instead of peak values in V_dc formulas.
- Forgetting two diode drops in a bridge.
- Choosing diodes with PIV below 2V_m in a centre-tap rectifier.

activity.prompt: Rectifier → characteristic

quiz.why: For a full-wave rectifier, V_dc = 2V_m/π, about 0.637V_m.

quiz.q: Ripple frequency of a 50 Hz bridge rectifier
quiz.why: A bridge rectifier produces two pulses per input cycle, so the ripple frequency is twice 50 Hz = 100 Hz.
A larger capacitor holds the voltage better between pulses, so ripple is reduced. Ripple is proportional to 1/C.
A half-wave rectifier's diode must withstand the peak input in reverse, so PIV = V_m.
The maximum efficiency of a full-wave rectifier is 81.2% (a half-wave one is 40.6%).

scenes.text: A temperature sensor needs a steady 5.1 V even when the battery sags.
A Zener diode in reverse breakdown holds the voltage nearly constant.

steps.title: Zener shunt regulator
steps.body:
Source V_s through series R to the Zener (reverse-biased) in parallel with the load. In breakdown, V_Z ≈ constant. I_R = (V_s − V_Z)/R = I_Z + I_L.
Design: keep I_Z ≥ I_Z,min at minimum V_s and maximum I_L; check P_Z = V_Z I_Z,max ≤ rating at maximum V_s and minimum I_L.
Line regulation = ΔV_o/ΔV_s; load regulation = (V_NL − V_FL)/V_FL × 100%.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V_s = 12 V, V_Z = 5.1 V, R = 330 Ω, R_L = 1 kΩ: I_R = 20.9 mA, I_L = 5.1 mA, I_Z = 15.8 mA, P_Z = 81 mW.

**Example 2.** If R_L is removed: I_Z = 20.9 mA, P_Z = 107 mW (worst case for the Zener).

**Example 3.** Minimum R_L for regulation with I_Z,min = 1 mA: I_L,max = 19.9 mA ⇒ R_L,min = 5.1/0.0199 = 256 Ω.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forward-biasing the Zener (it then acts as an ordinary 0.7 V diode).
- Ignoring the no-load case when checking power.
- Forgetting that the Zener stops regulating if V_s falls too low.

activity.prompt: Zener regulator: Vs = 15 V, Vz = 6 V, R = 450 Ω, no load. Zener current (mA)?

quiz.why: A Zener diode is used in reverse breakdown, where the voltage stays almost constant. That is how it regulates.

quiz.q: I_R in a shunt regulator equals
quiz.why: By KCL, the current through the series resistor splits into the Zener current and the load current: I_R = I_Z + I_L.
The Zener current is largest when the supply voltage is highest and the load current is lowest. That gives the worst-case power.
options: max V_s and min load current

quiz.q: Zener breakdown dominates for V_Z below about
quiz.why: Below about 5–6 V, Zener (tunnelling) breakdown dominates. Above, avalanche breakdown dominates.

quiz.q: Line regulation measures change in V_o due to
quiz.why: Line regulation measures how much the output changes when the input (line) voltage changes.

scenes.text: A 3.3 V microcontroller input must survive a 12 V spike.
A clipper with diodes to the rails cuts the excess.

steps.title: Clippers
steps.body: Series or shunt diodes (with bias V_B) remove parts of a waveform above/below a level. Positive shunt clipper with bias V_B: output limited to V_B + 0.7 V. Double clipper (two diodes, two biases) limits both sides.

steps.title: Clampers and multipliers
steps.body:
Clamper (C + diode + R, RC ≫ T) shifts the DC level without changing shape: positive clamper puts the negative peak at ≈ 0 (or bias), output swings 0 to 2V_m.
Voltage doubler (half-wave): two diodes + two capacitors ⇒ ≈ 2V_m; tripler/quadrupler by cascading stages.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 10 V peak sine into a shunt clipper with diode + 3 V battery (Si): output clipped at 3.7 V on the positive side.

**Example 2.** Positive clamper on a 5 V peak square wave: output 0 to 10 V (ideal).

**Example 3.** Doubler from a 12 V RMS secondary: ≈ 2 × 16.97 = 33.9 V DC (ideal, light load).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 0.7 V drop in the clipping level.
- Choosing RC comparable to the period in a clamper (it then distorts).
- Confusing clipper (changes shape) with clamper (shifts level).

activity.prompt: Clipper or clamper?

items.text: Removes the part of the signal above 5 V
Shifts a waveform so its minimum sits at 0 V
Needs a capacitor with RC ≫ T
Limits both peaks with two diodes

quiz.why: A clamper shifts the DC level of a signal without changing its shape.

quiz.q: Shunt clipper with 2 V bias (Si) clips at
quiz.why: A shunt clipper clips when the diode conducts: bias plus the 0.7 V drop. So 2 V + 0.7 V = 2.7 V.

quiz.q: Ideal positive clamper output for ±V_m input
quiz.why: An ideal positive clamper shifts the whole waveform up so its negative peak is at 0. A ±V_m input becomes 0 to 2V_m.
A voltage doubler charges a capacitor to V_m and adds it to the next peak. The output is about 2V_m.
A clamper needs a long discharge time, RC ≫ T, so the capacitor keeps its charge across the cycle.

questions.why: A diode conducts when forward biased with a voltage above its cut-in value (about 0.7 V for silicon).

questions.why: A Zener diode is mainly used for voltage regulation.
For a half-wave rectifier, V_dc = V_m/π = 31.4/3.14 = 10 V.
A half-wave rectifier gives one pulse per cycle, so the ripple frequency equals the supply frequency, 60 Hz.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Centre-tap rectifier diodes need PIV of 2V_m.  Reason (R): When one diode conducts, the other sees both half-windings in reverse.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

Bridge with 9 V RMS secondary and 0.7 V diodes: peak output
questions.why: The peak of a 9 V RMS secondary is 9√2 ≈ 12.73 V. A bridge has two diodes in the path, so subtract 1.4 V: ≈ 11.3 V.

questions.q: Case: A 5 V Zener (1 W) is fed from 12 V through 100 Ω with no load. Is it safe?
questions.why: The current is (12 − 5)/100 = 70 mA. Zener power = 5 V × 0.07 A = 0.35 W, which is below the 1 W rating, so it is safe.
options: Yes — P_Z ≈ 0.35 W, below the 1 W rating

questions.q: Minimum R_L for Zener: V_s 15, V_Z 9, R 200 Ω, I_Z,min 5 mA
questions.why: I_R = (15 − 9)/200 = 30 mA. At least 5 mA must flow in the Zener, so the load can take at most 25 mA. Minimum R_L = 9/0.025 = 360 Ω.

questions.q: Diode current with I_s = 10⁻¹³ A at 0.6 V (V_T = 25 mV)
Ripple factor of full-wave with capacitor: f = 50, C = 1000 µF, R = 100 Ω
questions.why: For a full-wave rectifier with capacitor, r = 1/(4√3 fCR) = 1/(4 × 1.732 × 50 × 10⁻³ × 100) = 1/34.6 ≈ 0.0289.

questions.q: Diode current rises about 10× for each additional
questions.why: From I = I_s e^(V/V_T), the current rises 10× for each ΔV = V_T ln 10 ≈ 26 mV × 2.3 ≈ 60 mV.

scenes.text: A microcontroller pin (a few mA) switches a 200 mA LED strip through a transistor.
A small base current controls a much larger collector current.

steps.title: Operation
steps.body:
NPN: emitter (heavily doped) injects electrons into a thin base; most reach the collector. I_E = I_B + I_C; I_C = βI_B = αI_E; α = β/(β + 1).
Regions: **active** (BE forward, BC reverse) — amplifier; **saturation** (both forward, V_CE ≈ 0.2 V) — switch ON; **cut-off** (both reverse) — switch OFF.
Early effect: I_C rises slightly with V_CE (output resistance r_o = V_A/I_C).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** β = 100, I_B = 20 µA: I_C = 2 mA, I_E = 2.02 mA, α = 0.990.

**Example 2.** Switch: V_CC = 12 V, LED load R_C = 60 Ω ⇒ I_C(sat) ≈ (12 − 0.2 − 2)/60 ≈ 0.16 A (2 V LED). With β = 100 need I_B > 1.6 mA; drive 3 mA for hard saturation (R_B = (5 − 0.7)/3 mA ≈ 1.4 kΩ from a 5 V pin).

steps.title: Configurations
steps.body: CE (common emitter): voltage and current gain, phase inversion. CB: voltage gain, current gain ≈ 1, low input resistance. CC (emitter follower): voltage gain ≈ 1, high input, low output resistance — buffer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming I_C = βI_B in saturation (it is less).
- Swapping α and β.
- Forgetting the base–emitter drop (≈ 0.7 V) when finding I_B.

activity.prompt: β = 150 and I_C = 3 mA. Base current in µA?

quiz.why: By KCL, the emitter current is the sum of the base and collector currents: I_E = I_B + I_C.
In the active region, the base–emitter junction is forward biased and the base–collector junction is reverse biased.
An emitter follower (common collector) has voltage gain close to 1. It is used as a buffer.
A transistor used as a switch is ON in saturation, where V_CE is about 0.2 V.

scenes.text: An amplifier designed in winter distorts on hot afternoons.
β and V_BE change with temperature; good biasing keeps the Q-point steady.

steps.title: Load line and Q-point
steps.body:
DC load line: V_CE = V_CC − I_C(R_C + R_E). Q-point (I_CQ, V_CEQ) near the middle for maximum symmetric swing.
Fixed bias: I_B = (V_CC − 0.7)/R_B — Q-point depends strongly on β (poor).
Voltage-divider bias: Thevenin V_TH = V_CC R₂/(R₁ + R₂), R_TH = R₁ ∥ R₂; I_B = (V_TH − 0.7)/(R_TH + (β + 1)R_E). If βR_E ≥ 10R₂, I_C ≈ (V_TH − 0.7)/R_E — nearly independent of β.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** V_CC = 12 V, R₁ = 47 kΩ, R₂ = 10 kΩ, R_C = 2.2 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ, β = 100.
V_TH = 2.105 V, R_TH = 8.25 kΩ; I_B = 1.405/(8.25k + 101k) = 12.9 µA; I_C = 1.29 mA (approx. method: 1.405 mA).
V_CE = 12 − 1.29(3.2) = 7.9 V ⇒ active ✔.

**Example 2.** Fixed bias with R_B = 470 kΩ, V_CC = 12, β = 100 vs 200: I_C = 2.4 mA vs 4.8 mA — Q-point doubles (unstable).

steps.title: Stability factor
steps.body: S = ∂I_C/∂I_CO. Fixed bias S = β + 1 (poor); voltage divider S ≈ 1 + R_TH/R_E (good when small). Thermal runaway: rising I_C heats the junction ⇒ more I_C; R_E feedback prevents it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring (β + 1)R_E reflected into the base.
- Placing the Q-point near saturation.
- Forgetting to check V_CE > V_CE(sat).

activity.prompt: Analyse a voltage-divider bias circuit
items: Find V_TH and R_TH of the divider
Write base loop: V_TH = I_B R_TH + 0.7 + (β + 1)I_B R_E
Solve for I_B, then I_C = βI_B
Compute V_CE = V_CC − I_C R_C − I_E R_E
Confirm the transistor is in the active region

quiz.why: The voltage-divider bias with an emitter resistor gives negative feedback, so the Q-point is the most stable.

quiz.q: DC load line end on V_CE axis
quiz.why: On the DC load line, I_C = 0 at V_CE = V_CC. That is the point on the V_CE axis.
For fixed bias, the stability factor is about β + 1, which is poor (large) because the collector current varies a lot with β and temperature.

quiz.q: R_E reflected into the base loop as
quiz.why: The emitter current is (β + 1) times the base current. So R_E appears in the base loop as (β + 1)R_E.
The emitter resistor gives negative feedback. If current rises, voltage across R_E rises and reduces base drive, preventing thermal runaway.

lessons.title: Small-signal models and the CE amplifier

scenes.text: A microphone gives a few millivolts; a CE stage amplifies it 100 times.
The small-signal model predicts that gain.

steps.title: Hybrid-π / re model
steps.body:
g_m = I_C/V_T (≈ I_C/26 mV); r_π = β/g_m; r_e = V_T/I_E ≈ 26 mV/I_E; r_o = V_A/I_C.
h-parameters (CE): h_ie ≈ r_π, h_fe ≈ β.

steps.title: CE amplifier (R_E bypassed)
steps.body:
A_v = −g_m(R_C ∥ R_L ∥ r_o) ≈ −(R_C ∥ R_L)/r_e. R_in = R₁ ∥ R₂ ∥ r_π. R_out ≈ R_C.
Unbypassed R_E (degeneration): A_v ≈ −R_C/(r_e + R_E) — lower but more stable gain, higher R_in = R₁ ∥ R₂ ∥ (β + 1)(r_e + R_E).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** I_C = 1.3 mA: g_m = 50 mA/V; r_e = 20 Ω; β = 100 ⇒ r_π = 2 kΩ. R_C = 2.2 kΩ, R_L = 10 kΩ (R_E bypassed): A_v = −50m × (2.2k ∥ 10k = 1.8k) = −90.
R_in = 47k ∥ 10k ∥ 2k = 1.6 kΩ.

**Example 2.** With R_E = 1 kΩ unbypassed: A_v ≈ −1.8k/1.02k ≈ −1.8.

**Example 3.** Emitter follower, R_E = 1 kΩ: A_v = R_E/(r_e + R_E) ≈ 0.98.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using DC resistances in AC analysis without shorting capacitors and DC sources.
- Forgetting the load R_L in parallel with R_C.
- Dropping the minus sign (phase inversion) of the CE stage.

activity.prompt: I_C = 2.6 mA. Transconductance g_m = I_C/26 mV in mA/V?

quiz.why: The transconductance g_m = I_C/V_T, where V_T ≈ 26 mV.
The input resistance r_π = β/g_m, since g_m = I_C/V_T and I_B = I_C/β.
A common-emitter stage inverts the signal, giving a 180° phase shift.
A bypass capacitor across R_E makes the emitter AC ground. That removes AC feedback and raises the AC gain, while the DC bias stays the same.
An emitter follower has high input and low output resistance with gain near 1. So it works as a buffer.

lessons.title: CB, CC stages, multistage and frequency response basics

scenes.text: A hi-fi amplifier has a pre-amp, driver and buffer stages.
Cascading stages multiplies gains — and each stage's R_in loads the previous one.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
| | CE | CB | CC |
Voltage gain: high, high, ≈ 1
Current gain: β, α ≈ 1, β + 1
R_in: medium, low (≈ r_e), high
R_out: high (≈ R_C), high, low
Phase: 180°, 0°, 0°

Cascade: A_total = A₁A₂…, with each stage loaded by the next stage's R_in. In dB, gains add: 20 log|A|.

steps.title: Frequency response
steps.body: Low-frequency roll-off from coupling and bypass capacitors (f_L ≈ 1/(2πR_eqC)); high-frequency roll-off from junction capacitances and the Miller effect (C_M = C_μ(1 + |A_v|) at the input of a CE stage). Bandwidth = f_H − f_L; gain–bandwidth trade-off.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Two stages with gains −40 and −25: total 1000 (60 dB), in phase.

**Example 2.** Coupling cap: R_in = 1.6 kΩ, want f_L = 20 Hz ⇒ C = 1/(2π·20·1600) ≈ 5 µF.

**Example 3.** Miller: C_μ = 2 pF, A_v = −90 ⇒ C_M = 182 pF — dominates the input capacitance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying unloaded gains of stages.
- Forgetting the Miller multiplication in CE stages.
- Adding gains in linear form instead of dB.

activity.prompt: Configuration → property

quiz.why: The common-collector (emitter follower) stage has the highest input resistance, about (β + 1) times the emitter load. CE is medium, and CB is very low.
At low frequencies, the coupling and bypass capacitors act as high impedances and limit the gain. They set the low-frequency cut-off. Junction capacitances limit the high end.

quiz.q: Total gain of stages 20 dB and 30 dB
quiz.why: Gains in decibels add for cascaded stages. 20 dB + 30 dB = 50 dB.

quiz.q: Miller capacitance for C = 5 pF, A_v = −49
quiz.why: Miller effect: the effective input capacitance is C(1 + |A_v|) = 5 × (1 + 49) = 250 pF.

questions.why: The emitter is heavily doped so it can inject many carriers into the base. The base is thin and lightly doped.
Current gain β is the ratio of collector current to base current, I_C/I_B.
A common-collector (CC) amplifier is also called an emitter follower, because the emitter voltage follows the base.
The emitter resistance r_e = V_T/I_E = 26 mV/1 mA = 26 Ω.

questions.q: V_CE(sat) of a small Si BJT
questions.why: In saturation a small silicon BJT has V_CE(sat) of about 0.2 V.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Voltage-divider bias with a large R_E makes I_C nearly independent of β.  Reason (R): With βR_E ≫ R_TH, I_C ≈ (V_TH − V_BE)/R_E.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: With βR_E ≫ R_TH, the base current has little effect and I_C ≈ (V_TH − V_BE)/R_E, which does not depend on β. That is the reason for the assertion.

questions.q: V_TH for V_CC 15 V, R₁ 40 k, R₂ 10 k
I_C (approx) for that with R_E = 1.15 kΩ
CE gain with I_C = 1 mA, R_C ∥ R_L = 2.6 kΩ (bypassed)
questions.why: At I_C = 1 mA, g_m = I_C/V_T ≈ 38.5 mS. With a bypassed emitter, gain ≈ −g_m (R_C ∥ R_L) = −38.5 mS × 2.6 k ≈ −100.

questions.q: Case: A sensor buffer needs R_out < 50 Ω and gain ≈ 1. Best stage
questions.why: A buffer needs gain near 1 and low output resistance. An emitter follower (common collector) provides both.

questions.q: Coupling C for f_L = 10 Hz into R_in = 8 kΩ
questions.why: The cut-off is f_L = 1/(2πRC). So C = 1/(2π × 10 × 8000) ≈ 2 µF.

questions.q: Unbypassed CE: R_C = 4.7 kΩ, R_E = 470 Ω, r_e = 10 Ω: A_v
questions.why: Without a bypass, the emitter resistance is in the AC path: A_v ≈ −R_C/(R_E + r_e) = −4.7 k/480 ≈ −9.8.

questions.q: Overall gain of 3 stages with −10, +0.9 (CC), −20 into each other (loaded values)
questions.why: Overall gain is the product of stage gains: (−10)(0.9)(−20) = +180. Two negative signs give a positive result.

questions.q: Required I_B to saturate: I_C(sat) = 50 mA, β_min = 50 (overdrive ×2)
questions.why: To saturate, I_B must be at least I_C/β_min = 50 mA/50 = 1 mA. With 2× overdrive, I_B = 2 mA.

courses.title: Analog Electronics · Unit 3 · Field-effect transistors (JFET and MOSFET)
courses.summary: JFET operation and Shockley's equation, enhancement and depletion MOSFETs, square-law model, regions of operation, biasing (self-bias, voltage-divider), small-signal model, common-source and source-follower amplifiers, and the CMOS inverter as a switch.
outcomes: Use Shockley's equation and the MOSFET square law
Determine region of operation and bias point
Compute g_m, gain, R_in and R_out of CS and CD stages
Explain CMOS inverter operation and power
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A phone processor holds billions of MOSFETs.
Their gate draws almost no current — ideal for dense, low-power logic.

steps.title: JFET
steps.body: Voltage-controlled: I_D = I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)² for V_P ≤ V_GS ≤ 0 (n-channel). Gate–channel junction reverse biased ⇒ very high input resistance. g_m = (2I_DSS/|V_P|)(1 − V_GS/V_P).

steps.title: MOSFET (n-channel enhancement)
steps.body:
Insulated gate (SiO₂ or high-k). Channel forms for V_GS > V_T (threshold).
- Cut-off: V_GS < V_T, I_D ≈ 0.
- Triode (linear): V_DS < V_GS − V_T, I_D = k′(W/L)[(V_GS − V_T)V_DS − V_DS²/2].
- Saturation: V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T, I_D = ½k′(W/L)(V_GS − V_T)² (1 + λV_DS).
Depletion MOSFET has a built-in channel (conducts at V_GS = 0).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** JFET I_DSS = 10 mA, V_P = −4 V, V_GS = −2 V: I_D = 10(0.5)² = 2.5 mA; g_m = (20/4)(0.5) = 2.5 mS.

**Example 2.** MOSFET k′W/L = 2 mA/V², V_T = 1 V, V_GS = 3 V, V_DS = 5 V: saturation (5 > 2) ⇒ I_D = ½·2·4 = 4 mA.

**Example 3.** Same with V_DS = 1 V: triode ⇒ I_D = 2[(2)(1) − 0.5] = 3 mA.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the saturation equation without checking V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T.
- Sign errors for p-channel devices.
- Confusing BJT 'saturation' (switch on) with MOSFET 'saturation' (constant-current, amplifier region).

activity.prompt: JFET: I_DSS = 12 mA, V_P = −6 V, V_GS = −3 V. I_D (mA)?

quiz.why: A FET's drain current is controlled by the gate voltage, so it is a voltage-controlled device. A BJT is current-controlled.
A MOSFET is in saturation (pinch-off) when V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_T. Below that, it is in the triode region.
At V_GS = 0 a JFET carries its maximum drain current, I_DSS (Shockley equation).
An enhancement MOSFET has no channel at V_GS = 0. It conducts only when V_GS exceeds the threshold V_T.
The MOSFET gate is insulated by an oxide layer, so the gate current is practically zero.

story.title: Bias for a radio front end

scenes.text: An FM receiver's front end uses a JFET for low noise.
Self-bias sets V_GS automatically through a source resistor.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
**JFET self-bias:** V_GS = −I_D R_S; solve with Shockley (quadratic, pick root with V_P < V_GS < 0).
**Voltage-divider (MOSFET/JFET):** V_G = V_DD R₂/(R₁ + R₂); V_GS = V_G − I_D R_S; solve with the device equation.
Drain feedback for enhancement MOSFETs: V_GS = V_DS (always saturated).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (self-bias).** I_DSS = 8 mA, V_P = −4 V, R_S = 1 kΩ: I_D = 8(1 − I_D/4)² (I_D in mA) ⇒ I_D² − 10I_D + 16 = 0 ⇒ I_D = 2 mA (8 rejected) ⇒ V_GS = −2 V.

**Example 2 (E-MOSFET divider).** V_DD = 12, V_G = 4 V, R_S = 1 kΩ, ½k′W/L = 1 mA/V², V_T = 1 V: I_D = (4 − I_D − 1)² ⇒ I_D² − 7I_D + 9 = 0 ⇒ I_D = 1.70 mA (other root 5.3 gives V_GS < V_T, reject). V_GS = 2.30 V.

steps.title: Root selection
steps.body: Always reject the root that puts V_GS outside the valid range (beyond pinch-off for JFETs, below V_T for E-MOSFETs).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Keeping both roots.
- Forgetting V_GS = −I_D R_S is negative for n-JFET self-bias.
- Not checking saturation after finding I_D.

activity.prompt: JFET self-bias analysis
items: Write V_GS = −I_D R_S
Substitute into I_D = I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)²
Solve the quadratic for I_D
Reject the root giving |V_GS| > |V_P|
Compute V_DS and check saturation

quiz.why: In JFET self-bias, the drain current through R_S makes the source positive. With the gate at 0 V, V_GS = −I_D R_S.
With the gate tied to the drain, V_DS = V_GS, which is above V_GS − V_T. So the enhancement MOSFET stays in saturation.
Self-bias gives two roots. The valid one has |V_GS| ≤ |V_P| (the JFET is on). A root with |V_GS| > |V_P| would mean the JFET is cut off, so it is rejected.
The FET gate draws negligible current, so a gate divider has only a tiny effect and gives a stable bias with high input resistance.

scenes.text: A pH electrode has megaohms of source resistance.
A FET input stage barely loads it — perfect.

steps.title: Model and stages
steps.body:
Small-signal: g_m (MOSFET sat: g_m = k′(W/L)(V_GS − V_T) = 2I_D/(V_GS − V_T) = √(2k′(W/L)I_D)), r_o = 1/(λI_D).
**Common source (R_S bypassed):** A_v = −g_m(R_D ∥ R_L ∥ r_o); R_in = R_G (divider); R_out ≈ R_D.
**CS with unbypassed R_S:** A_v = −g_mR_D/(1 + g_mR_S).
**Source follower (CD):** A_v = g_mR_S/(1 + g_mR_S) < 1; R_out ≈ 1/g_m ∥ R_S.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** g_m = 2 mS, R_D = 5 kΩ, R_L = 20 kΩ: A_v = −2m × 4k = −8.

**Example 2.** Unbypassed R_S = 1 kΩ: A_v = −2m × 5k/(1 + 2) = −3.33.

**Example 3.** Source follower R_S = 2 kΩ, g_m = 4 mS: A_v = 8/9 = 0.89; R_out ≈ 250 Ω ∥ 2k = 222 Ω.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using BJT formulas with r_π for FETs (FET input is open).
- Forgetting R_L in parallel with R_D.
- Calculating g_m from the triode equation for a saturated device.

activity.prompt: CS amplifier: g_m = 3 mS, R_D ∥ R_L = 4 kΩ (R_S bypassed). |A_v|?

quiz.why: A common-source amplifier has voltage gain A_v = −g_m R_D, an inverting stage.
A source follower has gain slightly below 1, so it works as a buffer.

quiz.q: FET amplifier input resistance is set mainly by
quiz.why: The gate takes no current, so the amplifier's input resistance is set mainly by the gate bias resistors.

quiz.q: g_m for I_D = 2 mA, V_GS − V_T = 1 V
quiz.why: For a MOSFET in saturation, g_m = 2I_D/V_ov = 2 × 2 mA/1 V = 4 mS.
An unbypassed R_S gives source degeneration (negative feedback). It lowers the gain but makes it more stable.

lessons.title: MOSFET as a switch and the CMOS inverter

scenes.text: A laptop CPU flips billions of CMOS switches every second.
CMOS draws power mainly while switching — that is why it dominates digital design.

steps.title: CMOS inverter
steps.body:
PMOS from V_DD to output, NMOS from output to ground, gates tied together. Input high ⇒ NMOS on, PMOS off ⇒ output 0. Input low ⇒ PMOS on ⇒ output V_DD. Static current ≈ 0 (only leakage).
Voltage-transfer characteristic: switching threshold ≈ V_DD/2 for matched devices; noise margins NM_H = V_OH − V_IH, NM_L = V_IL − V_OL.

steps.title: Power and switching
steps.body: Dynamic power P = αC_L V_DD² f (α = activity factor). Halving V_DD cuts dynamic power to one quarter — why chips use low supply voltages. Power MOSFET switch: conduction loss I²R_DS(on); use a gate driver for fast switching; flyback diode across inductive loads.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** C_L = 10 fF, V_DD = 1 V, f = 2 GHz, α = 0.1: P = 0.1 × 10⁻¹⁴ × 1 × 2×10⁹ = 2 µW per gate.

**Example 2.** MOSFET with R_DS(on) = 20 mΩ carrying 10 A: P = 2 W ⇒ needs a heat sink.

**Example 3.** Same circuit at V_DD = 0.8 V instead of 1 V: dynamic power × 0.64.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Driving a relay coil from a MOSFET without a flyback diode.
- Thinking CMOS has zero power (dynamic and leakage power exist).
- Leaving MOSFET gates floating (they pick up charge and switch unpredictably).

statements.s: A CMOS inverter draws large static current.
Dynamic power is proportional to V_DD².
A flyback diode protects a switch driving an inductor.
NMOS conducts when its gate is low.

quiz.q: When CMOS inverter input is high
quiz.why: When a CMOS inverter's input is high, the NMOS turns on and the PMOS turns off. The output is pulled low.
CMOS dynamic power is P = αC V_DD² f, with activity factor α, load capacitance C and frequency f.

quiz.q: Conduction loss of a MOSFET switch
quiz.why: When a MOSFET switch is on, it behaves like a small resistance R_DS(on). The conduction loss is I² R_DS(on).

quiz.q: Halving V_DD changes dynamic power by
quiz.why: Dynamic power depends on V_DD². Halving the supply voltage gives (1/2)² = 1/4 of the power.
The high noise margin is NM_H = V_OH − V_IH: how much the output high level can drop and still be read as high.

questions.why: The FET gate is insulated or reverse-biased, so the input resistance is very high.
CMOS (complementary MOS) uses NMOS and PMOS transistors together.
The JFET pinch-off voltage is written V_P.

questions.q: JFET I_DSS = 16 mA, V_P = −4 V, V_GS = −1 V: I_D
MOSFET (½k′W/L = 0.5 mA/V², V_T = 2 V) at V_GS = 4 V, saturated: I_D
Is the device saturated if V_DS = 1 V in that case?
questions.why: V_ov = V_GS − V_T = 2 V. Saturation needs V_DS ≥ 2 V, but V_DS = 1 V, so it is in the triode region.

questions.q: Assertion (A): MOSFET 'saturation' is the region used for amplification.  Reason (R): In saturation, I_D is nearly independent of V_DS.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: In saturation, I_D hardly changes with V_DS (a current-source behaviour), which gives good gain. So saturation is used for amplification, and R explains A.

questions.q: g_m of the JFET at V_GS = −1 V (I_DSS 16 mA, V_P −4 V)
CS gain with g_m = 5 mS, R_D = 10 kΩ, R_S = 1 kΩ unbypassed
questions.why: With an unbypassed source resistor, A_v = −g_m R_D/(1 + g_m R_S) = −(5 mS × 10 k)/(1 + 5) = −50/6 ≈ −8.33.

questions.q: Self-bias: I_DSS = 9 mA, V_P = −3 V, R_S = 1 kΩ. I_D
questions.why: I = 9(1 − I/3)² ⇒ I² − 7I + 9 = 0 ⇒ I ≈ 1.70 mA (the 5.30 mA root gives |V_GS| > |V_P|).

questions.q: Case: A 3.3 V microcontroller must switch a 12 V, 2 A solenoid. Best choice
questions.why: A logic-level N-MOSFET can be turned fully on by 3.3 V, with a low R_DS(on). A flyback diode protects against the solenoid's inductive spike.

questions.q: Dynamic power of 10⁹ gates, C = 1 fF, V_DD = 1 V, f = 1 GHz, α = 0.1
questions.why: P = α N C V_DD² f = 0.1 × 10⁹ × 10⁻¹⁵ F × 1² × 10⁹ = 100 W.

questions.q: Source follower R_S = 1 kΩ, g_m = 9 mS: A_v
r_o for λ = 0.02 V⁻¹, I_D = 1 mA
questions.why: The output resistance r_o = 1/(λI_D) = 1/(0.02 × 1 mA) = 50 kΩ.
A depletion-mode MOSFET has a built-in channel, so it conducts at V_GS = 0.

courses.title: Analog Electronics · Unit 4 · Op-amps, feedback and oscillators
courses.summary: Ideal and practical op-amp parameters, inverting, non-inverting, summing, difference and instrumentation amplifiers, integrator and differentiator, comparators and Schmitt trigger, negative feedback topologies and their effects, and oscillators using the Barkhausen criterion (RC phase-shift, Wien bridge, LC).
outcomes: Analyse op-amp circuits using virtual short
Design inverting/non-inverting/summing/difference amplifiers
Explain effects of negative feedback on gain, bandwidth and impedances
Design RC phase-shift and Wien-bridge oscillators
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A weighing scale's strain gauge gives millivolts.
An op-amp with two resistors sets an exact, stable gain.

steps.title: Ideal op-amp and golden rules
steps.body: Infinite open-loop gain, infinite R_in, zero R_out, infinite bandwidth. With negative feedback: (1) V₊ = V₋ (virtual short), (2) input currents = 0.

steps.title: Basic configurations
steps.body:
- **Inverting:** A_v = −R_f/R₁; R_in = R₁.
- **Non-inverting:** A_v = 1 + R_f/R₁; R_in very high.
- **Voltage follower:** A_v = 1.
- **Summing (inverting):** V_o = −R_f(V₁/R₁ + V₂/R₂ + …).
- **Difference:** with R₁ = R₃, R_f = R₄: V_o = (R_f/R₁)(V₂ − V₁).
- **Instrumentation amp (3 op-amp):** gain = (1 + 2R/R_G)(R₃/R₂), high CMRR, high R_in.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Inverting R₁ = 10 kΩ, R_f = 100 kΩ, V_in = 0.2 V: V_o = −2 V.

**Example 2.** Non-inverting R₁ = 1 kΩ, R_f = 9 kΩ: gain 10.

**Example 3.** Summing R_f = 10 kΩ, R₁ = R₂ = 10 kΩ, V₁ = 1 V, V₂ = 2 V: V_o = −3 V (an audio mixer).

**Example 4.** Output saturates near the rails: with ±12 V supplies and gain 100, a 0.2 V input would clip at about ±11 V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the virtual short to circuits without negative feedback (comparators).
- Forgetting the 1 in the non-inverting gain.
- Ignoring output saturation at the supply rails.

activity.prompt: Non-inverting amplifier: R₁ = 2 kΩ, R_f = 18 kΩ, V_in = 0.3 V. V_o (V)?

quiz.why: An inverting op-amp amplifier has gain −R_f/R₁.
With negative feedback and a high open-loop gain, the two inputs sit at nearly the same voltage, V₊ ≈ V₋. This is the virtual short.
A voltage follower has gain 1. It copies the input and works as a buffer.

quiz.q: Summing amp with R_f = R = 10 k, inputs 0.5 V and 1.5 V
quiz.why: The summing amplifier output is −(R_f/R)(V₁ + V₂) = −(0.5 + 1.5) = −2 V.
Instrumentation amplifiers have high common-mode rejection and very high input impedance, so they suit small sensor signals.

lessons.title: Integrator, differentiator, comparators and practical parameters

scenes.text: A function generator makes triangles by integrating square waves.
A comparator with hysteresis makes the squares.

steps.title: Integrator and differentiator
steps.body: Integrator: V_o = −(1/RC)∫V_in dt (add R_f across C to limit DC gain). Differentiator: V_o = −RC dV_in/dt (add series R to limit high-frequency gain/noise).

steps.title: Comparators and Schmitt trigger
steps.body: Open-loop comparator: output ±V_sat depending on sign of V₊ − V₋. Schmitt trigger (positive feedback) has two thresholds: V_UT, V_LT = ±βV_sat with β = R₂/(R₁ + R₂) (inverting type, symmetric supplies); hysteresis V_H = 2βV_sat — rejects noise.

steps.title: Practical parameters
steps.body: Input offset voltage, bias current, CMRR = A_d/A_cm (dB), **slew rate** SR (V/µs): full-power bandwidth f_max = SR/(2πV_p). Gain–bandwidth product GBW constant for a dominant-pole op-amp (e.g. 1 MHz): closed-loop bandwidth = GBW/noise gain.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Integrator R = 10 kΩ, C = 0.1 µF, V_in = +1 V step: ramp of −1000 V/s (−1 V per ms) until saturation.

**Example 2.** Schmitt: R₁ = 9 kΩ, R₂ = 1 kΩ, V_sat = ±12 V: thresholds ±1.2 V, hysteresis 2.4 V.

**Example 3.** SR = 0.5 V/µs, 10 V peak output: f_max = 0.5×10⁶/(2π·10) ≈ 8 kHz.

**Example 4.** GBW 1 MHz, gain 100: bandwidth 10 kHz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting full output swing at high frequency despite slew-rate limits.
- Using negative-feedback rules for a Schmitt trigger.
- Forgetting the minus sign of the inverting integrator.

activity.prompt: Circuit → function

quiz.why: An integrator integrates its input. A constant input gives a linear ramp at the output.

quiz.q: Hysteresis width of Schmitt (β = 0.1, V_sat = ±10 V)
quiz.why: The Schmitt trigger's hysteresis width is 2βV_sat = 2 × 0.1 × 10 = 2 V.
The full-power bandwidth is the highest frequency at which a full-amplitude sine is not slew-limited: f_max = SR/(2πV_p).

quiz.q: Closed-loop BW for GBW 2 MHz, gain 20

quiz.why: Comparators work in open loop or with positive feedback, driving the output into saturation. They do not use the linear region.

scenes.text: Raw transistor gain varies with temperature and part tolerance.
Feeding back a fraction of the output trades some gain for accuracy and bandwidth.

steps.title: Basic feedback equation
steps.body: A_f = A/(1 + Aβ). Loop gain T = Aβ. If Aβ ≫ 1, A_f ≈ 1/β (set by passive components). Desensitivity D = 1 + Aβ: dA_f/A_f = (1/D)·dA/A. Bandwidth × D; distortion and noise inside the loop ÷ D.

steps.title: Topologies (sampling–mixing)
steps.body:
- Voltage-series (series–shunt): voltage amplifier — R_in ×D, R_out ÷D (non-inverting op-amp).
- Current-series: transconductance — R_in ×D, R_out ×D.
- Voltage-shunt: transresistance — R_in ÷D, R_out ÷D (inverting op-amp).
- Current-shunt: current amplifier — R_in ÷D, R_out ×D.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A = 10⁵, β = 0.01: A_f = 10⁵/1001 ≈ 99.9.

**Example 2.** If A drops 50% to 5×10⁴: A_f = 5×10⁴/501 = 99.8 — only 0.1% change.

**Example 3.** Amplifier BW 10 kHz, D = 100 ⇒ closed-loop BW ≈ 1 MHz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking feedback increases gain (negative feedback reduces it).
- Mixing up which topology raises or lowers R_in/R_out.
- Ignoring stability: too much phase shift turns negative feedback into positive (oscillation).

activity.prompt: Effect of negative feedback

quiz.why: With feedback, the closed-loop gain is A_f = A/(1 + Aβ).
When Aβ ≫ 1, the closed-loop gain approaches 1/β, which depends only on the passive feedback network.
A non-inverting op-amp samples the output voltage and mixes the feedback in series with the input. That is the voltage-series topology.
Negative feedback keeps the gain–bandwidth product constant, so bandwidth increases by (1 + Aβ) as gain falls by the same factor.

quiz.q: Excess loop phase shift can cause
quiz.why: If the loop phase shift grows too large at a frequency where loop gain is still at least 1, negative feedback becomes positive. The circuit can oscillate.

scenes.text: Every radio and microcontroller needs a stable oscillator.
An amplifier with positive feedback of exactly the right gain and phase sustains a sine wave.

steps.title: Barkhausen criterion
steps.body: |Aβ| = 1 and ∠Aβ = 0° (or 360°) at the oscillation frequency. In practice |Aβ| slightly > 1 to start, with amplitude limiting (non-linearity, AGC, lamp/thermistor).

steps.title: Common circuits
steps.body:
- **RC phase-shift (3 equal RC sections, inverting amp):** f = 1/(2πRC√6); β = 1/29 ⇒ amplifier gain ≥ 29.
- **Wien bridge (non-inverting amp):** f = 1/(2πRC); β = 1/3 ⇒ gain ≥ 3 (R_f = 2R₁).
- **LC (Colpitts):** f = 1/(2π√(L C_eq)), C_eq = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂). **Hartley:** L_eq = L₁ + L₂ (+2M).
- **Crystal:** very high Q, frequency stability ~ppm — used for clocks.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Wien bridge R = 10 kΩ, C = 16 nF: f = 1/(2π × 1.6×10⁻⁴) ≈ 995 Hz; set R_f = 2R₁ (slightly more for start-up).

**Example 2.** RC phase-shift R = 10 kΩ, C = 10 nF: f = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁴ × 2.449) ≈ 650 Hz; need |A| ≥ 29.

**Example 3.** Colpitts L = 100 µH, C₁ = C₂ = 2 nF: C_eq = 1 nF ⇒ f ≈ 503 kHz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using gain exactly = 3 (Wien) — oscillation won't start reliably; use slightly more with limiting.
- Forgetting √6 in the phase-shift formula.
- Adding Colpitts capacitances directly (they are in series).

activity.prompt: Wien-bridge oscillator: R = 1 kΩ, C = 0.159 µF. Frequency (Hz, ≈)?

quiz.why: The Barkhausen criterion for sustained oscillation is |Aβ| = 1 and a loop phase shift of 0° (or 360°).
The Wien bridge feedback network attenuates by 1/3 at the oscillation frequency. So the amplifier needs a gain of at least 3.
An RC phase-shift network attenuates by 1/29 at the oscillation frequency, so the amplifier gain must be at least 29.
A crystal has a very high Q, giving excellent frequency stability. The tuning range is small.

quiz.q: Colpitts C_eq for 1 nF and 1 nF
quiz.why: The two capacitors are in series: C_eq = (1 × 1)/(1 + 1) = 0.5 nF.

questions.why: An ideal op-amp has infinite input resistance, so it draws no input current.

questions.q: Inverting amp R₁ = 1 k, R_f = 47 k: gain
questions.why: The inverting gain is −R_f/R₁ = −47 k/1 k = −47.
Oscillators use positive feedback so the output sustains itself, with loop gain 1 and zero phase shift.

questions.q: Difference amp (R_f/R₁ = 5), V₂ = 1.2 V, V₁ = 1.0 V: V_o
questions.why: The difference amplifier output is (R_f/R₁)(V₂ − V₁) = 5 × (1.2 − 1.0) = 1 V.

questions.q: Integrator R = 100 kΩ, C = 1 µF, V_in = −0.5 V for 2 s: ΔV_o
Assertion (A): Negative feedback reduces gain sensitivity to component changes.  Reason (R): A_f ≈ 1/β depends only on passive components when loop gain is large.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: With high loop gain, A_f ≈ 1/β, set by passive components. So the gain hardly changes when the active device varies, i.e. lower sensitivity. R explains A.

questions.q: Phase-shift oscillator R = 6.5 kΩ, C = 10 nF: f
questions.why: For an RC phase-shift oscillator, f = 1/(2πRC√6) = 1/(2π × 6.5 k × 10 nF × 2.449) ≈ 1 kHz.

questions.q: Slew rate 1 V/µs, 5 V peak sine: max frequency
questions.why: The slew-rate limit is f_max = SR/(2πV_p) = 10⁶/(2π × 5) ≈ 31.8 kHz.

questions.q: Case: A Wien oscillator distorts badly (clipped sine). Most likely fix
questions.why: If the Wien oscillator's loop gain is too large, the output clips and distorts. Reduce the gain close to 3 and stabilise the amplitude.
options: reduce amplifier gain closer to 3 with amplitude stabilisation

questions.q: Inverting summer with R_f = 20 k, R₁ = 10 k (V₁ = 0.5), R₂ = 20 k (V₂ = 1)
Schmitt trigger thresholds for R₁ = 10 k, R₂ = 2.2 k, V_sat = ±13 V (β = R₂/(R₁ + R₂))
questions.why: β = R₂/(R₁ + R₂) = 2.2/12.2 ≈ 0.18. The thresholds are ±βV_sat = ±0.18 × 13 ≈ ±2.34 V.

questions.q: Op-amp GBW 3 MHz used at gain 150: bandwidth
Hartley L₁ = 1 mH, L₂ = 3 mH (M = 0), C = 1 nF: f

Solve mixed-unit problems under time
Diagnose weak units from mock results

scenes.text: Ananya has one evening to revise Analog Electronics.
She works through a one-page sheet, then tests herself.

steps.title: Diodes
steps.body:
- I = I_s(e^(V/ηV_T) − 1); r_d = ηV_T/I
- HW V_m/π, FW 2V_m/π; ripple 1.21/0.482; PIV V_m (HW, bridge), 2V_m (CT)
- V_r ≈ I/(2fC) full-wave; Zener I_R = I_Z + I_L

steps.title: Transistors
steps.body:
- I_C = βI_B, α = β/(β + 1); g_m = I_C/V_T; r_π = β/g_m
- Divider bias: V_TH, R_TH, I_B = (V_TH − 0.7)/(R_TH + (β + 1)R_E)
- CE A_v = −g_m R_C∥R_L; degenerated −R_C/(r_e + R_E)
- JFET I_D = I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)²; MOSFET sat I_D = ½k′(W/L)V_ov²; g_m = 2I_D/V_ov

steps.title: How to use this sheet
steps.body:
- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.
- For every formula, say its conditions of validity aloud (units, assumptions, ranges).
- Re-solve one worked example from the matching unit without looking.

steps.title: Common slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Mixing units (kN vs N, mm vs m, km/h vs m/s, degrees vs radians).
- Using a formula outside its assumptions.
- Dropping signs or factors such as 2, ½, π or √3.

quiz.why: For a full-wave bridge rectifier, V_dc = 2V_m/π = 2 × 15.7/3.14 = 10 V.

quiz.q: MOSFET V_ov = 0.5 V, I_D = 1 mA: g_m
quiz.why: For a MOSFET in saturation, g_m = 2I_D/V_ov = 2 × 1 mA/0.5 V = 4 mS.

quiz.why: A non-inverting amplifier has gain 1 + R_f/R₁ = 1 + 4 = 5.

quiz.why: The Wien oscillator frequency is f = 1/(2πRC) = 1/(2π × 10 k × 10 nF) ≈ 1.59 kHz.
