activity.prompt: Before the real exam
items: Formula sheet revised twice
One full mock done under time
Wrong answers re-solved without looking
Derivations listed in the syllabus practised once

quiz.why: A silicon diode starts to conduct at about 0.7 V.
A full-wave rectifier gives two pulses per cycle, so the ripple frequency is twice the supply frequency: 100 Hz.
A common-emitter stage inverts the signal, a 180° phase shift.
At V_GS = V_P, the JFET channel is pinched off and I_D = 0.

quiz.q: Mock 1: Inverting R₁ = 2k, R_f = 10k, V_in = −0.4 V
quiz.why: The inverting gain is −R_f/R₁ = −10k/2k = −5. With V_in = −0.4 V, V_o = −5 × (−0.4) = +2 V.
For sustained oscillation, the loop phase shift must be 0° (or 360°), so the feedback is positive.
A Schmitt trigger uses positive feedback, which gives two different switching thresholds (hysteresis).

questions.why: A Zener diode regulates in reverse breakdown, where its voltage is nearly constant.
A transistor amplifies in the active region. Cut-off and saturation are the OFF and ON switch states.
An op-amp voltage follower has a gain of 1.
In CMOS, one transistor is off in each static state, so static power is near zero. Power is used mostly when switching.
For 12 V RMS, V_m = 12√2 ≈ 16.97 V. Half-wave V_dc = V_m/π ≈ 5.4 V.

questions.q: JFET I_DSS = 10 mA, V_P = −5 V at V_GS = −2.5 V
Zener: V_s 18 V, V_Z 12 V, R 300 Ω, R_L 1.2 kΩ: I_Z
Assertion (A): Bypassing the emitter resistor increases CE voltage gain.  Reason (R): The bypass capacitor removes R_E from the AC path.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A bypass capacitor across R_E makes the emitter AC ground, removing R_E's feedback in the AC path. The gain therefore increases, so R explains A.

questions.q: MOSFET ½k′W/L = 1 mA/V², V_T = 0.7 V, V_GS = 1.7 V (sat): I_D
Filter C for 0.2 A, 50 Hz full-wave, 0.5 V ripple
questions.why: For a full-wave rectifier, C = I/(2fV_r) = 0.2/(2 × 50 × 0.5) = 0.004 F = 4000 µF.

questions.q: Divider bias: V_TH 2.2 V, R_TH 9 k, R_E 1 k, β 150: I_C
questions.why: I_B = (V_TH − V_BE)/(R_TH + (β + 1)R_E) = 1.5/(9k + 151k) ≈ 9.4 µA. Then I_C = βI_B ≈ 1.4 mA.

questions.q: Case: An ECG front end must amplify a 1 mV difference while rejecting 1 V of 50 Hz common-mode noise. Best circuit
questions.why: A tiny 1 mV signal must be amplified while large common-mode noise is rejected. An instrumentation amplifier has high CMRR and high input impedance.

questions.q: Phase-shift oscillator with C = 1 nF for f = 6.5 kHz: R
questions.why: For an RC phase-shift oscillator, f = 1/(2πRC√6). So R = 1/(2π × 6500 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.449) ≈ 10 kΩ.

questions.q: Unbypassed CS: g_m 4 mS, R_D 6 kΩ, R_S 500 Ω: A_v
questions.why: With an unbypassed source resistor, A_v = −g_mR_D/(1 + g_mR_S) = −(4 mS × 6 k)/(1 + 2) = −24/3 = −8.

questions.q: Self-bias JFET I_DSS 12 mA, V_P −4 V, R_S 500 Ω: I_D
questions.why: I = 12(1 − I/8)² ⇒ 3I² − 64I + 192 = 0 ⇒ I ≈ 3.61 mA (V_GS ≈ −1.8 V); the other root is invalid.

questions.q: Integrator R = 1 kΩ, C = 1 µF with a 1 kHz ±1 V square input: peak-to-peak triangle output
questions.why: The slope is V/(RC) = 1 V/1 ms = 1000 V/s. Over a half period of 0.5 ms, the output changes by 0.5 V, so the triangle is 0.5 V peak to peak.

questions.q: Dynamic power ratio when f doubles and V_DD falls from 1.2 to 0.9 V
questions.why: Dynamic power scales with f and V². Ratio = 2 × (0.9/1.2)² = 2 × 0.5625 = 1.125.

courses.title: Digital Electronics · Unit 1 · Number systems, codes and Boolean algebra
courses.summary: Binary, octal, hexadecimal conversions, signed numbers and complements, binary arithmetic, BCD, Gray and ASCII codes, Boolean laws and De Morgan's theorems, canonical SOP/POS forms and Karnaugh-map minimisation with don't-cares.
outcomes: Convert between number systems and do binary arithmetic
Represent signed numbers in 1's and 2's complement
Use BCD, Gray and parity codes
Simplify Boolean functions with algebra and K-maps
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: A web designer writes colours as #FF8800.
That is hexadecimal: FF = 255 red, 88 = 136 green, 00 blue.

steps.title: Positional systems
steps.body: Value = Σ dᵢ × baseⁱ. Decimal → binary: repeated division by 2 (integer part), repeated multiplication by 2 (fraction). Binary ↔ octal: group 3 bits; binary ↔ hex: group 4 bits from the binary point.

steps.title: Binary arithmetic
steps.body: Addition rules 0+0 = 0, 1+1 = 10 (carry). Subtraction via complements. Multiplication = shift and add.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading remainders top-down instead of bottom-up.
- Grouping bits from the wrong end.
- Using digits ≥ base (e.g. 8 in octal).

activity.prompt: Write a function to_bin(n) that converts a non-negative integer to a binary string WITHOUT using bin(); print to_bin(45).
activity.starter:
def to_bin(n):
    if n == 0:
        return '0'
    s = ''
    # repeated division by 2
    return s

print(to_bin(45))
activity.hint: Prepend n % 2 to the string and integer-divide n by 2 until it becomes 0.

quiz.why: Group the bits in 3s: 111 101 is 7 and 5, so the octal number is 75.
Group in 4s: 1011 = B and 1110 = E, so the hex is BE.

scenes.text: A digital thermometer stores −12 °C in 8 bits.
Computers store negatives in 2's complement so that the same adder does subtraction.

steps.title: Representations (n bits)
steps.body:
- Sign-magnitude: MSB sign; range −(2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1)…+(2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1); two zeros.
- 1's complement: invert all bits; two zeros.
- **2's complement:** invert and add 1; range −2ⁿ⁻¹…+(2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1); one zero. 8-bit: −128 to +127.
Subtraction A − B = A + (2's complement of B); discard the final carry.
Overflow: adding two numbers of the same sign gives a result of the opposite sign (carry into MSB ≠ carry out).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to add 1 for 2's complement.
- Treating the final carry as part of the answer.
- Missing overflow when signs agree.

activity.prompt: 8-bit 2's complement
activity.text: Range is ___ to +127, and −1 is written as ___ (8 bits).

quiz.why: To get the 2's complement of 0101, invert it to 1010 and add 1, giving 1011.
1's complement has two zeros, +0 (all 0s) and −0 (all 1s). That is its weakness.
Overflow can occur when adding two numbers of the same sign, if the result goes out of range and has the wrong sign. Numbers of opposite sign cannot overflow.
options: two numbers of the same sign

quiz.why: The leading 1 means negative. Invert 11110110 to get 00001001 and add 1 to get 00001010 = 10. So the value is −10.

lessons.title: Codes: BCD, Gray, excess-3, parity and ASCII

scenes.text: A volume knob's position sensor uses Gray code.
Only one bit changes between positions, so no glitchy readings.

steps.title: Codes
steps.body:
- **BCD (8421):** each decimal digit in 4 bits (1010–1111 invalid). 59 = 0101 1001.
- **Excess-3:** BCD + 0011 (self-complementing).
- **Gray code:** g = b ⊕ (b >> 1); successive values differ in one bit. Gray→binary: b_MSB = g_MSB, bᵢ = bᵢ₊₁ ⊕ gᵢ.
- **Parity:** even parity makes the total number of 1s even — detects single-bit errors.
- **ASCII:** 7-bit character code ('A' = 65 = 1000001, '0' = 48).
- Hamming code adds parity bits to correct single-bit errors.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Binary 1011 → Gray 1110 (1, 1⊕0, 0⊕1, 1⊕1).

**Example 2.** Gray 1101 → binary 1001 (1; 1⊕1 = 0; 0⊕0 = 0; 0⊕1 = 1).

**Example 3.** BCD addition 7 + 5: 0111 + 0101 = 1100 (> 9) ⇒ add 0110 ⇒ 1 0010 = 12 in BCD.

**Example 4.** Even-parity bit for 1011001: four 1s ⇒ parity 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Converting a whole number to binary instead of digit-by-digit for BCD.
- Forgetting the +6 correction in BCD addition.
- Gray→binary: XOR with the previous *binary* bit, not the previous Gray bit.

activity.prompt: Print the 4-bit Gray code of the number 11 (binary 1011) using g = b ^ (b >> 1), formatted as 4 bits.
activity.hint: Use the XOR operator ^ and right shift >>.

quiz.why: BCD encodes each decimal digit in 4 bits. 4 is 0100 and 7 is 0111, so 47 is 0100 0111.
Gray code: the first bit is the same, and each next bit is the XOR of adjacent binary bits. 0110 gives 0, 0⊕1 = 1, 1⊕1 = 0, 1⊕0 = 1, i.e. 0101.
A single parity bit detects any single-bit error, but cannot correct it and may miss 2-bit errors.

scenes.text: A chip designer cuts a 10-gate circuit to 4 gates — less area, power and delay.
Boolean algebra and K-maps find the simplest form.

steps.title: Laws
steps.body:
Identity A + 0 = A, A·1 = A; null A + 1 = 1, A·0 = 0; idempotent A + A = A; complement A + A′ = 1, AA′ = 0; absorption A + AB = A, A(A + B) = A; A + A′B = A + B; consensus AB + A′C + BC = AB + A′C.
**De Morgan:** (A + B)′ = A′B′, (AB)′ = A′ + B′. NAND and NOR are universal gates.

steps.title: Canonical forms and K-maps
steps.body: SOP minterms Σm(…), POS maxterms ΠM(…). K-map: Gray-ordered cells; group 1, 2, 4, 8 adjacent 1s (wrapping at edges), as large as possible; each group gives a product term; don't-cares (X) may be used to enlarge groups.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** F = AB + AB′ + A′B = A + A′B = A + B.

**Example 2.** F(A,B,C) = Σm(0, 2, 4, 5, 6): group m0, m2, m4, m6 (the C′ column pair, corners) ⇒ C′; group m4, m5 ⇒ AB′. F = C′ + AB′.

**Example 3.** F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(1, 3, 5, 7, 9) + d(11, 13, 15): quad m1, m3, m5, m7 ⇒ A′D; with don't-cares, the octet of all odd minterms ⇒ F = D.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing K-map columns in binary order (00, 01, 10, 11) instead of Gray (00, 01, 11, 10).
- Missing wrap-around groups at the edges and corners.
- Forcing don't-cares to be 1 when they don't help.

activity.prompt: Boolean identity → simplified form

quiz.why: NAND and NOR are universal gates. Any logic function can be built from either one alone.
A variable ANDed with its complement is always 0: A·A′ = 0.
K-map cells are arranged in Gray code order so that neighbouring cells differ by one bit. That allows grouping.

quiz.q: Group of 4 ones in a 4-variable K-map eliminates
quiz.why: A group of 4 = 2² cells eliminates 2 variables, since 2 of the variables change within the group.
The sum of all four minterms of a 2-variable function is 1.

questions.why: Gray of 1000: keep the first bit 1, then 1⊕0 = 1, 0⊕0 = 0, 0⊕0 = 0, giving 1100.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 2's complement allows subtraction with an adder.  Reason (R): A − B = A + (B′ + 1).
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: In 2's complement, A − B = A + (B′ + 1), so a single adder can do subtraction. That is what simplifies hardware.
Combine terms: A′B′C + A′BC = A′C, and A′B′C + AB′C = B′C. The expression simplifies to A′C + B′C.
8 + 7 = 15, which is above 9, so add 6 for BCD correction. 15 becomes 0001 0101 (decimal 15).
Minterms 1, 3, 5, 7 are all those where C = 1. So F = C.

questions.q: Case: 8-bit signed adder computes 01111111 + 00000001. Result and flag
questions.why: 127 + 1 = 128, which does not fit in 8-bit signed. The result 10000000 means −128, with overflow set.
Minterms 0, 2, 8, 10 are the four corners of the K-map. They share B = 0 and D = 0, so F = B′D′.

questions.q: Minimum NAND gates to implement XOR
questions.why: An XOR gate can be built from 4 two-input NAND gates, which is the classic minimum.
The minterms 0–7 cover the half of the map where A = 0, and the don't-care at 8 does not help. So F = A′.

courses.title: Digital Electronics · Unit 2 · Combinational circuits
courses.summary: Design procedure for combinational logic, half and full adders/subtractors, ripple-carry and carry-look-ahead adders, multiplexers and demultiplexers, decoders and encoders (including priority encoders), magnitude comparators, code converters and hazards.
outcomes: Design combinational circuits from truth tables
Build adders/subtractors and compare ripple vs look-ahead
Implement functions with MUX and decoders
Design comparators, encoders and code converters; recognise hazards
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Every CPU adds numbers billions of times per second.
It starts with a full adder: three input bits, sum and carry out.

steps.title: Half and full adder
steps.body:
Half adder: S = A ⊕ B, C = AB.
Full adder: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cᵢₙ, C_out = AB + Cᵢₙ(A ⊕ B) (= AB + BCᵢₙ + ACᵢₙ). Built from two half adders and an OR gate.
Half subtractor: D = A ⊕ B, Borrow = A′B. Full subtractor: D = A ⊕ B ⊕ Bᵢₙ, B_out = A′B + Bᵢₙ(A ⊕ B)′.

steps.title: Multi-bit adders
steps.body: Ripple-carry: n full adders chained — delay grows linearly with n. **Carry look-ahead:** generate Gᵢ = AᵢBᵢ, propagate Pᵢ = Aᵢ ⊕ Bᵢ; Cᵢ₊₁ = Gᵢ + PᵢCᵢ, expanded so all carries are computed in parallel (two-level logic). Adder–subtractor: XOR each B bit with a mode line M and set C₀ = M.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A = 1, B = 1, Cᵢₙ = 1: S = 1, C_out = 1.

**Example 2.** 4-bit ripple adder, each full adder carry delay 2 gate delays ⇒ ~8 gate delays for the carry chain.

**Example 3.** C₂ in look-ahead: C₂ = G₁ + P₁G₀ + P₁P₀C₀.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing C_out = A ⊕ B.
- Forgetting C₀ = 1 when subtracting with the 2's-complement method.
- Confusing propagate (XOR) with generate (AND).

activity.prompt: Write full_adder(a, b, cin) returning (sum, carry) using ^, & and |. Print full_adder(1, 1, 1) and full_adder(1, 0, 0).
activity.starter:
def full_adder(a, b, cin):
    s = 0
    c = 0
    return s, c

print(full_adder(1, 1, 1))
print(full_adder(1, 0, 0))
activity.solution:
def full_adder(a, b, cin):
    s = a ^ b ^ cin
    c = (a & b) | (cin & (a ^ b))
    return s, c

print(full_adder(1, 1, 1))
print(full_adder(1, 0, 0))
activity.hint: Sum is the XOR of all three; carry is ab OR cin(a XOR b).

quiz.why: A half adder's sum is A XOR B, and its carry is AB.
A full adder can be built from two half adders and an OR gate for the carry.
options: two half adders and an OR gate

quiz.why: A carry look-ahead adder computes all carries in parallel from the generate and propagate terms. It does not wait for a ripple.
A half subtractor's borrow is A′B: a borrow is needed when A = 0 and B = 1.
The propagate signal is P_i = A_i ⊕ B_i. It shows that a carry in is passed on.

scenes.text: Several sensors share one ADC channel through a selector.
A multiplexer picks one of many inputs using select lines.

steps.title: MUX and DEMUX
steps.body:
2ⁿ:1 MUX has n select lines: Y = Σ mᵢ Iᵢ (minterm of selects × data). 4:1 MUX: Y = S₁′S₀′I₀ + S₁′S₀I₁ + S₁S₀′I₂ + S₁S₀I₃.
DEMUX 1:2ⁿ routes one input to the selected output (a decoder with enable).
Trees: 8:1 from two 4:1 + one 2:1.

steps.title: Function implementation with a MUX
steps.body: An n-variable function can be built with a 2ⁿ⁻¹:1 MUX: use n − 1 variables as selects; each data input is 0, 1, the last variable or its complement (from the implementation table).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** F(A,B,C) = Σm(1, 2, 6, 7) with a 4:1 MUX, selects A, B: AB = 00 → m0, m1 ⇒ I₀ = C; 01 → m2, m3 ⇒ I₁ = C′; 10 → m4, m5 ⇒ I₂ = 0; 11 → m6, m7 ⇒ I₃ = 1.

**Example 2.** 16:1 MUX needs 4 select lines; from 4:1 MUXes: five devices (four + one).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong order of select lines (MSB vs LSB).
- Forgetting the enable input on cascaded devices.
- Counting data inputs wrongly (2ⁿ for n selects).

activity.prompt: Number of select lines for a 32:1 multiplexer?

quiz.why: An 8:1 MUX has 8 inputs, so it needs log₂ 8 = 3 select lines.
A demultiplexer sends one input to one of several outputs. It is equivalent to a decoder with an enable input used as data.
A 16:1 MUX built from 4:1 MUXes needs 4 in the first layer and 1 in the second: 5.

quiz.q: MUX implementing a 4-variable function needs at least
quiz.why: A 4-variable function can be implemented with an 8:1 MUX (n − 1 select lines), using the 4th variable on the data inputs.
For the MUX table, both minterms of the pair (6 and 7) are 1 for I₃, so I₃ = 1 regardless of the last variable.

scenes.text: A digital clock turns BCD digits into lit segments.
A decoder maps each code to exactly one active output.

steps.title: Decoders and encoders
steps.body:
n:2ⁿ decoder: each output is one minterm — with an OR gate it implements any SOP function. Enable inputs allow cascading (two 3:8 → one 4:16).
Encoder 2ⁿ:n: output is the code of the active input. **Priority encoder** gives the highest-priority active input and a valid bit.
BCD-to-7-segment decoder drives displays (common anode or cathode).

steps.title: Magnitude comparator
steps.body: 1-bit: (A > B) = AB′, (A < B) = A′B, (A = B) = (A ⊕ B)′. Multi-bit: equality xᵢ = (Aᵢ ⊕ Bᵢ)′; A = B ⇔ all xᵢ; A > B = A₃B₃′ + x₃A₂B₂′ + x₃x₂A₁B₁′ + …

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Full adder with a 3:8 decoder: S = Σm(1, 2, 4, 7), C = Σm(3, 5, 6, 7) — two OR gates on decoder outputs.

**Example 2.** 4:2 priority encoder with inputs D₃ (highest)…D₀: D₂ = 1, D₁ = 1 ⇒ output 10 (D₂ wins), valid = 1.

**Example 3.** Compare A = 1011, B = 1001: x₃ = 1, x₂ = 1, A₁B₁′ = 1 ⇒ A > B.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring active-low outputs (common in IC decoders).
- Ordinary encoders give wrong codes for multiple active inputs (need priority).
- Forgetting the valid/enable line.

activity.prompt: Which block?

items.text: Gives code of the active input
Outputs A > B, A = B, A < B

quiz.why: A priority encoder handles several active inputs at once, by outputting the code of the highest-priority one.
A 1-bit equality output is high when A = B. That is XNOR, (A ⊕ B)′.
A 4:16 decoder can be made from two 3:8 decoders, using the extra input bit as an enable for each.
A decoder gives all minterms. An OR gate over the minterms of a function implements any sum-of-products function.

scenes.text: A display flickers a wrong digit for a few nanoseconds when inputs change.
That is a hazard — caused by unequal path delays — and can be removed with redundant terms.

steps.title: Code converters
steps.body:
Design steps: truth table (inputs → outputs, unused codes as don't-cares), K-map each output, implement.
- BCD → excess-3: add 0011.
- Binary → Gray: gᵢ = bᵢ₊₁ ⊕ bᵢ (XOR chain).
- Gray → binary: bᵢ = bᵢ₊₁ ⊕ gᵢ (cascaded XORs).

steps.title: Hazards
steps.body:
Static-1 hazard: output should stay 1 but glitches to 0 during an input change (SOP with adjacent groups not overlapping). Fix: add the consensus term covering the transition.
Static-0 hazard: dual for POS. Dynamic hazard: multiple transitions when one is expected (multi-level circuits).
Example: F = AB + A′C has a static-1 hazard when B = C = 1 and A changes; add BC.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 4-bit binary → Gray: g₃ = b₃, g₂ = b₃ ⊕ b₂, g₁ = b₂ ⊕ b₁, g₀ = b₁ ⊕ b₀ (3 XOR gates).

**Example 2.** BCD to excess-3 output E₃ = B₃ + B₂B₀ + B₂B₁ (using don't-cares 10–15).

**Example 3.** Hazard-free F = AB + A′C + BC.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving unused BCD combinations as 0 instead of don't-cares (bigger circuits).
- Assuming minimal SOP is always hazard-free.
- Cascading XORs in the wrong direction for Gray → binary.

activity.prompt: Combinational design procedure
items: State the problem and assign input/output variables
Write the truth table (mark don't-cares)
Simplify each output with a K-map
Draw the logic diagram
Check for hazards and verify by simulation

quiz.why: For a 4-bit binary-to-Gray conversion, the MSB passes through and the other 3 bits each need one XOR, so 3 XOR gates.
A static-1 hazard is removed by adding the consensus (redundant) term, which covers the transition between two product terms.

quiz.q: Unused BCD codes are treated as
quiz.why: Unused BCD codes (10–15) never occur, so they are treated as don't-cares to simplify the logic.
Hazards come from unequal propagation delays through different paths. They cause brief glitches.
For F = AB + A′C, adding the consensus term BC gives a hazard-free form: AB + A′C + BC.

questions.why: A full adder has 3 inputs: A, B and the carry in.

questions.q: MUX with 2 select lines has data inputs
questions.why: A multiplexer with 2 select lines can choose among 2² = 4 data inputs.
Each decoder output is high for exactly one input combination, so each is a minterm.

questions.q: Carry out of a full adder for 1, 0, 1
questions.why: Carry out = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B). For A = 1, B = 0, Cin = 1: 0 + 1·1 = 1.

questions.q: Gray code is obtained from binary using
questions.why: Gray code is obtained by XORing adjacent bits of the binary number.

questions.q: 2:4 decoder with enable can act as
questions.why: A 2:4 decoder with an enable input can act as a 1:4 demultiplexer, with the data on the enable and the select on the address inputs.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Carry look-ahead adders reduce delay compared with ripple-carry.  Reason (R): They compute every carry from G and P terms in two levels of logic.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: A look-ahead adder computes every carry in parallel from G and P in two logic levels, so no ripple delay builds up. So R explains A.

questions.q: Implement F(A,B,C) = Σm(0, 3, 5, 6) with 3:8 decoder: OR of outputs
questions.why: A decoder gives one output per minterm. To implement F = Σm(0, 3, 5, 6), OR the outputs 0, 3, 5 and 6.
A = 0110 and B = 0111 differ only in the last bit, where A has 0 and B has 1. So A < B.

questions.q: 8:1 MUX implementing F(A,B,C,D) uses selects A, B, C. If minterms 6 and 7 are 1 (ABC = 011), I₃ =
questions.why: With the selects ABC = 011, minterms 6 and 7 are both 1 for D = 0 and D = 1. So I₃ = 1.

questions.q: Case: A 4-bit adder must work at 1 GHz but ripple delay is 1.6 ns. Best fix
questions.why: Ripple carry delay is too long at 1 GHz. A carry look-ahead adder computes carries in parallel, shortening the critical path.

questions.q: Ripple adder of 16 bits with 2-gate-delay carry per bit: worst-case carry delay
questions.why: The carry ripples through 16 bits at 2 gate delays each: 16 × 2 = 32 gate delays.

questions.q: Number of 2:1 MUXes to build a 16:1 MUX
questions.why: A 16:1 MUX tree of 2:1 MUXes needs 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15.

questions.q: Priority encoder (D₇ highest) with D₅ and D₂ high outputs
questions.why: The priority encoder outputs the code of the highest active input. D₅ is higher than D₂, so the output is 5 = 101.

questions.q: Static hazard in F = AB′ + BC occurs when A = C = 1 and B changes; fix by adding
questions.why: For F = AB′ + BC with A = C = 1, B changes and a static-1 hazard occurs. Adding the consensus term AC covers the transition.

courses.title: Digital Electronics · Unit 3 · Sequential circuits
courses.summary: Latches and flip-flops (SR, D, JK, T, master–slave and edge-triggered), characteristic and excitation tables, timing parameters, shift registers, asynchronous and synchronous counters, and design of synchronous sequential circuits (Moore/Mealy state machines).
outcomes: Explain latch and flip-flop operation and timing
Use characteristic and excitation tables
Design registers and synchronous/asynchronous counters
Design simple Moore and Mealy state machines
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

scenes.text: Every register in a CPU is a row of flip-flops.
They store one bit and change only on a clock edge.

steps.title: Latches
steps.body: SR latch (cross-coupled NOR): S = 1 sets Q = 1, R = 1 resets, S = R = 0 holds, S = R = 1 invalid (NOR). Gated D latch: Q follows D while enable is high (transparent) — a problem in synchronous systems.

steps.title: Flip-flops and characteristic equations
steps.body:
Edge-triggered (sample at the clock edge):
- D: Q⁺ = D
- JK: Q⁺ = JQ′ + K′Q (J = K = 1 toggles)
- T: Q⁺ = T ⊕ Q
- SR: Q⁺ = S + R′Q (SR = 0)
Master–slave JK removes the race-around problem of level-triggered JK.
Timing: setup time t_su, hold time t_h, clock-to-Q t_cq. Max clock f_max = 1/(t_cq + t_logic + t_su).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** JK with J = 1, K = 1, Q = 0 ⇒ after edge Q = 1 (toggle).

**Example 2.** T flip-flop with T = 1 halves the clock frequency (divide-by-2).

**Example 3.** t_cq = 1 ns, logic 6 ns, t_su = 1 ns ⇒ f_max = 125 MHz.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a latch as edge-triggered.
- Violating setup/hold times (metastability).
- Forgetting that S = R = 1 is forbidden for SR.

activity.prompt: Flip-flop → characteristic equation

quiz.why: A JK flip-flop with J = K = 1 toggles on every clock edge.
A D latch is level-sensitive. It is transparent (follows D) when its enable is high.
Race-around happens in a level-triggered JK with J = K = 1. It is avoided by master–slave or edge-triggered flip-flops.
The minimum clock period is t_cq + logic + t_su = 2 + 8 + 2 = 12 ns. So f_max = 1/12 ns ≈ 83 MHz.

quiz.q: T flip-flop with T = 1 acts as
quiz.why: A T flip-flop with T = 1 toggles each clock edge, so its output frequency is half of the clock: divide by 2.

scenes.text: A lab only has JK flip-flops but the design needs a D flip-flop.
Excitation tables let you convert one type into another.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** JK → D: J = D, K = D′.

**Example 2.** JK → T: J = K = T.

**Example 3.** D → T: D = T ⊕ Q.

**Example 4.** SR → JK: S = JQ′, R = KQ.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Write the required next state from the target flip-flop's characteristic table, look up the excitation of the available flip-flop, K-map each input in terms of the target inputs and Q.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the characteristic table where the excitation table is required.
- Ignoring don't-cares in JK excitation (they simplify a lot).
- Forgetting Q as a K-map variable.

activity.prompt: Flip-flop conversions
activity.text: JK to T: J = K = ___ ; D to T: D = T ⊕ ___.

quiz.why: For a JK flip-flop 0 → 1, J must be 1 and K can be anything (X): J = 1, K = X.
A JK flip-flop acts as a D flip-flop with J = D and K = D′.
The excitation table gives the inputs needed to make a given state transition. The characteristic table gives the next state for given inputs.
For an SR flip-flop 1 → 0, S = 0 and R = 1 (reset).

scenes.text: A watch divides a 32 768 Hz crystal down to 1 Hz.
A chain of 15 toggle stages (÷2¹⁵) does exactly that.

steps.title: Registers
steps.body: Shift registers: SISO, SIPO, PISO, PIPO; universal shift register (shift left/right, parallel load). Ring counter (n flip-flops, n states, one-hot). Johnson (twisted-ring) counter: 2n states.

steps.title: Counters
steps.body:
**Asynchronous (ripple):** each flip-flop clocked by the previous output; simple but delays accumulate (glitches in decoding). Mod-N: reset at count N using a NAND on the outputs.
**Synchronous:** all flip-flops share the clock; T inputs: T₀ = 1, T₁ = Q₀, T₂ = Q₀Q₁, … (up counter). Design arbitrary sequences with excitation tables and K-maps.
Number of flip-flops for mod-N: smallest n with 2ⁿ ≥ N.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 32 768 Hz ÷ 2¹⁵ = 1 Hz ⇒ 15 flip-flops.

**Example 2.** Mod-10 ripple counter: 4 flip-flops, reset when Q₃Q₁ = 1 (count 1010).

**Example 3.** 3-bit synchronous up counter with T flip-flops: T₀ = 1, T₁ = Q₀, T₂ = Q₁Q₀.

**Example 4.** 4-bit Johnson counter: 8 states 0000 → 1000 → 1100 → 1110 → 1111 → 0111 → 0011 → 0001.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Decoding ripple-counter outputs without accounting for glitches.
- Choosing too few flip-flops for mod-N.
- Mixing ring (n states) and Johnson (2n states).

activity.prompt: Flip-flops needed for a mod-50 counter?

quiz.why: A 4-bit ring counter circulates a single 1, so it has 4 states.
An n-bit Johnson counter has 2n states. For 4 bits, 8 states.
A synchronous counter clocks all flip-flops together. So the delays do not add up as they do in a ripple counter.
A mod-6 counter has 6 states, which need 3 flip-flops since 2³ = 8 ≥ 6.
SIPO means Serial-In, Parallel-Out. It converts a serial stream to parallel outputs.

scenes.text: A digital lock opens only when the bits 1-0-1 arrive in order.
A finite-state machine remembers how much of the pattern it has seen.

steps.title: Moore vs Mealy
steps.body:
Moore: outputs depend only on present state (output changes on clock edge; may need more states). Mealy: outputs depend on state and input (fewer states, output can change between edges).
Design steps: state diagram → state table → state minimisation → state assignment → excitation table → K-maps → circuit.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1 (Mealy 101 detector, overlapping).** States: S0 (nothing), S1 (got 1), S2 (got 10).
S0: x = 1 → S1/0; x = 0 → S0/0. S1: x = 0 → S2/0; x = 1 → S1/0. S2: x = 1 → S1/1 (detected, overlap keeps the final 1); x = 0 → S0/0. Two flip-flops suffice.

**Example 2.** A Moore version needs a fourth state S3 (detected) whose output is 1.

**Example 3.** Input 1 0 1 0 1: Mealy outputs 0 0 1 0 1 (detections at the 3rd and 5th bits).

steps.title: State assignment and minimisation
steps.body: n flip-flops encode up to 2ⁿ states; equivalent states (same outputs, same next-state classes) can be merged; good assignments place related states at adjacent codes to simplify logic; one-hot encoding (one flip-flop per state) is popular in FPGAs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting overlap handling in sequence detectors.
- Moore outputs drawn on transitions (they belong to states).
- Leaving unused states without a safe next state (lock-up).

activity.prompt: Simulate the overlapping Mealy '101' detector: for input '10101' print the output string.
activity.starter:
def detect(bits):
    state = 0  # 0: none, 1: got 1, 2: got 10
    out = ''
    for b in bits:
        # update state and append '1' or '0'
        pass
    return out

print(detect('10101'))
activity.hint: Track three states; output 1 only when in 'got 10' and the input is 1.

quiz.why: In a Moore machine, the outputs depend only on the present state.
Mealy outputs depend on the state and input, so a Mealy machine usually needs fewer states than the equivalent Moore machine.
5 states need ⌈log₂ 5⌉ = 3 flip-flops with binary encoding (2³ = 8 ≥ 5).
One-hot encoding uses one flip-flop per state, with exactly one set at a time.
Unused states should lead back to a valid state, so the machine cannot get stuck (lock-up) after a glitch.

questions.why: A D flip-flop's next state equals the input D: Q⁺ = D.
In an asynchronous (ripple) counter, each flip-flop is clocked by the output of the previous one.

questions.q: Clock 1 MHz into a 4-bit ripple counter: MSB frequency
questions.why: A 4-bit counter divides by 2⁴ = 16 at the MSB. So 1 MHz/16 = 62.5 kHz.

questions.q: Invalid input of NOR SR latch
questions.why: For a NOR SR latch, S = R = 1 is invalid, since it forces both outputs to 0, and releasing both gives an unpredictable result.
A T flip-flop toggles when T = 1. Using a D flip-flop, D = T ⊕ Q.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Ripple counters can produce decoding glitches.  Reason (R): Flip-flops change one after another, so outputs pass through intermediate states.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: In a ripple counter, flip-flops change one after another. The outputs pass through brief intermediate states, which cause glitches when decoded. So R explains A.
A mod-12 counter needs 4 flip-flops, since 2⁴ = 16 ≥ 12.
In a synchronous up counter, the 4th bit toggles only when all lower bits are 1. So T₃ = Q₀Q₁Q₂.

questions.q: f_max: t_cq 0.5 ns, logic 3 ns, t_su 0.5 ns
questions.why: T_min = t_cq + logic + t_su = 0.5 + 3 + 0.5 = 4 ns. So f_max = 250 MHz.

questions.q: Case: A 10 MHz clock must produce a 1 kHz tick. Ideal divide ratio and minimum flip-flops (binary counter mod-N)
questions.why: 10 MHz/1 kHz = 10,000. A binary counter needs ⌈log₂ 10,000⌉ = 14 flip-flops (2¹⁴ = 16,384 ≥ 10,000).
For a JK flip-flop staying at 1 (1 → 1), J can be anything and K must be 0: J = X, K = 0.

questions.q: Johnson counter 3-bit state after 001 (shift right, Q₀ = complement of Q₂ fed back) starting 000 → 100 → 110 → 111 → 011 → ?
questions.why: The Johnson sequence is 000, 100, 110, 111, 011, 001, then back to 000. So after 011 comes 001.
For input 1101101, the pattern 101 is completed at positions 4 and 7. So the output is 0001001.

questions.q: Minimum states for a Moore '11' detector (overlapping)
questions.why: A Moore detector for 11 (overlapping) needs states for: no progress, seen one 1, and seen 11 (output 1). That is 3 states.

courses.title: Digital Electronics · Unit 4 · Logic families, memories and data converters
courses.summary: Logic family parameters (fan-out, noise margin, propagation delay, power, figure of merit), TTL and CMOS basics, open-collector/tri-state outputs, semiconductor memories (ROM, PROM, EPROM, flash, SRAM, DRAM) and memory expansion, PLDs, and DAC/ADC types and specifications.
outcomes: Compare logic families using standard parameters
Explain tri-state and open-drain outputs
Classify memories and design memory expansion
Compute DAC/ADC resolution and conversion times
courses.note: topic order may differ by edition

lessons.title: Logic family parameters, TTL and CMOS

scenes.text: A 5 V sensor board must talk to a 3.3 V microcontroller.
Logic levels and noise margins decide whether they understand each other.

steps.title: Parameters
steps.body:
- V_OH(min), V_OL(max), V_IH(min), V_IL(max); noise margins NM_H = V_OH − V_IH, NM_L = V_IL − V_OL
- Fan-out = min(I_OH/I_IH, I_OL/I_IL)
- Propagation delay t_pd = (t_PHL + t_PLH)/2
- Power dissipation; speed–power product (figure of merit) = t_pd × P

steps.title: Families
steps.body:
**TTL (74 series):** BJT-based, 5 V, V_OH 2.4, V_OL 0.4, V_IH 2.0, V_IL 0.8 ⇒ NM 0.4 V; totem-pole output.
**CMOS (74HC, 4000):** very low static power, wide supply range, high fan-out (capacitive limit), NM ≈ 30–45% of V_DD.
**ECL:** fastest classic family, non-saturating, high power.
Open-collector/open-drain outputs allow wired-AND and level shifting (need pull-up). Tri-state outputs (0, 1, high-Z) allow bus sharing.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** TTL: NM_H = 2.4 − 2.0 = 0.4 V; NM_L = 0.8 − 0.4 = 0.4 V.

**Example 2.** Fan-out with I_OL = 16 mA, I_IL = 1.6 mA; I_OH = 400 µA, I_IH = 40 µA ⇒ 10.

**Example 3.** t_pd = 10 ns, P = 10 mW ⇒ speed–power product 100 pJ.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Driving a 3.3 V input with 5 V without checking tolerance.
- Leaving CMOS inputs floating.
- Connecting totem-pole outputs together (bus contention).

activity.prompt: I_OL = 8 mA, I_IL = 0.4 mA, I_OH = 0.4 mA, I_IH = 20 µA. Fan-out?

quiz.why: The high noise margin is NM_H = V_OH − V_IH.
CMOS has the lowest static power, as one transistor is always off, so almost no current flows when not switching.
A tri-state output has a third state, high impedance (Hi-Z), where it is effectively disconnected. This lets many drivers share a bus.
Open-collector outputs cannot pull the line high themselves, so they need an external pull-up resistor.
The speed–power product is delay times power, which has units of energy (joules, e.g. pJ).

scenes.text: Your phone keeps photos in flash memory and runs apps from DRAM.
Each memory type trades speed, density, cost and volatility.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **ROM** (mask), **PROM** (one-time), **EPROM** (UV erase), **EEPROM** (electrical, byte-wise), **Flash** (block erase; NAND for storage, NOR for code) — non-volatile.
- **SRAM:** 6-transistor cell (latch), fast, no refresh, used for caches.
- **DRAM:** 1 transistor + 1 capacitor, dense, needs periodic refresh (charge leaks), main memory.
Volatile = loses data without power (SRAM, DRAM).

steps.title: Organisation and expansion
steps.body: A memory with k address lines and n data lines stores 2ᵏ × n bits. **Word-size expansion:** chips in parallel share address lines (e.g. two 1K×4 → 1K×8). **Capacity expansion:** extra address lines feed a decoder that selects chips (e.g. four 1K×8 → 4K×8 with a 2:4 decoder).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 64K × 8 memory: 16 address lines, 8 data lines, 512 Kbit.

**Example 2.** Build 8K × 16 from 2K × 8 chips: (8/2) × (16/8) = 8 chips; 11 address lines to each chip, 2 more to a 2:4 decoder.

**Example 3.** A 4 Gbit DRAM refreshed every 64 ms across 8192 rows ⇒ one row refresh every ~7.8 µs.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing bits and bytes in capacity.
- Thinking flash is volatile.
- Forgetting the decoder when expanding capacity.

activity.prompt: Volatile or non-volatile?

quiz.why: 1M words = 2²⁰, so 20 address lines are needed.
A DRAM cell stores charge on a capacitor, which leaks away. It must be refreshed periodically.
An SRAM cell is a latch made of about 6 transistors. A DRAM cell uses 1 transistor and 1 capacitor.
Flash memory is erased in blocks, but written in smaller units (pages).

scenes.text: A startup prototypes its motor controller logic on an FPGA before making a chip.
Programmable devices let hardware be 'rewritten' like software.

steps.title: PLD families
steps.body:
- **PROM:** fixed AND (decoder), programmable OR — implements any truth table.
- **PLA:** programmable AND and OR arrays — shares product terms.
- **PAL:** programmable AND, fixed OR — faster, simpler.
- **CPLD:** several PAL-like blocks with interconnect, non-volatile.
- **FPGA:** array of look-up tables (LUTs), flip-flops, routing, block RAM, DSP slices — usually SRAM-configured (reloaded at power-up). Designs are written in HDLs (Verilog/VHDL).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A 4-input LUT stores 16 bits — it can implement any 4-variable function.

**Example 2.** Full adder in a PLA: S needs 4 product terms, C needs 3 (AB, AC_in, BC_in) — 7 terms; with sharing none overlap, so 7 AND terms + 2 OR outputs.

**Example 3.** 3-input, 2-output function in a PROM: 8 × 2 bits.

steps.title: Choosing
steps.body: Small glue logic → CPLD; large/fast parallel designs → FPGA; high-volume products → ASIC (after FPGA prototyping).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing PLA (both arrays programmable) with PAL (only AND programmable).
- Forgetting FPGAs usually need configuration memory at power-up.
- Thinking LUT size limits the total function size (LUTs are combined).

activity.prompt: Device → programmable arrays

quiz.why: A PAL has a programmable AND array and a fixed OR array. A PROM is the reverse.
A k-input LUT stores the truth table, so it can implement any function of k variables.
SRAM-based FPGAs lose their configuration at power-off, so they load it from external non-volatile memory at power-up.
HDL stands for hardware description language, e.g. Verilog or VHDL.
In a PROM, the AND array is a fixed decoder producing all minterms, and the OR array is programmable.

scenes.text: Your phone's ADC records your voice; its DAC plays music back.
Resolution and speed decide the quality.

steps.title: DAC
steps.body:
Output V_o = V_ref × (D/2ⁿ) (or D × step). Resolution (step) = V_ref/2ⁿ (or full-scale/(2ⁿ − 1)). Types: binary-weighted resistor (needs wide resistor range), **R-2R ladder** (only two resistor values — preferred).
Specs: resolution, accuracy, settling time, linearity, monotonicity.

steps.title: ADC
steps.body:
Quantisation step q = V_FS/2ⁿ; quantisation error ±q/2; ideal SNR ≈ 6.02n + 1.76 dB.
Types: **flash** (2ⁿ − 1 comparators, fastest), **successive approximation (SAR)** (n clock cycles, common in microcontrollers), **dual-slope** (slow, accurate, rejects noise — multimeters), **counter/ramp** (up to 2ⁿ cycles), **sigma-delta** (high resolution audio).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** 8-bit DAC, V_ref = 5.12 V: step = 20 mV; D = 100 ⇒ 2.0 V.

**Example 2.** 10-bit SAR ADC at 1 MHz clock: conversion ≈ 10 µs (plus overhead).

**Example 3.** Flash ADC 6-bit needs 63 comparators.

**Example 4.** 12-bit ADC, 3.3 V full scale: q = 0.806 mV; SNR ≈ 74 dB.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 2ⁿ − 1 vs 2ⁿ inconsistently (state the convention).
- Thinking more bits always mean faster conversion.
- Ignoring the need for an anti-aliasing filter before the ADC.

activity.prompt: 8-bit DAC with V_ref = 2.56 V (step = Vref/256). Output for D = 200 (V)?

quiz.why: A flash ADC compares the input with all thresholds in parallel using many comparators. It is the fastest type.

quiz.q: Comparators in an n-bit flash ADC
quiz.why: An n-bit flash ADC has 2ⁿ levels, needing 2ⁿ − 1 threshold comparators.
A successive-approximation (SAR) ADC does a binary search, deciding one bit per clock. So it takes n clock cycles for n bits.
An R-2R ladder DAC needs only two resistor values, R and 2R, which is easier to match than binary-weighted resistors.

questions.why: DRAM is volatile: it loses its data when power is removed. ROM, EPROM and Flash keep data.
ECL is the fastest of the classic families, because its transistors do not saturate.
A DAC converts a digital code to an analog voltage or current.

questions.q: Step of a 10-bit DAC with V_ref = 10.24 V
questions.why: A 10-bit DAC has 1024 steps. Step size = V_ref/1024 = 10.24/1024 = 10 mV.
A memory with 256K = 2¹⁸ locations needs 18 address lines, because n lines select 2ⁿ locations. The 16 is the data width (bits per word), which does not affect the address count.
The low-level noise margin is NM_L = V_IL − V_OL = 0.8 − 0.4 = 0.4 V. It is how much noise a LOW output can tolerate before the next gate misreads it as HIGH.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Dual-slope ADCs are used in digital multimeters.  Reason (R): They are accurate and average out noise, though slow.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both statements are true. A dual-slope ADC integrates the input over a fixed time, so noise averages out and accuracy is high, but conversion is slow. That is exactly why it suits slowly changing readings in digital multimeters, so R explains A.
Chips needed = (total bits)/(bits per chip) = (16K×8)/(4K×4) = (16/4) rows × (8/4) columns = 4 × 2 = 8. Two chips side by side widen the word to 8 bits, and four such pairs extend the depth to 16K.

questions.q: 12-bit SAR at 2 MHz clock: approx. conversion time
questions.why: A SAR ADC needs one clock cycle per bit, so 12 bits take 12 cycles. With a 2 MHz clock (0.5 µs per cycle), time = 12/2 MHz = 6 µs.
A flash ADC compares the input with every threshold in parallel. An n-bit converter has 2ⁿ levels and so needs 2ⁿ − 1 comparators: 2⁸ − 1 = 255.

questions.q: Case: A 5 V open-drain sensor output must feed a 3.3 V MCU. Correct approach
questions.why: An open-drain output only pulls the line low and relies on a pull-up resistor for the high level. Pulling up to 3.3 V keeps the high level within the MCU's safe range, so the open-drain line does the level shifting. Connecting a 5 V totem-pole output directly could overstress the 3.3 V input.
options: pull-up to 3.3 V on the open-drain line

questions.q: Quantisation error of an 8-bit ADC with 5.12 V full scale
questions.why: Step size q = 5.12 V/2⁸ = 5.12/256 = 20 mV. Quantisation error is at most half a step, ±q/2 = ±10 mV.

questions.q: Speed–power product: t_pd 4 ns, P 2 mW
questions.why: The speed–power product is propagation delay × power: 4 ns × 2 mW = 4×10⁻⁹ × 2×10⁻³ = 8×10⁻¹² J = 8 pJ. Mixing up the prefixes is what gives wrong answers like nJ.

questions.q: DRAM with 8192 rows refreshed every 64 ms: interval between row refreshes
questions.why: All 8192 rows must be refreshed within 64 ms, so one row is refreshed every 64 ms/8192 ≈ 7.8 µs. Dividing in ms and forgetting to convert is the usual slip.

questions.q: Bits of ADC needed for ≈ 74 dB ideal SNR
questions.why: Ideal SNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB, so N = (74 − 1.76)/6.02 ≈ 12 bits. Each extra bit adds about 6 dB of SNR.

scenes.text: Ananya has one evening to revise Digital Electronics.
She works through a one-page sheet, then tests herself.

steps.title: Numbers and codes
steps.body:
- 2's complement = invert + 1; n-bit range −2ⁿ⁻¹…2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1
- Overflow: same-sign inputs, opposite-sign result
- Gray g = b ⊕ (b >> 1); BCD +6 correction
- De Morgan; A + A′B = A + B; consensus

steps.title: Combinational
steps.body:
- HA: S = A ⊕ B, C = AB; FA: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ C, C = AB + C(A ⊕ B)
- CLA: G = AB, P = A ⊕ B, Cᵢ₊₁ = Gᵢ + PᵢCᵢ
- 2ⁿ:1 MUX n selects; decoder + OR = SOP

steps.title: How to use this sheet
steps.body:
- Cover the right-hand side of each formula and try to recall it.
- For every formula, say its conditions of validity aloud (units, assumptions, ranges).
- Re-solve one worked example from the matching unit without looking.

steps.title: Common slips to avoid
steps.body:
- Mixing units (kN vs N, mm vs m, km/h vs m/s, degrees vs radians).
- Using a formula outside its assumptions.
- Dropping signs or factors such as 2, ½, π or √3.

quiz.why: 7F in hex = 7×16 + 15 = 112 + 15 = 127. F stands for 15 in the units place.
A 64:1 MUX picks one of 64 inputs, so it needs n select lines with 2ⁿ = 64. Since 2⁶ = 64, n = 6.
Factor out A: AB + AB′ = A(B + B′) = A·1 = A. B + B′ is always 1, so the result does not depend on B.

steps.body:

- Ring n states; Johnson 2n; mod-N needs ⌈log₂N⌉ FFs

steps.title: How to use this sheet

steps.title: Common slips to avoid

statements.s: PAL has a programmable OR array.

quiz.why: A mod-20 counter needs 20 distinct states. With n flip-flops you get 2ⁿ states, and 2⁵ = 32 ≥ 20 while 2⁴ = 16 is too few, so 5 flip-flops.
A flash ADC needs 2ⁿ − 1 comparators. For 4 bits: 2⁴ − 1 = 15. Sixteen is the number of output codes, not comparators.
The JK characteristic equation is Q⁺ = JQ′ + K′Q. With J = K = 1 this becomes Q′, so the output toggles on every clock. J = K = 0 holds the state.

scenes.text: Set a 30-minute timer and attempt every question before checking.
Read each explanation, even for the ones you got right.

activity.prompt: Before the real exam
items: Formula sheet revised twice
One full mock done under time
Wrong answers re-solved without looking
Derivations listed in the syllabus practised once

quiz.why: De Morgan's law: the complement of an OR is the AND of the complements, so (A + B)′ = A′B′.
+5 is 0101. Invert to get 1010, then add 1 to get 1011, which is −5 in 4-bit two's complement. Check: 1011 = −8 + 3 = −5.
A half adder adds two bits. The carry is 1 only when both inputs are 1, so Carry = AB (AND). The sum is A ⊕ B.
A 3:8 decoder turns 3 input bits into one of 2³ = 8 output lines, and exactly one is active for each input code.
A D flip-flop copies its D input to the output at the clock edge, so the next state Q⁺ = D, whatever the present Q.
A DRAM cell stores a bit as charge on a capacitor, switched by a single transistor, so it is 1 transistor + 1 capacitor. A 6-transistor cell is SRAM, and a floating gate is used in flash/EPROM.
An n-bit DAC has 2ⁿ input codes. For 8 bits that is 2⁸ = 256 codes (levels). The number of intervals between them would be 255.

questions.why: Octal is base 8, so each digit can be only 0 to 7. The digits 8 and 9 do not exist in octal.
NAND is a universal gate: NOT, AND and OR can all be built from NAND gates alone (for example, tying the inputs together gives NOT). So any logic function can be made with NANDs only.
A ring counter circulates a single 1 through its flip-flops, so n flip-flops give only n states. Five flip-flops give 5 states, not 2⁵ = 32.
A flash ADC uses one comparator per level, all working in parallel, so it converts in one step. That makes it the fastest, but it needs many comparators.
Group the bits in fours from the right: 110110 = 0011 0110 = 3 and 6, so 36 in hex.
Convert Gray to binary: the first bit is copied (0). Each next binary bit = previous binary bit ⊕ next Gray bit: 0⊕1 = 1, 1⊕1 = 0, 0⊕1 = 1. This gives 0101.
A′B + AB′ + AB = A′B + A(B′ + B) = A′B + A = A + B, using the identity A + A′B = A + B. The only input giving 0 is A = B = 0, which is OR.
The select lines 10 form the binary number 2, so the MUX routes input I₂ to the output.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A Mealy machine can respond to an input within the same clock cycle.  Reason (R): Its outputs depend directly on the present input as well as the state.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.why: Both statements are true. In a Mealy machine the output is a function of both state and current input, so a change at the input can change the output straight away, within the same clock cycle. So R explains A.
The minterms 5, 7, 13, 15 are 0101, 0111, 1101, 1111. B = 1 and D = 1 in all of them while A and C change, so the 4-cell group simplifies to BD.
11111100 is −4 in two's complement and 00000101 is +5. Their sum is −4 + 5 = 1 = 00000001, with no overflow because the operands have opposite signs.
Chips needed = (4K×8)/(1K×4) = 4 (depth) × 2 (width) = 8. Two chips give an 8-bit word and four such pairs give 4K locations.

questions.q: f_max with t_cq 2 ns, logic 15 ns, t_su 3 ns
questions.why: The minimum clock period is t_cq + logic + t_su = 2 + 15 + 3 = 20 ns, so f_max = 1/20 ns = 50 MHz.

questions.q: 10-bit ADC, 5 V full scale: code for 2.5 V (V/q, q = 5/1024)
questions.why: Step q = 5/1024 ≈ 0.00488 V. The code for 2.5 V is 2.5/0.00488 = 512, which is exactly half of the 1024 codes.

questions.q: Case: A keypad sends codes when several keys are pressed together. Best encoder
questions.why: A priority encoder gives a valid code even when several inputs are active by choosing the highest-priority one. A simple encoder gives wrong outputs for multiple active inputs.

questions.q: Synchronous mod-8 up counter with JK: J₂ = K₂ =
questions.why: In a synchronous counter, a bit toggles only when all lower bits are 1. So the most significant flip-flop has J₂ = K₂ = Q₁Q₀ (toggle when both lower bits are 1).
An 8:1 MUX tree uses 4 MUXes in the first stage, 2 in the second and 1 in the last: 4 + 2 + 1 = 7 MUXes of 2:1.

questions.q: Fan-out: I_OL 20 mA / I_IL 0.5 mA; I_OH 1 mA / I_IH 50 µA
questions.why: Fan-out is the smaller of the two limits. Low state: 20/0.5 = 40. High state: 1 mA/50 µA = 20. The smaller one limits the gate, so fan-out = 20.
Ideal SNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB. For N = 10: 60.2 + 1.76 ≈ 62 dB. The 74 dB figure belongs to a 12-bit ADC.

questions.q: Hazard-free SOP for F = A′C′ + AB
questions.why: F = A′C′ + AB has a hazard when A changes with B = 1 and C = 0. Adding the consensus term BC′ covers that transition, giving A′C′ + AB + BC′ without changing the function.

lessons.title: Digital communication model, sampling and quantization

scenes.text: When you speak into a phone, the microphone voltage is sampled 8000 times per second and each sample is rounded to one of 256 levels. Only numbers travel to the other end.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: System model
steps.body: Source → source encoder (sampling, quantization, compression) → channel encoder (adds redundancy) → modulator → **channel** (noise, fading) → demodulator → channel decoder → source decoder → destination. Advantages of digital: regenerative repeaters (noise does not accumulate), error control, encryption, TDM and flexible mixing of voice/data. Cost: larger bandwidth and synchronisation needs.

steps.title: Quantization
steps.body: A uniform quantizer with n bits has L = 2ⁿ levels over (−V_max, V_max): **step Δ = 2V_max/L**. Error uniformly distributed in (−Δ/2, Δ/2): **noise power N_q = Δ²/12**. For a full-scale sinusoid signal power V_max²/2: **SQNR = 1.5 L² = (6.02n + 1.76) dB**. Each extra bit adds 6 dB. For general signals SQNR = 6.02n + 4.77 − 20log(V_max/σ_x).

steps.title: Example 2 — bits needed
steps.body: Required SQNR 60 dB for a full-scale sine: n ≥ (60 − 1.76)/6.02 = 9.67 → **10 bits**.

steps.title: Example 3 — error bound
steps.body: Max error Δ/2 = 19.5 mV, i.e. 0.39 % of full scale.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using V_max instead of 2V_max for the total range in Δ.
- Applying 6.02n+1.76 to speech with low average level — SQNR is worse.

activity.prompt: SQNR (dB) for an 8-bit uniform quantizer with a full-scale sinusoid.

lessons.title: Pulse-code modulation, companding and TDM hierarchies

story.title: Why a phone call is exactly 64 kb/s

scenes.text: 8 000 samples/s × 8 bits = 64 000 b/s — the DS0 channel that every digital telephone network is built from.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: PCM chain
steps.body: Anti-alias LPF → sample & hold → quantizer → encoder (n bits/sample). **Bit rate R_b = n f_s**; transmission bandwidth for binary PCM ≥ R_b/2 (Nyquist), commonly ≈ R_b (NRZ) or n f_m (≥ nW). Speech has a high peak-to-average ratio: non-uniform quantization via **companding**: compress → uniform quantizer → expand. **µ-law** (North America/Japan, µ = 255): y = ln(1+µ|x|)/ln(1+µ)·sgn x; **A-law** (India, Europe, A = 87.6) with a linear segment for small x. 8-bit companded PCM gives SQNR ≈ 38 dB over a wide dynamic range.

steps.title: Hierarchies
steps.body: E1 (used in India): 32 time slots × 8 bits per 125 µs = **2.048 Mb/s** (30 voice + sync + signalling). T1: 24 × 8 + 1 framing bit = 193 bits per 125 µs = **1.544 Mb/s**. Higher orders multiplex further (E2 8.448 Mb/s, E3 34.368 Mb/s).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: Audio: 20 kHz, f_s = 44.1 kHz, 16 bits, 2 channels: R_b = 44.1×16×2 = **1.411 Mb/s**.

steps.title: Example 2 — bandwidth
steps.body: Telephone PCM: R_b = 64 kb/s; Nyquist BW 32 kHz; practical NRZ ≈ 64 kHz. Compare with 4 kHz analog: BW expansion = 8–16×.

steps.title: Example 3 — E1
steps.body: 256 bits per 125 µs = 2.048 Mb/s; 30 channels × 64 kb/s = 1.92 Mb/s; remaining 128 kb/s is framing and signalling.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting the 1 framing bit in T1 (193, not 192).

activity.prompt: CD stereo bit rate (Mb/s): f_s = 44.1 kHz, 16 bits, 2 channels.

options: uniform SQNR for weak and strong signals

scenes.text: Instead of sending the value, send only whether the signal went up or down: a staircase tracks the signal with one bit per sample.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: DM
steps.body: At each sample, transmit 1 if x(nT) > staircase estimate, else 0; the staircase steps ±Δ. Receiver: integrator (accumulator) + LPF. Errors: **granular noise** (Δ too large; noise power ≈ Δ²/3 over band) and **slope overload** (Δ too small). No overload if **Δ/T_s ≥ max|dx/dt|**; for a sinusoid: **Δ ≥ 2πf_m A_m/f_s**. Adaptive DM varies Δ; DPCM quantizes the prediction error x[n] − x̂[n] with fewer bits (e.g. 4 bits instead of 8 → 32 kb/s ADPCM speech, ITU G.726).

steps.title: Example 2 — bit rate
steps.body: DM at 64 kb/s for speech vs PCM 64 kb/s: DM needs f_s ≈ 64 kHz, 1 bit — comparable quality to 7-bit PCM only at much higher f_s.

steps.title: Example 3 — DPCM gain
steps.body: Prediction gain G_p = σ_x²/σ_e² = 10 → 10 dB ≈ 1.7 bits saved; so 8-bit PCM quality in ≈ 6.3 bits.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Increasing Δ cures slope overload but worsens granular noise — they trade off.

activity.prompt: Minimum step size Δ (V) to avoid slope overload: A_m=1 V, f_m=1 kHz, f_s=32 kHz.

Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Rounding instead of flooring in a mid-rise quantizer index.

Serialise and add framing

courses.title: Unit 2 · Baseband transmission, ISI and equalization
courses.summary: Line codes and their spectra, inter-symbol interference, Nyquist criteria, raised-cosine pulses, eye diagrams and zero-forcing equalization.
outcomes: Encode bit streams in NRZ, RZ, AMI, Manchester and HDB3
Compute bandwidth of line codes
Apply the Nyquist criterion with raised-cosine pulses
Design a zero-forcing equalizer

scenes.text: Classic 10 Mb/s Ethernet encoded each bit as a mid-bit transition so the receiver could recover the clock even for long strings of identical bits.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Desirable properties
steps.body: Self-clocking (enough transitions), no DC component, narrow bandwidth, error-detection capability, immunity to polarity inversion, transparency (any data pattern).

steps.title: Common codes
steps.body:
- **Unipolar NRZ:** 1 → +A, 0 → 0; has DC; long runs lose clock.
- **Polar NRZ-L:** ±A; best noise margin (distance 2A) but DC for unbalanced data.
- **RZ:** pulse returns to zero mid-bit; bandwidth doubles.
- **AMI (bipolar):** 0 → 0, 1 → alternating +A/−A; no DC, error detection by violations; long 0-runs lose clock.
- **HDB3:** AMI with substitution of four zeros by 000V or B00V to keep clock and DC balance (E1).
- **Manchester (biphase):** 1 → high-to-low, 0 → low-to-high (IEEE 802.3); transition each bit; no DC; bandwidth 2×.
- **Differential Manchester, MLT-3, 4B/5B, 8B/10B** in fast links.

steps.title: Example 1 — encoding
steps.body: Bits 1 0 1 1 0 0 1. **AMI:** +A, 0, −A, +A, 0, 0, −A. **Manchester (IEEE 802.3: 0 = low→high, 1 = high→low):** HL LH HL HL LH LH HL.

steps.title: Example 2 — HDB3
steps.body: 1 0 0 0 0 → +1 0 0 0 +V (V has the same polarity as the previous pulse, violating AMI so the receiver can find it). Next substitution alternates between 000V and B00V for DC balance.

steps.title: Example 3 — DC
steps.body: Unipolar NRZ with equal 1s and 0s has average A/2 → DC component A/2 blocked by transformers.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Believing AMI solves clock recovery for all-zero data; it needs HDB3/B8ZS.

activity.prompt: Which line codes have no DC component (for any data)?

lessons.title: Lab: Power spectral density and bandwidth of line codes

story.title: How much spectrum does my bit stream need?

scenes.text: A telecom engineer must fit 2.048 Mb/s E1 into a copper pair. The line code decides the bandwidth.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Results
steps.body:
For random equiprobable bits at rate R_b = 1/T_b with rectangular pulses:
- Polar NRZ: S(f) = A²T_b sinc²(fT_b); null-to-null BW = **R_b**.
- Unipolar NRZ: same continuous part plus a DC delta at f = 0.
- Polar RZ (50 %): BW (null) = **2R_b**.
- Manchester: BW (null) = **2R_b**, no DC, zero at f=0.
- AMI: BW = R_b, spectrum zero at DC.
Spectral efficiency (bits/s/Hz) ≈ R_b/BW. Practical bound from Nyquist: BW_min = R_b/2 for ideal binary signalling.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: R_b = 2.048 Mb/s with HDB3 (AMI-type): null BW = **2.048 MHz**; main-lobe power 90 %.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body: 10 Mb/s Manchester: null BW = 20 MHz; first null at 20 MHz; 10BASE-T cable bandwidth ≥ 10 MHz is practical because most power lies below 10 MHz.

steps.title: Example 3 — power
steps.body: Polar NRZ with A = 1 V, 1 Ω: average power 1 W; unipolar NRZ (0/A): 0.5A² = 0.5 W for equiprobable bits, i.e. 3 dB less energy distance than polar for the same peak.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using null-to-null BW as the minimum possible bandwidth; ideal minimum is R_b/2.

activity.prompt: Null-to-null bandwidth (MHz) of 10 Mb/s Manchester.

lessons.title: Inter-symbol interference and the Nyquist criterion

scenes.text: When a band-limited channel spreads each pulse, the tail of one symbol lands on the next one. If the tails do not vanish at the sampling instants, bits are corrupted even with no noise.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Nyquist criterion
steps.body: Received y(t) = Σ a_k p(t − kT) + noise. Sample at t = mT: y_m = a_m p(0) + Σ_{k≠m} a_k p((m−k)T). **Zero ISI** if p(kT) = 1 for k = 0 and 0 otherwise. In frequency: **Σ_n P(f − n/T) = T** (a constant). Minimum bandwidth solution: ideal rectangular P(f) of width 1/T → p(t) = sinc(t/T); **B_min = R_s/2** (Nyquist rate: R_s = 2B symbols/s). Sinc is non-causal with slowly decaying tails (1/t) → sensitive to timing jitter.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: Channel B = 4 kHz (ideal): max symbol rate 8000 sym/s; binary → 8 kb/s; with 16 levels (4 bits/symbol) → 32 kb/s.

steps.title: Example 2 — ISI
steps.body: Pulse samples p(0)=1, p(T)=0.3, p(−T)=0.1. Sequence a = +1, −1, +1: at the centre symbol: y = 1×(−1) + 0.3×(+1)(preceding) + 0.1×(+1)(following) → −0.6. Peak distortion D = 0.4 → noise margin reduced from 1 to 0.6.

steps.title: Example 3 — worst case
steps.body: Peak distortion = Σ_{k≠0}|p(kT)|; here 0.4; eye opening 1 − 0.4 = 0.6.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Confusing bit rate with symbol rate: R_b = R_s log₂M.

activity.prompt: Eye opening (normalised) for p(0)=1, p(±T)=0.3 and 0.1.

scenes.text: A modem sends a test pulse and measures the received samples: 0.1 before the main tap and 0.3 after. It then adjusts a 3-tap FIR filter to cancel them.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Zero-forcing
steps.body: Equalizer taps c_{−1}, c_0, c_1; combined response y_k = Σ_n c_n p_{k−n}. Force y_{−1} = 0, y_0 = 1, y_1 = 0. Limitations: noise enhancement; finite taps leave residual ISI. MMSE (Wiener) and decision-feedback equalizers balance noise; adaptive LMS: c ← c + μ e x.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Assuming a ZF equalizer removes all ISI; with a finite number of taps it only zeros the chosen samples.

activity.prompt: Centre tap c_0 of the 3-tap ZF equalizer (4 decimals).

questions.q: R_b=1 Mb/s polar NRZ null BW
α=1 RC BW for R_s=2 ksym/s

courses.title: Unit 4 · Digital passband modulation and spread spectrum
courses.summary: ASK, FSK, PSK, DPSK, QPSK, M-ary PSK and QAM, MSK, bandwidth efficiency, error performance and direct-sequence spread spectrum.
outcomes: Write signal sets and constellations for ASK/FSK/PSK/QAM
Compute bandwidth and spectral efficiency
Compare BER of coherent and non-coherent schemes
Compute DSSS processing gain and jamming margin

scenes.text: 3G, Wi-Fi and satellite TV all send bits as carrier phase changes: more bits per hertz than FSK with the same energy.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: BPSK
steps.body: s_{1,2}(t) = ±√(2E_b/T_b) cos ω_ct; one basis function; **P_e = Q(√(2E_b/N0))**; BW (null-to-null, rect pulses) = 2R_b. Coherent detection needs carrier recovery (Costas loop / squaring loop with 180° ambiguity → differential encoding).

steps.title: DPSK & QPSK
steps.body: **DPSK:** information in phase change between bits; no carrier recovery; **P_e = ½e^{−E_b/N0}**. **QPSK:** 2 bits/symbol; s = √(E_s/T_s)cos(ω_ct + (2k+1)π/4); I and Q carry independent BPSK streams of energy E_b; **P_e (per bit) = Q(√(2E_b/N0))** (same as BPSK); symbol rate R_b/2, null BW = R_b — **twice the spectral efficiency**. OQPSK offsets Q by T_b/2 to limit phase jumps to 90°; π/4-QPSK avoids zero crossings (used in IS-136, TETRA). Gray mapping gives one bit error per symbol error.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: R_b = 10 Mb/s QPSK: R_s = 5 Msym/s; null BW 10 MHz (rect) or with RC α = 0.35: 5×1.35 = **6.75 MHz**.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Quoting QPSK symbol error where bit error is meant: P_b ≈ P_s/2 with Gray coding.

activity.prompt: Symbol rate (Msym/s) of a 10 Mb/s QPSK link.

quiz.q: QPSK BER vs BPSK at same Eb/N0

lessons.title: Lab: Compare schemes — bandwidth, efficiency and BER

story.title: Choosing a modulation for a link

scenes.text: Given 1 Mb/s, 1 MHz of spectrum and 10 dB E_b/N0, which schemes fit?
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Table (null-to-null BW, rect pulses, R_b = 1 Mb/s)
steps.body:
| Scheme | BW | Eff (b/s/Hz) | P_e at Eb/N0=10 dB |
|---|---|---|---|
| BPSK | 2 MHz | 0.5 | 3.9×10⁻⁶ |
| QPSK | 1 MHz | 1 | 3.9×10⁻⁶ |
| 16-QAM | 0.5 MHz | 2 | ≈1.8×10⁻³ |
| Coherent BFSK | ≈ 1.5–3 MHz | ~0.4 | 7.8×10⁻⁴ |
| DPSK | 2 MHz | 0.5 | 2.3×10⁻⁵ |
With ideal Nyquist filtering efficiencies double (BPSK 1, QPSK 2, 16-QAM 4).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: 1 MHz available: QPSK (rect) fits exactly; BPSK needs 2 MHz or RC shaping with α=0 (impractical).

steps.title: Example 2 — Shannon limit
steps.body: Spectral efficiency 2 b/s/Hz needs E_b/N0 ≥ (2² − 1)/2 = 1.5 → 1.76 dB at the Shannon limit; QPSK at 10⁻⁵ needs 9.6 dB, a gap of ~8 dB closed by coding.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Comparing schemes at equal E_s/N0 rather than equal E_b/N0.

activity.prompt: Which schemes have constant envelope?

story.title: Hiding a signal below the noise

scenes.text: GPS signals arrive below the thermal noise floor; they can be recovered because each bit is spread by a long pseudo-noise code and de-spread at the receiver.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: DSSS
steps.body: Data (R_b) is multiplied by a PN chip sequence at R_c ≫ R_b; BW ≈ 2R_c; **processing gain G_p = R_c/R_b = BW_ss/BW_data**. At the receiver, de-spreading collapses the signal back and spreads interference. **Jamming margin = G_p(dB) − (E_b/N0)_req − L_sys**. Benefits: interference rejection, low probability of intercept, multipath resolution, CDMA multiple access. PN sequences: m-sequences of length 2ⁿ−1, balance and autocorrelation properties (e.g. length 127, 1023 for GPS C/A).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: R_c = 11 Mchip/s, R_b = 1 Mb/s: G_p = 11 = **10.4 dB**.

steps.title: Example 2 — GPS C/A
steps.body: Chip rate 1.023 Mchip/s, data 50 b/s: G_p = 20460 = 43.1 dB; code length 1023 repeats each 1 ms (20 code periods per data bit).

steps.title: Example 3 — margin
steps.body: G_p = 30 dB, (E_b/N0)_req = 10 dB, L = 2 dB: jamming margin = 18 dB — the jammer can be 18 dB stronger than the signal.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking spreading increases capacity; it trades bandwidth for interference rejection.

activity.prompt: Processing gain (dB) for 11 Mchip/s and 1 Mb/s (3 decimals if needed).

questions.q: G_p for R_c=100 Mcps, R_b=100 kb/s

courses.title: Unit 5 · Information theory and error-control coding
courses.summary: Entropy, source coding (Shannon–Fano, Huffman), mutual information, channel capacity and Shannon limit, linear block codes, Hamming and cyclic codes with CRC, convolutional codes and Viterbi decoding.
outcomes: Compute entropy, code efficiency and redundancy
Build Huffman codes
Compute channel capacity (BSC, AWGN)
Encode and decode Hamming, CRC and convolutional codes

scenes.text: If some letters are far more common than others, give short codes to the common ones. Morse code did it by hand with E = one dot; Huffman proved the best way.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Information measures
steps.body:
Self-information I(x) = −log₂ P(x) bits. **Entropy H(X) = −Σ P_i log₂P_i** (bits/symbol); 0 ≤ H ≤ log₂M, maximum for equiprobable symbols. Source-coding theorem: average code length L̄ ≥ H. **Efficiency η = H/L̄**, redundancy 1 − η. Prefix (instantaneous) codes satisfy Kraft: Σ2^{−l_i} ≤ 1.

**Huffman:** repeatedly merge the two least probable symbols, assigning 0/1; optimal prefix code.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using ln instead of log₂.
- Thinking Huffman codes are unique — ties give different but equally optimal codes.

activity.prompt: Entropy (bits) of a binary source with P(1)=0.1 (3 decimals).

story.title: The ultimate speed limit of a phone line

scenes.text: Dial-up modems reached 56 kb/s on a 3 kHz channel and no further: Shannon's formula says why.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Capacity
steps.body: I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y). Capacity C = max I. **BSC with crossover p:** C = 1 − H_b(p). **AWGN (band-limited): C = B log₂(1 + S/N) bits/s**, N = N0B. As B → ∞, C → (S/N0)log₂e = 1.44 S/N0. Reliable communication is possible at any R < C with suitable coding; impossible for R > C. **Shannon limit:** E_b/N0 ≥ ln2 = 0.693 = **−1.59 dB** (η → 0); in general E_b/N0 ≥ (2^η − 1)/η.

steps.title: Example 3 — required SNR
steps.body: Target 1 Mb/s in 200 kHz: S/N = 2^5 − 1 = 31 → 14.9 dB.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using SNR in dB inside the logarithm without converting to a ratio.

activity.prompt: Capacity (kb/s) for B = 3 kHz, S/N = 30 dB.

lessons.title: Lab: Linear block codes and Hamming (7,4)

story.title: Fixing a flipped bit in memory

scenes.text: ECC memory in servers uses Hamming-type codes: a single flipped bit is detected and corrected automatically.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body: (n,k) linear code: codeword c = mG; parity check H with cHᵀ = 0; syndrome s = rHᵀ. Minimum distance d_min = smallest nonzero codeword weight; detects d_min − 1 errors, corrects ⌊(d_min−1)/2⌋. **Hamming (7,4): d_min = 3**, rate 4/7, corrects 1 error. Positions 1–7: p₁ p₂ d₁ p₃ d₂ d₃ d₄ with p₁ = d₁⊕d₂⊕d₄ (covers 1,3,5,7), p₂ = d₁⊕d₃⊕d₄ (2,3,6,7), p₃ = d₂⊕d₃⊕d₄ (4,5,6,7). The syndrome (s₃s₂s₁) read as binary is the error position.

steps.title: Example — encode
steps.body: Data d₁d₂d₃d₄ = 1011: p₁ = 1⊕0⊕1 = 0; p₂ = 1⊕1⊕1 = 1; p₃ = 0⊕1⊕1 = 0. Codeword (positions 1–7): **0 1 1 0 0 1 1**.

steps.title: Example — decode
steps.body: Received 0 1 1 0 1 1 1 (error in position 5). Check 1 (pos 1,3,5,7) = 0⊕1⊕1⊕1 = 1; check 2 (2,3,6,7) = 1⊕1⊕1⊕1 = 0; check 3 (4,5,6,7) = 0⊕1⊕1⊕1 = 1. Syndrome s₃s₂s₁ = 101 = 5 → flip bit 5 → 0110011 ✓; data = 1011.

steps.title: Example — bounds
steps.body: Hamming bound for single-error correction: 2^{n−k} ≥ n + 1: for (7,4): 8 ≥ 8 — a perfect code.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Two errors in a Hamming codeword are mis-corrected (to a third error).

activity.prompt: Hamming (7,4): the minimum distance is ___ and the code can correct ___ error(s).

story.title: Every Ethernet frame ends in a CRC

scenes.text: The last 4 bytes of an Ethernet frame are a 32-bit CRC; any corrupted frame is dropped. The CRC is computed by polynomial division over GF(2).
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: A cyclic code is generated by g(x) of degree n−k. Systematic encoding: append n−k zeros to the message (multiply by x^{n−k}), divide by g(x) with XOR, append the remainder. Receiver divides the whole word; remainder 0 → no detected error. CRC-4 (x⁴ + x + 1 = 10011), CRC-16-CCITT (x¹⁶+x¹²+x⁵+1), CRC-32 (Ethernet). A CRC with r bits detects all burst errors ≤ r bits and all odd numbers of errors if g contains (x+1).

steps.title: Example — CRC-4
steps.body: Message 1101011011, g = 10011. Append 0000: 11010110110000. Long division (XOR): final remainder **1110**. Transmitted word: 1101011011 1110.

steps.title: Verify
steps.body: Dividing 11010110111110 by 10011 gives remainder 0000 ✓. Flip one bit and the remainder becomes nonzero.

steps.title: Burst detection
steps.body: CRC-32 detects all bursts up to 32 bits and 1 − 2⁻³² ≈ 99.99999998 % of longer bursts.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting to append the zeros before dividing — you would be dividing the message itself.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of CRC encoding.
items: Choose the generator polynomial g(x) of degree r
Append r zeros to the message
Divide (modulo-2) the extended message by g(x)
Take the r-bit remainder
Replace the appended zeros by the remainder and transmit

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — convolutional encoding and Viterbi decoding

story.title: How a deep-space probe talks home

scenes.text: Voyager-era links used rate-½ convolutional codes with Viterbi decoding to gain several dB over uncoded transmission.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Encoder
steps.body: Rate-½, constraint length K = 3 encoder with generators g₁ = 111 (7₈), g₂ = 101 (5₈): for input u and previous bits (u₁, u₂): out₁ = u⊕u₁⊕u₂; out₂ = u⊕u₂. The state is (u₁,u₂) — 4 states. **Viterbi:** at each step keep for every state the survivor path with the smallest accumulated Hamming (hard) or Euclidean (soft) metric; trace back from the best final state. Free distance d_free = 5 for this code; coding gain ≈ 3–5 dB at BER 10⁻⁵ (soft decisions ≈ 2 dB better than hard).

steps.title: Rate and bandwidth
steps.body: Rate ½ doubles the coded bits: 1 Mb/s data → 2 Mb/s coded; BPSK bandwidth doubles unless a higher-order modulation is used.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting to flush the encoder with K−1 zeros so the trellis terminates in state 00.

activity.prompt: Number of coded bits produced for a 1011 message followed by 2 flush zeros (rate ½).

quiz.q: Output for first input 1 from state 00

courses.title: Unit 6 · Revision, practicals & exam
courses.summary: Formula sheet, standard digital-communication laboratory experiments (PCM, delta modulation, line coding, ASK/FSK/PSK/QPSK, error coding), viva questions, exam-style problems and a 20-question exam.
outcomes: Recall all key digital-communication formulas
Plan and record standard laboratory experiments
Answer viva questions
Solve exam-style problems

scenes.text: Digital communication has about thirty formulas that cover almost every question.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Waveform coding
steps.body:
- Δ = 2V_max/2ⁿ; N_q = Δ²/12; SQNR = 6.02n + 1.76 dB (full-scale sine).
- R_b = n f_s; E1 = 2.048 Mb/s; T1 = 1.544 Mb/s; voice 64 kb/s.
- DM: no slope overload if Δ ≥ 2πf_mA_m/f_s.

steps.title: Baseband
steps.body:
- Nyquist: R_s ≤ 2B; raised cosine B = (1+α)R_s/2.
- Null BW: polar NRZ R_b; RZ and Manchester 2R_b.
- ZF equalizer: solve y_k = Σc_np_{k−n} = δ_k.

steps.title: Detection & modulation
steps.body:
- Matched filter: h = s(T−t); SNR_max = 2E/N0.
- BPSK/QPSK: Q(√(2E_b/N0)); coherent FSK/unipolar: Q(√(E_b/N0)); DPSK ½e^{−E_b/N0}; non-coherent FSK ½e^{−E_b/2N0}.
- BW: BPSK 2R_b; QPSK R_b; M-ary 2R_b/log₂M. G_p = R_c/R_b.

steps.title: Information & coding
steps.body:
- H = −ΣP log₂P; η = H/L̄.
- C = B log₂(1+S/N); Shannon limit −1.59 dB.
- Hamming (7,4) d=3; t = ⌊(d−1)/2⌋; CRC = remainder of m·x^r / g.

steps.title: Top slips
steps.body: 1) dB vs ratio. 2) R_b vs R_s. 3) Peak vs average E_b. 4) ln vs log₂. 5) Forgetting appended zeros in CRC. 6) Forgetting 1 framing bit in T1.

activity.prompt: Match scheme and BER formula.

scenes.text: On a trainer kit, sample a 1 kHz sine, encode with an ADC, transmit serially, and decode with a DAC.

DM: set step size; observe slope overload when amplitude/frequency increase; note granular noise. Line codes: apply data pattern 1011 0010; observe NRZ, RZ, AMI, Manchester on the CRO and measure the transition density.

lessons.title: Lab: ASK, FSK, PSK and QPSK modulation/demodulation

scenes.text: Generate each scheme from the same data stream and observe the waveform, spectrum and constellation.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) ASK: switch a 100 kHz carrier by data (analog switch). 2) FSK: VCO or two oscillators + switch; tones 100 and 200 kHz at 10 kb/s. 3) BPSK: balanced modulator with ±1 data; observe 180° phase jumps. 4) QPSK: split data into I and Q; carriers 90° apart; observe constellation on X-Y mode. 5) Demodulate: envelope detector (ASK), PLL/discriminator (FSK), coherent detector with carrier recovery (BPSK), I/Q correlators (QPSK). 6) Measure bandwidth on the spectrum analyser.

steps.title: Observation table
steps.body:
| Scheme | Rb (kb/s) | Measured null BW (kHz) | Theory |
|---|---|---|---|
| ASK | 10 | 20 | 2Rb |
| BPSK | 10 | 20 | 2Rb |
| QPSK | 10 | 10 | Rb |
| FSK (Sunde) | 10 | ≈ 30 | 3Rb |

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body: Lock carrier phase for coherent detection; trigger on the data clock; avoid overdriving the balanced modulator.

activity.prompt: Order the QPSK modulator steps.
items: Serial bits are split into odd and even streams
Each stream is converted to ±1 levels
I stream multiplies cos(ω_ct)
Q stream multiplies sin(ω_ct)
Sum the two products to get the QPSK wave

lessons.title: Lab: Error-control coding experiments and viva

scenes.text: Implement a Hamming (7,4) encoder/decoder and a CRC checker on hardware or software, inject single and double errors and observe.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Encode 16 data words with Hamming (7,4). 2) Inject a single-bit error in each position and verify syndrome = position. 3) Inject two errors and show mis-correction. 4) CRC-4: compute remainder for 1101011011 → 1110; flip a bit; observe nonzero remainder. 5) Count BER with and without coding on a noisy channel (e.g. noise generator at different SNR).

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body: Count enough bits (≥ 100 errors) for a trustworthy BER.

activity.prompt: Viva questions with answers.

items.q: Why does digital communication tolerate noise better than analog?
items.a: Regenerative repeaters make decisions and re-create clean pulses, so noise does not accumulate.

items.q: What is ISI and how is it removed?
items.a: Overlap of pulse tails at sampling instants; Nyquist pulse shaping and equalization remove it.

items.q: Why is Eb/N0 used?
items.a: It normalises SNR by bit rate, allowing fair comparison between schemes.

items.q: What does a matched filter maximise?
items.a: The output SNR at the sampling instant, equal to 2E/N0.

items.q: Why does QPSK double spectral efficiency?
items.a: Two orthogonal BPSK signals (I and Q) share the same bandwidth.

scenes.text: Typical paper: PCM numericals, line codes, Nyquist, BER, entropy/Huffman, Hamming/CRC.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Q2 (8)

lessons.title: Coulomb's law and electric field intensity

scenes.text: A photocopier drum charges toner particles with small charges; the tiny forces between charges pick up and place toner exactly where the image is.
Those forces are given by Coulomb's law, the starting point of electromagnetics.

steps.title: Law and field
steps.body: **F = Q1Q2 / (4πε0R²) a_R**, with ε0 = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m, 1/(4πε0) ≈ 9×10⁹ N·m²/C². Field intensity: **E = F/Q** (V/m). Point charge: E = Q/(4πε0R²) a_R. Superposition holds for many charges; for continuous distributions integrate: line (ρL), surface (ρS), volume (ρV).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body: Two 1 µC charges are 3 cm apart in air. F = 9×10⁹ × (10⁻⁶)² / (0.03)² = 9×10⁹×10⁻¹²/9×10⁻⁴ = **10 N** (repulsive).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — field of a finite line
steps.body: Infinite line ρL: E = ρL/(2πε0 ρ) a_ρ. For ρL = 10 nC/m at ρ = 2 m: E = 10⁻⁸/(2π×8.854×10⁻¹²×2) = **89.9 V/m**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — infinite sheet
steps.body: E = ρS/(2ε0) a_n, independent of distance. ρS = 1 µC/m² gives 56.5 kV/m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding magnitudes instead of vectors.
- Using cm instead of m.
- Forgetting direction: field of a negative charge points inward.
