lessons.title: Lab: Gauss's law and flux density

story.title: Why a car is safe in lightning

scenes.text: Inside a metal car the field from a lightning strike is zero — Gauss's law explains why charge sits on the outside.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body:
**∮ D·dS = Q_enclosed**, D = εE. Differential form: **∇·D = ρV**. Use on symmetric charge: spherical (D = Q/(4πr²)), cylindrical (D = ρL/(2πρ)), planar (D = ρS/2).

Procedure: (1) identify symmetry, (2) choose a Gaussian surface where D is constant or perpendicular, (3) evaluate Q_enc, (4) solve.

steps.title: Example 1 — uniformly charged sphere
steps.body: Radius a, total Q. Outside r > a: E = Q/(4πε0r²). Inside r < a: Q_enc = Q(r/a)³ → E = Qr/(4πε0a³). At r = a both equal Q/(4πε0a²).

steps.title: Example 2 — coaxial
steps.body: Inner conductor ρL = 2 nC/m. Between conductors D = ρL/(2πρ); at ρ=1 cm in air: E = 2×10⁻⁹/(2π×8.854×10⁻¹²×0.01) = 3595 V/m.

steps.title: Example 3 — divergence
steps.body: D = 2x a_x C/m². ∇·D = 2 → ρV = 2 C/m³ everywhere. Charge in a 1 m cube = 2 C.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Gauss's law without symmetry.
- Counting charges outside the surface.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **V_AB = −∫_B^A E·dl** (work per unit charge). **E = −∇V**; conservative: ∇×E = 0. Point charge: V = Q/(4πε0r). Dipole: V = p cosθ/(4πε0r²). Energy of a charge system W = ½ΣQ_kV_k; of a field W = ½∫ε E² dv.

steps.title: Example 3 — energy
steps.body: A 2 µF capacitor at 100 V stores ½CV² = 0.5×2×10⁻⁶×10⁴ = 10 mJ.

steps.title: Common mistake

lessons.title: Lab: Dielectrics, capacitance and boundary conditions

scenes.text: A tiny ceramic capacitor has a very high εr, so a small area stores enough charge to smooth the supply.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Results
steps.body: D = ε0E + P = ε0εrE. Parallel plate: **C = εA/d**. Coax: **C = 2πε/ln(b/a)** per metre. Sphere pair: C = 4πε ab/(b−a). Boundary conditions at a dielectric interface: E_t1 = E_t2; D_n1 − D_n2 = ρS (zero if no free charge → ε1E_n1 = ε2E_n2). At a conductor surface: E_t = 0, D_n = ρS.

steps.title: Example 3 — boundary
steps.body: Air (z>0) to εr = 4 (z<0). E in air: E_t = 10, E_n = 20 V/m. In dielectric: E_t = 10; ε1E_n1 = ε2E_n2 → E_n2 = 20/4 = 5. |E2| = √125 = 11.18 V/m.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Mixing which component is continuous: tangential E, normal D (no free charge).

scenes.text: Electrodes in an old CRT shape the beam. Engineers solve ∇²V = 0 between them to get the field.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Poisson & Laplace
steps.body: ∇²V = −ρV/ε; in charge-free regions ∇²V = 0. Uniqueness theorem: a solution satisfying the boundary conditions is the only solution. Method: integrate directly using symmetry, apply boundary conditions.

steps.title: Example — parallel plates
steps.body: V = 0 at x = 0 and V = 50 V at x = 2 mm; V depends only on x: d²V/dx² = 0 → V = Ax + B → V = 25000x. E = −25 kV/m a_x.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using Cartesian ∇² for cylindrical problems.

courses.summary: Biot–Savart and Ampère laws, magnetic forces, inductance, Faraday's law, displacement current, Maxwell's equations, boundary conditions and the Poynting theorem.

scenes.text: A scrapyard crane lifts cars with an electromagnet: current in a coil makes a strong magnetic field.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Laws
steps.body:
**Biot–Savart:** dH = I dl × a_R/(4πR²). **Ampère:** ∮H·dl = I_enc; ∇×H = J (static). B = μH, μ0 = 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m, ∇·B = 0.

Standard results: infinite wire H = I/(2πρ); circular loop on axis H = Ia²/[2(a²+z²)^{3/2}]; solenoid (long) H = NI/l; toroid H = NI/(2πρ).

steps.title: Example 2 — loop centre
steps.body: Loop radius 5 cm, I = 2 A: H = I/2a = 20 A/m; B = 25.1 µT.

steps.title: Example 3 — solenoid
steps.body: N = 500 turns, l = 0.25 m, I = 2 A: H = 4000 A/m, B = 5.03 mT (air core).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Ampère without symmetry.
- Forgetting μ0 when asked for B.

scenes.text: A voice coil sits in a radial magnetic field. Current through it makes a force that moves the cone.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Lorentz force **F = Q(E + v × B)**; on a wire **F = I L × B**; torque on loop T = m × B, m = IA. Inductance **L = Λ/I = NΦ/I**; energy W = ½LI² = ½∫B·H dv. Solenoid L = μN²A/l; coax L = (μ/2π)ln(b/a) per length; mutual inductance M = k√(L1L2).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Magnetic force does no work on a charge: it changes direction, not speed.

story.title: Four lines that run the world

scenes.text: Radio, radar, Wi-Fi, fibre and every antenna on earth are consequences of four equations.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Equations
steps.body:
Point form: ∇·D = ρV; ∇·B = 0; ∇×E = −∂B/∂t; ∇×H = J + ∂D/∂t. Integral forms: ∮D·dS = Q; ∮B·dS = 0; ∮E·dl = −dΦ/dt; ∮H·dl = I + dΨ/dt. Phasor (e^{jωt}): ∇×E = −jωμH; ∇×H = (σ + jωε)E. Continuity: ∇·J = −∂ρV/∂t.

Boundary conditions: E_t1 = E_t2; H_t1 − H_t2 = K (surface current); D_n1 − D_n2 = ρS; B_n1 = B_n2. At a perfect conductor: E_t = 0, B_n = 0, D_n = ρS, H_t = K.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: In free space E = 100 sin(ωt − βz) a_x V/m. From ∇×E = −μ0∂H/∂t: H_y amplitude = E0/η0 = 100/377 = **0.265 A/m**, same phase; H = 0.265 sin(ωt − βz) a_y.

steps.title: Example 2 — check consistency
steps.body: E = 100 sin(ωt − βz) a_x requires β = ω√(μ0ε0) = ω/c. At f = 300 MHz: β = 2π×3×10⁸/3×10⁸ = 6.28 rad/m.

steps.title: Example 3 — conducting plane
steps.body: At a perfect conductor E_t = 0, so a normal field E_n = ρS/ε0. With ρS = 2 nC/m² : E_n = 2×10⁻⁹/8.854×10⁻¹² = 226 V/m.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Mixing static (∇×E = 0) with time-varying forms.

activity.prompt: H amplitude (A/m) for E0 = 100 V/m in free space.

scenes.text: A router radiates 100 mW. A safety engineer wants the field strength at 1 m to compare with exposure limits.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Poynting
steps.body: **S = E × H** (W/m²); Poynting theorem: −∮S·dS = d/dt∫(½εE² + ½μH²)dv + ∫σE²dv. Time average for plane wave: S_av = E0²/(2η) = E_rms²/η.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using peak amplitude in S = E²/η (that gives twice the average).

story.title: Why FM radio fits in a car

scenes.text: An FM station at 100 MHz has wavelength 3 m, so a car-roof antenna of 0.75 m (quarter-wave) works well. Wavelength comes straight from the wave equation.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Wave equation
steps.body: Source-free, lossless: ∇²E = με ∂²E/∂t². Uniform plane wave E = E0 cos(ωt − βz) a_x with **β = ω√(με)**, **v = 1/√(με) = c/√(εrμr)**, **λ = v/f = 2π/β**, **η = √(μ/ε) = 377√(μr/εr) Ω**. E, H and direction of travel are mutually perpendicular (TEM): H = (1/η) a_z × E.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using f instead of ω in β = ω√(με).
- Writing η = √(ε/μ).

lessons.title: Lab: Lossy media, skin depth and good conductors

scenes.text: Sea water is a conductor; radio waves are attenuated quickly, so submarines use very low frequencies near the surface.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Propagation constant
steps.body: γ = α + jβ = √(jωμ(σ + jωε)). Loss tangent tanδ = σ/ωε. Good conductor (σ ≫ ωε): α = β = √(πfμσ), η = (1+j)√(πfμ/σ), **skin depth δ = 1/α = 1/√(πfμσ)**; fields fall as e^{−z/δ}. Surface resistance R_s = 1/(σδ).

steps.title: Example 3 — depth
steps.body: Field falls to 1/e at δ, to 1 % at 4.6δ. In sea water at 1 MHz, 4.6δ = 1.16 m.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using the good-conductor formula when σ/ωε is not ≫ 1.

activity.prompt: Skin depth (m) of sea water (σ=4 S/m) at 1 MHz.

scenes.text: Polarised sunglasses block glare because reflected light is mostly horizontally polarised. 3D cinema glasses use circular polarisation.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Types
steps.body: E = (E_x a_x + E_y e^{jφ} a_y)e^{−jβz}. **Linear**: φ = 0 or π. **Circular**: E_x = E_y and φ = ±90° (LHC/RHC by rotation sense viewed from the source/IEEE convention). **Elliptical**: all other. Axial ratio AR = major/minor (1 circular, ∞ linear). Satellite links often use circular polarisation to avoid Faraday rotation.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: E = 3 cos(ωt − βz)a_x + 3 sin(ωt − βz) a_y → equal amplitudes, 90° phase → circular.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body: E_x = 4, E_y = 3, φ=0 → linear at angle tan⁻¹(3/4) = 36.9° with |E| = 5.

steps.title: Example 3 — loss
steps.body: Linear receive antenna with circular wave: polarisation loss 3 dB (factor ½). Cross-polarised linear: ideally infinite loss.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Equal amplitudes alone do not make circular; the 90° phase difference is needed.

activity.prompt: Classify each wave.

lessons.title: Lab: Normal incidence — reflection, transmission, VSWR

scenes.text: A window reflects about 4 % of normally incident light even though it is transparent. The mismatch of wave impedances is the cause.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body: Interface η1 → η2: **Γ = (η2 − η1)/(η2 + η1)**, **τ = 1 + Γ = 2η2/(η2+η1)**. Power reflected |Γ|², transmitted 1 − |Γ|². Standing wave ratio **S = (1+|Γ|)/(1−|Γ|)**. Perfect conductor: Γ = −1. Quarter-wave coating η_c = √(η1η2) removes reflection.

steps.title: Example 3 — coating
steps.body: Air to glass: coating index √1.5 = 1.225; thickness λ/4n: for λ = 550 nm, d = 550/(4×1.225) = 112 nm.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using η1−η2 in the numerator (sign changes meaning).

activity.prompt: Reflection coefficient Γ for air → εr=4 dielectric (3 decimals).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — oblique incidence, Snell, Brewster and critical angles

scenes.text: In an optical fibre light hits the core–cladding boundary beyond the critical angle and is totally reflected, travelling kilometres.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Laws
steps.body: Snell: n1 sinθi = n2 sinθt (μr=1). Perpendicular (TE) and parallel (TM) polarisation. **Brewster angle** (TM, no reflection): tanθB = n2/n1. **Critical angle** (n1 > n2): sinθc = n2/n1; beyond it total internal reflection with evanescent field.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body: Fibre core 1.48, cladding 1.46: θc = sin⁻¹(1.46/1.48) = 80.6°; NA = √(1.48²−1.46²) = 0.243; acceptance half-angle = sin⁻¹0.243 = 14.1°.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Brewster angle exists for parallel (TM) polarisation only (for non-magnetic media).

lessons.title: Line parameters and the telegrapher's equations

story.title: Why the TV cable has a number on it

scenes.text: Coaxial cable is labelled 75 Ω; Ethernet pairs are 100 Ω; lab cables 50 Ω. That number is the characteristic impedance, set by geometry, not by length.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Model
steps.body: A short length Δz has series R, L and shunt G, C (per metre). **dV/dz = −(R + jωL)I; dI/dz = −(G + jωC)V.** Then γ = α + jβ = √((R + jωL)(G + jωC)), **Z0 = √((R + jωL)/(G + jωC))**. Lossless: **Z0 = √(L/C)**, **β = ω√(LC)**, **v = 1/√(LC)**. Low-loss: α ≈ R/(2Z0) + GZ0/2. Distortionless (Heaviside): R/L = G/C.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Characteristic impedance is not the resistance you would measure with a meter on a long cable.

activity.prompt: Z0 (Ω) for L = 250 nH/m and C = 100 pF/m.

scenes.text: Before computers, RF engineers solved matching on a circular chart. Today the same chart is on every network analyser screen.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body: The Smith chart plots Γ in the unit circle and overlays constant-resistance and constant-reactance circles for z = Z/Z0 = r + jx. Centre = matched (z=1). **Constant-|Γ| circle = constant VSWR.** Moving toward the generator = clockwise, one full turn = λ/2. Rotating 180° converts z to y (admittance). Right real axis crossing gives S; left real-axis point gives 1/S.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Normalise z_L = Z_L/Z0. 2) Mark on chart. 3) Draw |Γ| circle. 4) Read S at the right-hand real-axis crossing. 5) Rotate clockwise by 2βd (wavelengths toward generator scale) to get z_in. 6) For y, rotate 180°.

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body: Real load z = 2: the point lies on the real axis; S = 2; after λ/4 z = 0.5 (Z = 25 Ω).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Rotating counter-clockwise (toward load) when moving toward generator.

activity.prompt: Order the Smith chart steps to find Z_in at distance d from the load.
items: Normalise the load: z_L = Z_L/Z0
Plot z_L on the chart
Draw the constant-|Γ| circle through it
Rotate clockwise by 2βd (d/λ on wavelengths-toward-generator scale)
Read normalised z_in and multiply by Z0

story.title: Tuning a TV antenna with a spare cable

scenes.text: A short length of cable soldered across the line cancels the antenna's reactance — a stub.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: Shunt stub (admittance). Move from the load a distance d to where y = 1 + jb. Add a stub with susceptance −jb. Short-circuited stub: y = −j cot βl; open: y = +j tan βl. Choose l accordingly.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: Z0 = 50 Ω, Z_L = 100 Ω: y_L = 0.5, |Γ| = 1/3. Need Re y = 1: cosφ = −|Γ| = −1/3 → φ = −109.5° → 2βd = 109.5° → **d = 0.152λ**. There y = 1 + j0.707. Stub must supply −j0.707: cot βl = 0.707 → βl = 54.7° → **l = 0.152λ** (short-circuited). At 300 MHz (λ = 1 m in air): d = 15.2 cm, l = 15.2 cm.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Mixing impedance and admittance moves; shunt stubs add admittance.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — locate a cable fault with TDR

story.title: The broken cable under the floor

scenes.text: A 50 Ω coax run is intermittently dropping signal. A technician sends a fast step and watches for the echo.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: TDR
steps.body: A step launched into the cable reflects at impedance discontinuities. Fault distance **D = v·t/2**, v = VF·c. Polarity: positive echo = higher impedance (open), negative = lower (short). Γ = (Z − Z0)/(Z + Z0).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: Echo returns after 202 ns on cable VF = 0.66: v = 1.98×10⁸ m/s → D = 1.98×10⁸×202×10⁻⁹/2 = **20 m**. Positive reflection of +0.9 → open circuit.

steps.title: Example 2 — delay
steps.body: 10 m of VF 0.66 cable has one-way delay 10/1.98×10⁸ = 50.5 ns.

steps.title: Example 3 — impedance step
steps.body: Echo amplitude +0.2 of the step on a 50 Ω line: Γ = 0.2 → Z = 50×1.2/0.8 = 75 Ω (a 75 Ω section spliced in).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting to halve the round-trip time.

activity.prompt: Distance to fault (m) for 202 ns echo with VF 0.66.

lessons.title: Rectangular waveguide: modes, cutoff and velocities

scenes.text: A magnetron's 2.45 GHz power travels through a hollow metal waveguide into the oven cavity. Below a cutoff frequency, waves cannot propagate at all.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Results
steps.body: Dimensions a × b (a > b). Modes TE_mn (E_z = 0) and TM_mn (H_z = 0). **f_c = (c/2)√((m/a)² + (n/b)²)**. Dominant mode TE10: f_c = c/2a. For f > f_c: β_g = β√(1 − (f_c/f)²); **λ_g = λ/√(1 − (f_c/f)²)**; **v_p = c/√(1−(f_c/f)²)** > c; **v_g = c√(1−(f_c/f)²)** < c; v_p v_g = c². Wave impedance TE: η_TE = η/√(1−(f_c/f)²); TM: η√(1−(f_c/f)²). No TEM mode in a single hollow conductor; TM00/TE00 do not exist, TE_m0 and TE_0n exist.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming v_g > c (energy never exceeds c; v_p can).
- Using a smaller dimension in TE10 cutoff.

activity.prompt: Guide wavelength (mm) of TE10 in WR-90 at 10 GHz.

lessons.title: Lab: Resonant cavities and guide power

scenes.text: A cavity is a waveguide closed at both ends; it stores energy only at special resonant frequencies. Q measures how sharply.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Resonance
steps.body: Rectangular cavity a × b × d: **f_r = (c/2)√((m/a)² + (n/b)² + (p/d)²)**. Quality factor Q = ω0 × (energy stored)/(power lost); bandwidth BW = f_0/Q. TE101 is dominant.

steps.title: Example 2 — Q
steps.body: f0 = 10 GHz, Q = 5000 → BW = 2 MHz.

steps.title: Example 3 — attenuation by cutoff
steps.body: Guide lengths used as high-pass filter; e.g. a WR-90 guide passes 8–12 GHz and blocks 5 GHz.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting that two indices cannot both be zero in a TE/TM cavity (TE101 uses m=1,n=0,p=1).

activity.prompt: TE101 resonant frequency (GHz) of a 3 cm cubic cavity.

story.title: Why Wi-Fi routers have two sticks

scenes.text: The sticks are dipoles; their donut-shaped pattern sends energy sideways rather than up or down — directivity at work.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: Radiation pattern; HPBW; **directivity D = 4π/Ω_A = U_max/U_avg**; **gain G = η_rad D**; radiation resistance R_r from P_rad = ½I²R_r. Effective aperture **A_e = λ²G/(4π)**. Hertzian dipole: R_r = 80π²(l/λ)², D = 1.5. Half-wave dipole: **R_r ≈ 73 Ω, D = 1.64 (2.15 dBi)**, length ≈ 0.47λ in practice. Isotropic: D = 1. Reciprocity: same pattern in transmit and receive.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: f = 900 MHz: λ = 0.333 m; half-wave dipole ≈ 16.7 cm (≈ 15.7 cm after end-effect 0.47λ). A_e = 0.111×1.64/(4π) = 0.0145 m².

steps.title: Example 3 — efficiency

story.title: Will the drone video reach the car?

scenes.text: A drone sends video on 2.4 GHz with 10 W (extreme case) over 1 km. A link budget tells whether the receiver gets enough signal.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Friis
steps.body: **P_r = P_t G_t G_r (λ/4πR)²**. Free-space path loss **FSPL = 20log(4πR/λ) dB = 32.44 + 20log f(MHz) + 20log d(km)**. Link budget (dB): P_r = P_t + G_t + G_r − FSPL − other losses. Receiver sensitivity and fade margin decide viability.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Friis assumes far field and line of sight; ignoring polarisation and obstacle losses overestimates P_r.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — arrays and a 5.8 GHz point-to-point link

scenes.text: A village wants broadband from a fibre hub 10 km away on a hill. You design the radio link.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Array factor
steps.body: Two isotropic elements spaced d with phase δ: AF = 2cos(ψ/2), ψ = kd cosθ + δ. In-phase, d = λ/2: broadside maximum, nulls along the array axis (end-fire). N-element uniform array: gain ≈ N× element gain.

steps.title: Link design
steps.body: 5.8 GHz, 10 km: FSPL = 32.44 + 20log5800 + 20log10 = 32.44 + 75.27 + 20 = 127.7 dB. Dishes 28.6 dBi each, P_t = 25 dBm: P_r = 25 + 28.6 + 28.6 − 127.7 = −45.5 dBm. With sensitivity −80 dBm, fade margin = 34.5 dB — comfortable.

steps.title: Fresnel clearance
steps.body: First Fresnel radius at mid-path: r = √(λ d1 d2/(d1+d2)) = √(0.0517×5000×5000/10000) = 11.4 m; keep ≥ 60 % clear (6.8 m).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Ignoring earth curvature and Fresnel zones on long links.

steps.title: Statics and Maxwell

scenes.text: A microwave bench with Gunn oscillator, isolator, attenuator and slotted line is used to measure an unknown load.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Aim and procedure
steps.body: Aim: measure VSWR, λg and load impedance. 1) Set the Gunn source to ≈ 10 GHz, square-wave modulate at 1 kHz. 2) Short the slotted line; note positions of voltage minima (spacing = λg/2). 3) Replace with the unknown load; note V_max, V_min and the position of a minimum. 4) VSWR = V_max/V_min (square-law detector: S = √(V_max/V_min) for readings in square-law region). 5) Find shift of minimum with respect to short-circuit minimum; compute Γ phase and Z_L from Smith chart.

steps.title: Observation table
steps.body:
| Reading | Value |
|---|---|
| Short minima | 8.10 cm, 10.09 cm |
| λg/2 | 1.99 cm → λg = 3.98 cm |
| V_max / V_min (load) | 10 mV / 4 mV |
| VSWR (linear detector) | 2.5 |
| |Γ| | (2.5−1)/(3.5) = 0.4286 |

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body: Operate detector in the square-law region; avoid loose cable connections; keep the probe depth small.

steps.title: Procedure

steps.title: Precautions

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Place transmitting horn and receiving test antenna in far field: R > 2D²/λ. 2) Rotate in 10° steps; record P_r in dB relative to maximum. 3) Plot polar pattern; HPBW = angle between −3 dB points. 4) Gain by comparison method: G_x = G_ref + (P_x − P_ref) dB.

steps.title: Observation

items.q: Why is a hollow waveguide a high-pass filter?
items.a: Only frequencies above the cutoff propagate; below it the wave is evanescent.

items.q: What is VSWR and its value for a matched line?
items.a: Ratio of maximum to minimum voltage on the line; 1 for a matched line.

items.q: What is the far-field distance?
items.a: R > 2D²/λ for an antenna of largest dimension D.

items.q: Why use an isolator?

items.q: Why coaxial cable at 75 Ω for TV?
items.a: Lowest attenuation occurs near 77 Ω for air-spaced coax; 50 Ω is a power-handling compromise.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Semiconductor physics
courses.summary: Energy bands, intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors, carrier concentrations, drift and diffusion, Einstein relation, continuity and the Hall effect.
outcomes: Explain band structure of conductors, semiconductors and insulators
Compute electron and hole concentrations using mass-action law
Calculate conductivity, diffusion coefficient and diffusion length
Use the Hall effect to find carrier type and density

scenes.text: Almost every chip is made of silicon, not germanium, which was used in the first transistors.
The reason is the band gap and how fast thermal leakage grows with temperature.

steps.title: Bands
steps.body:
In a crystal, atomic levels broaden into bands. The **valence band** (filled at 0 K) and the **conduction band** are separated by a forbidden gap E_g.

- Insulator: E_g > ~5 eV.
- Semiconductor: E_g ≈ 0.5–3 eV (Ge 0.67 eV, Si 1.12 eV, GaAs 1.42 eV at 300 K).
- Metal: bands overlap or the conduction band is partly filled.

E_g decreases slightly with temperature.

steps.title: Intrinsic carriers
steps.body: In a pure crystal, thermal energy creates electron–hole pairs: n = p = n_i. The mass-action law holds: **n·p = n_i²**, with n_i ∝ T^(3/2) e^(−E_g/2kT). Silicon: n_i ≈ 1.5×10¹⁰ cm⁻³ at 300 K; Ge: 2.4×10¹³ cm⁻³. Thermal voltage V_T = kT/q = 25.85 mV at 300 K (k = 8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K).

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: Why Ge leaks more: n_i(Ge)/n_i(Si) = 2.4×10¹³/1.5×10¹⁰ ≈ 1600 at 300 K, because its smaller gap makes e^(−E_g/2kT) larger.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using temperature in °C in V_T; assuming n_i is the same for all semiconductors; forgetting E_g shrinks as T rises.

activity.prompt: Compute the thermal voltage V_T = kT/q at 300 K (k = 8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K). Answer in mV.

steps.title: Doping
steps.body:
**n-type**: donors (P, As, Sb — group V) give electrons; N_D⁺ ions fixed. **p-type**: acceptors (B, Ga, In — group III) give holes.

Charge neutrality: p + N_D = n + N_A. For N_D ≫ n_i (n-type): n ≈ N_D, p = n_i²/N_D. For p-type: p ≈ N_A, n = n_i²/N_A.

Fermi level moves toward E_c in n-type and toward E_v in p-type; E_F = E_i + kT ln(n/n_i).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying the n-type crystal is negatively charged (it is neutral); using n = N_D when N_D is comparable to n_i.

steps.title: Drift current
steps.body:
Drift velocity v_d = μE. Current density J = q(nμ_n + pμ_p)E = σE, so **σ = q(nμ_n + pμ_p)** (S/cm), ρ = 1/σ.

Si at 300 K (low doping): μ_n ≈ 1350, μ_p ≈ 480 cm²/V·s; mobility falls with temperature (lattice scattering ~T^(−3/2)) and with heavy doping (impurity scattering).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing cm and m (mobility in cm²/V·s vs m²/V·s differ by 10⁴); forgetting the minority-carrier term is negligible in doped material.

lessons.title: Lab: Diffusion, Einstein relation and continuity

scenes.text: Inject excess carriers at one end of a bar and they spread even with no field.
The distance they travel before recombining is the diffusion length.

steps.title: Diffusion
steps.body:
Diffusion current density: J_n = qD_n dn/dx, J_p = −qD_p dp/dx. **Einstein relation**: D/μ = kT/q = V_T.

For holes injected into n-type with lifetime τ_p: steady state p'(x) = p'(0) e^(−x/L_p), **L_p = √(D_pτ_p)**. Continuity: ∂p/∂t = −(1/q)∂J_p/∂x − p'/τ_p + G.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
D_n = μ_nV_T = 1350 × 0.02585 = **34.9 cm²/s**. With τ = 1 µs: L_n = √(34.9 × 10⁻⁶) = 5.9×10⁻³ cm = **59 µm**.

Total current: J = qn μ_nE + qD_n dn/dx.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the sign (holes diffuse down the gradient so J_p carries a minus); applying Einstein's relation with T in °C.

steps.title: Hall effect
steps.body:
A current I flows along a bar of thickness t in a perpendicular field B. The Lorentz force deflects carriers and builds a transverse field E_H = v_d B.

**V_H = IB/(n q t)** (n-type; p replaces n for p-type), **R_H = 1/(nq)** (m³/C) or −1/(nq) for electrons. Hall mobility μ = |R_H|σ. The sign of V_H tells the carrier type.

steps.title: Applications
steps.body: Hall sensors in motor commutation, current sensors, magnetometers in phones.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using t as the width; ignoring the sign (electrons give negative R_H).

courses.title: Unit 2 · The PN junction diode and special diodes
courses.summary: PN junction in equilibrium, built-in potential and depletion width, diode equation, temperature effects, breakdown, junction and diffusion capacitance, Zener regulation, and LED, photodiode, solar cell, Schottky and varactor diodes.
outcomes: Compute built-in potential and depletion width

scenes.text: Join p-type and n-type silicon and a potential barrier forms with no battery.
Its height and width set diode behaviour.

steps.title: Equilibrium
steps.body:
Electrons diffuse from n to p and holes from p to n, leaving fixed ionised donors (+) and acceptors (−): the **depletion region** with a built-in field. At equilibrium drift balances diffusion, net current is zero and the Fermi level is flat.

**V₀ = V_T ln(N_A N_D/n_i²)**.
Width: **W = √[(2ε V₀/q)(1/N_A + 1/N_D)]**, extending x_n = W N_A/(N_A+N_D) into n-side and x_p = W N_D/(N_A+N_D) into p-side (the lightly doped side gets the wider share). Under bias V: replace V₀ by V₀ − V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Believing the built-in voltage can be measured with a voltmeter (contact potentials cancel it); using the wrong dopant in the x_n, x_p split.

quiz.why: Mobile carriers have been swept out.

steps.title: Shockley equation
steps.body:
**I = I_s (e^(V/ηV_T) − 1)**, η = 1–2. Reverse bias (V ≪ −V_T): I ≈ −I_s. Forward (V ≫ V_T): I ≈ I_s e^(V/ηV_T).

Temperature: I_s doubles per ~10 °C rise; at constant current V_D falls about **2 mV/°C**. Dynamic resistance r_d = ηV_T/I (26 Ω at 1 mA, η=1).

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: r_d at 12 mA = 25.85 mV/12 mA = **2.15 Ω**. A 40 °C rise lowers V_D at fixed I by ≈ 80 mV.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using 0.7 V for every diode (Ge 0.2–0.3 V, Schottky ~0.3 V, LEDs 1.8–3.3 V); forgetting the −1 term at low voltage.

scenes.text: A varactor diode changes its capacitance with reverse voltage in a radio tuner.

steps.title: Breakdown
steps.body:
- **Zener breakdown** (V_Z < ~5 V): heavy doping, narrow depletion, quantum tunnelling; negative temperature coefficient.
- **Avalanche breakdown** (V_Z > ~7 V): impact ionisation multiplies carriers; positive temperature coefficient.
- Near 5–6 V the two cancel: ~zero TC.

Breakdown is non-destructive if power is limited.

steps.title: Capacitances
steps.body: **Transition (junction) capacitance** under reverse bias: C_j = C_j0/(1 + V_R/V₀)^m, m = ½ (abrupt), ⅓ (graded). **Diffusion capacitance** under forward bias: C_D = τI/V_T (dominates).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling all breakdown 'Zener effect'; thinking junction capacitance rises with reverse bias.

steps.title: Design rules
steps.body:
Series resistor R_s drops V_in − V_Z. Zener current I_Z = I_s − I_L where I_s = (V_in − V_Z)/R_s. Requirements: I_Z ≥ I_Z,min (knee) for the worst case (low V_in, max I_L), and P_Z = V_Z I_Z,max ≤ rating for the best case (high V_in, no load).

Line regulation depends on r_z: ΔV_out ≈ ΔV_in·r_z/(R_s + r_z).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
V_in = 12 V, V_Z = 5.1 V, R_s = 220 Ω, R_L = 1 kΩ.

- I_L = 5.1 mA; I_s = 6.9/220 = 31.36 mA.
- **I_Z = 26.0 mA**; P_Z = 5.1 × 26.0 mA = 132.6 mW (a 500 mW part is fine).
- If the load is removed: I_Z = 31.4 mA, P = 160 mW.
- With r_z = 7 Ω, a 1 V input change moves V_out by 7/227 = 31 mV.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Omitting R_s (the Zener burns out); sizing R_s for nominal not worst-case conditions.

steps.title: Special diodes
steps.body:
- **LED**: forward bias, radiative recombination; direct-gap materials (GaAs, GaP, GaN); V_f ≈ 1.8 V red, ~3 V blue/white. Wavelength λ(µm) ≈ 1.24/E_g(eV).
- **Photodiode**: reverse biased; photons create pairs → photocurrent ∝ light.
- **Solar cell**: photovoltaic mode, no bias; open-circuit V_oc ≈ 0.6 V Si, I_sc ∝ irradiance.
- **Schottky**: metal–semiconductor, majority carriers only, V_f ≈ 0.3 V, no storage time → fast.
- **Tunnel/varactor/PIN** for microwave, tuning and RF switches.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:

courses.title: Unit 3 · Diode circuits: rectifiers, filters, clippers, clampers
courses.summary: Half-wave, full-wave and bridge rectifiers with all performance parameters, capacitor filters and ripple, clippers, clampers and voltage multipliers, ending with a power-supply design.
outcomes: Compute V_dc, V_rms, ripple factor, efficiency and PIV of rectifiers

scenes.text: Mains AC must become DC. The simplest idea: block the negative half-cycles with a diode.
How good is the DC that results?

steps.title: Half-wave formulas
steps.body:
Input v = V_m sin ωt, ideal diode, load R_L.

- I_dc = I_m/π, **V_dc = V_m/π** = 0.318 V_m
- I_rms = I_m/2, V_rms = V_m/2
- Ripple factor γ = √((I_rms/I_dc)² − 1) = **1.21**
- Rectification efficiency η = P_dc/P_ac = 4/π² = **40.6 %**
- PIV = V_m; ripple frequency = f (50 Hz); form factor 1.57.
With a diode drop V_γ: V_m → V_m − V_γ.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
V_m = 10 V, R_L = 1 kΩ, ideal diode.

- V_dc = 10/π = **3.183 V**; I_dc = 3.18 mA.

With 0.7 V drop: V_dc = 9.3/π = 2.96 V.

steps.title: Capacitor filter
steps.body:
The capacitor charges to V_m and discharges through R_L between peaks. Approximation (triangle ripple): **V_r(p-p) = I_dc/(f_r C)**, with f_r = ripple frequency (2f for full-wave). V_dc ≈ V_m − V_r/2; ripple factor γ ≈ 1/(2√3 f_r C R_L).

Larger C or higher f_r → lower ripple. Surge current at switch-on needs a transformer resistance or inrush limiter.

steps.title: Wave shaping
steps.body:
**Clipper**: removes part of the waveform. Series positive clipper (diode in series) blanks positive peaks; shunt clipper with reference V_R limits at V_R + V_γ. **Clamper**: adds a DC level without changing shape: diode + capacitor + (R); positive clamper shifts the waveform up so its negative peak sits near 0 V; its time constant RC ≫ T.

**Voltage doubler** (Greinacher): V_out ≈ 2(V_m − V_γ). Tripler/quadrupler by cascading.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Negative clamper, ideal diode, input ±5 V (10 V p-p): output swings from **−10 V to 0 V**.
Voltage doubler: V_m = 12 V, V_γ = 0.7 V → V_out ≈ 2 × 11.3 = **22.6 V** (no load).

steps.body: Thinking a clamper changes the peak-to-peak amplitude; neglecting the load on multipliers (output sags rapidly).

courses.summary: BJT physics and current relations, input/output characteristics and regions, Early effect, DC biasing and stability factor, and the small-signal hybrid-π model of the common-emitter amplifier.

lessons.title: Lab: BJT operation, α, β and configurations

story.title: One small current controls a big one

scenes.text: A tiny base current opens the way for a much bigger collector current, like a tap controlling a pipe.
α and β quantify how big that multiplication is.

steps.title: Operation
steps.body:
An NPN BJT has a heavily doped emitter, a thin lightly-doped base and a collector. In the **active region**: base–emitter junction forward biased, base–collector reverse biased. The emitter injects electrons; most cross the thin base and are swept into the collector, a few recombine (I_B).

I_E = I_C + I_B; **α = I_C/I_E** (0.95–0.995); **β = I_C/I_B = α/(1 − α)**; I_C = βI_B + (1+β)I_CBO.

steps.title: Configurations
steps.body:
- **CE**: voltage and current gain, phase inversion, most used.
- **CB**: no current gain, high voltage gain, good at high frequency, low input impedance.
- **CC (emitter follower)**: voltage gain ≈ 1, high input and low output impedance, a buffer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thinking two back-to-back diodes make a transistor (the thin base is essential); assuming β is constant (varies with I_C, T, device).

activity.prompt: A transistor has α = 0.98. Find β.

lessons.title: Lab: BJT characteristics, regions and Early effect

scenes.text: The datasheet shows I_C versus V_CE for several base currents.
Cut-off, active and saturation are the three operating zones.

steps.title: Regions
steps.body:
| Region | BE | BC | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cut-off | rev | rev | switch OFF |
| Active | fwd | rev | amplifier |
| Saturation | fwd | fwd | switch ON (V_CE,sat ≈ 0.2 V) |

Input characteristic ≈ diode: V_BE ≈ 0.7 V (−2 mV/°C). Output curves nearly flat in active region.

steps.title: Early effect
steps.body: Raising V_CE widens the C–B depletion region, narrowing the base: I_C rises slightly: I_C = βI_B(1 + V_CE/V_A). Output resistance **r_o = V_A/I_C** (V_A Early voltage, ~50–200 V).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
V_A = 100 V, I_C = 2 mA → **r_o = 50 kΩ**.
Switch check: V_CC = 5 V, R_C = 1 kΩ, β = 100, V_CE,sat = 0.2 V: I_C,sat = 4.8 mA → I_B,min = 48 µA; use ≈ 5× overdrive.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using β·I_B in saturation (I_C is fixed by the load there); ignoring the temperature drift of V_BE.

story.title: A bias point that survives summer

scenes.text: An amplifier's bias drifts when the box heats up and its β rises 50 %.
Voltage-divider bias keeps I_C nearly constant.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
1. Thevenin of the divider: V_TH = V_CC R₂/(R₁+R₂), R_TH = R₁∥R₂.
2. Base loop: V_TH = I_B R_TH + V_BE + I_E R_E, with I_E = (1+β)I_B → I_B = (V_TH − V_BE)/(R_TH + (1+β)R_E).
3. I_C = βI_B; V_CE = V_CC − I_C R_C − I_E R_E.
Good design: R_TH ≪ (1+β)R_E so I_C ≈ (V_TH − V_BE)/R_E independent of β. Rule: V_E ≈ V_CC/10, divider current ≈ 10 I_B.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting (1+β) multiplying R_E in the base loop; assuming V_BE = 0.7 V for a high-current power BJT.

lessons.title: Lab: Hybrid-π model and CE amplifier gain

scenes.text: A microphone gives a few millivolts. A CE amplifier must boost it to a few hundred.

steps.title: Hybrid-π
steps.body:
At the Q-point: **g_m = I_C/V_T**, **r_π = β/g_m**, r_o = V_A/I_C. Small-signal current i_c = g_m v_be.

CE with bypassed emitter: **A_v = −g_m(R_C ∥ r_o ∥ R_L)**, R_in = R_TH ∥ r_π, R_out ≈ R_C ∥ r_o.
With unbypassed R_E: A_v ≈ −R_C/(r_e + R_E), where r_e = V_T/I_E.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the load in the gain; forgetting that bypassing R_E gives high gain but sets the gain by I_C (temperature-dependent).

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — stability factor and thermal runaway

scenes.text: A power stage's collector current rises as it warms, which makes it hotter still.
The stability factor S predicts how sensitive I_C is to leakage and temperature.

steps.title: Stability factor
steps.body:
**S = ∂I_C/∂I_CO**. For emitter-bias networks: **S = (1+β)(1 + R_TH/R_E)/(1 + β + R_TH/R_E)**. Fixed bias: S = 1 + β (worst). The lower S, the more stable (ideal S = 1).

Other stability factors: S′ = ∂I_C/∂V_BE, S″ = ∂I_C/∂β. **Thermal runaway**: T↑ → I_CO↑ → I_C↑ → power↑ → T↑; prevented by R_E, heat sinks, and S small.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Using the voltage-divider design (R_TH = 8.246 kΩ, R_E = 1 kΩ, β = 100):

R_TH/R_E = 8.246.
S = 101 × 9.246/(101 + 8.246) = 933.8/109.25 = **8.55**.
Fixed-bias S would be 101. A 0.1 µA rise in I_CO → ΔI_C = 0.855 µA only.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming S is dimensionless-zero-ideal (ideal is 1); forgetting I_CO doubles every 10 °C for silicon.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Field-effect transistors: JFET, MOSFET and CMOS
courses.summary: JFET operation and square-law, the MOS capacitor and oxide capacitance, MOSFET I–V in triode and saturation, small-signal common-source gain, and the CMOS inverter.
outcomes: Apply the JFET and MOSFET square-law equations
Compute C_ox, k′ₙ and drain currents

scenes.text: Squeeze a garden hose and the flow drops. A JFET squeezes a semiconductor channel with a reverse-biased gate.
The input draws almost no current.

steps.title: Operation
steps.body:
An n-channel JFET has an n-type channel between source and drain with a p⁺ gate on each side. Reverse gate bias widens the depletion regions and **pinches off** the channel at V_GS = V_P (negative for n-channel, e.g. −4 V). I_G ≈ 0 (reverse-biased junction), so R_in ~10⁹ Ω.

Saturation (V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_P): **I_D = I_DSS(1 − V_GS/V_P)²**; transconductance g_m = g_m0(1 − V_GS/V_P), g_m0 = 2I_DSS/|V_P|.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using positive V_P for an n-channel; forgetting that forward-biasing the gate junction destroys the high input resistance.

lessons.title: Lab: The MOS capacitor and threshold voltage

scenes.text: Put a metal plate over an oxide-covered p-type wafer and apply positive voltage.
Holes are pushed away; at high enough voltage electrons form a thin channel.

steps.title: MOS capacitor
steps.body:
Metal (or poly-Si) – SiO₂ – semiconductor. For p-type substrate: **accumulation** (V_G < 0), **depletion**, then **inversion** (V_G > V_T) where an n-type channel forms. Oxide capacitance per unit area **C_ox = ε_ox/t_ox**, ε_ox = 3.9 ε₀ = 3.45×10⁻¹¹ F/m.

Threshold V_T = V_FB + 2φ_F + Q_dep/C_ox. Body effect raises V_T when source–body is reverse biased.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
t_ox = 10 nm: C_ox = 3.453×10⁻¹¹/10⁻⁸ = 3.45×10⁻³ F/m² = **3.45 fF/µm²**.
For W×L = 10 µm × 1 µm, gate capacitance = 10 × 3.45 = 34.5 fF.
Fermi potential φ_F = V_T ln(N_A/n_i) = 0.02585 × ln(10¹⁷/1.5×10¹⁰) = 0.407 V.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing threshold voltage with the pinch-off voltage of a JFET; forgetting the oxide is an insulator, so I_G = 0 at DC.

activity.prompt: Find C_ox in fF/µm² for t_ox = 10 nm (ε_r = 3.9, ε₀ = 8.854 pF/m).

scenes.text: A designer measures V_GS and V_DS on a transistor and must decide triode or saturation before using a formula.
Compare V_DS with the overdrive voltage.

steps.title: Square-law model (n-channel enhancement)
steps.body:
Overdrive V_OV = V_GS − V_T.

- Cut-off: V_GS < V_T, I_D ≈ 0.
- **Triode**: V_DS < V_OV, I_D = k′ₙ(W/L)[V_OV V_DS − V_DS²/2].
- **Saturation**: V_DS ≥ V_OV, I_D = ½k′ₙ(W/L)V_OV²(1 + λV_DS).
k′ₙ = μₙC_ox. Triode with small V_DS acts as a resistor r_on = 1/[k′ₙ(W/L)V_OV].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using the saturation formula in triode; mixing up V_GS and V_OV; using μ in cm² with C_ox in F/m² without conversion.

activity.prompt: k′ₙ = 138 µA/V², W/L = 10, V_T = 0.5 V, V_GS = 1.5 V, V_DS = 1.5 V. Find I_D in saturation.

quiz.q: I_D in saturation is proportional to:

lessons.title: Lab: Small-signal model and common-source amplifier

scenes.text: A CMOS sensor chip needs a common-source stage to amplify a small signal.
Compute g_m at the bias point, then the gain.

steps.title: Small-signal parameters
steps.body:
g_m = ∂I_D/∂V_GS = k′ₙ(W/L)V_OV = **2I_D/V_OV** = √(2k′ₙ(W/L)I_D). r_o = 1/(λI_D). Body transconductance g_mb = χg_m.

Common-source: **A_v = −g_m(R_D ∥ r_o ∥ R_L)**; input resistance essentially infinite at low frequency; with a source resistor R_S: A_v ≈ −g_mR_D/(1 + g_mR_S). Source follower gain = g_mR/(1 + g_mR) < 1.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Using the bias above (I_D = 0.69 mA, V_OV = 1 V): g_m = 2 × 0.69/1 = **1.38 mS**.
With R_D = 5 kΩ (r_o large, no load): **A_v = −1.38 × 5 = −6.9**.
Compared with a BJT at the same current (g_m = 26.7 mS), the MOSFET has much lower g_m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using g_m = I_D/V_T (BJT formula) for a MOSFET; ignoring the negative sign.

scenes.text: A CPU is built from complementary pairs of NMOS and PMOS transistors.

steps.title: CMOS inverter
steps.body:
PMOS (to V_DD) and NMOS (to ground) share the gate (input) and drain (output). In = 0: PMOS on, NMOS off → out = V_DD. In = V_DD: NMOS on → out = 0.

Switching threshold V_M ≈ V_DD/2 for matched strengths (k_p = k_n needs W_p/W_n ≈ μₙ/μₚ ≈ 2–3). Dynamic power **P = αC_LV_DD²f**; short-circuit and leakage power are smaller (but leakage dominates in nanometre nodes).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
C_L = 10 fF, V_DD = 1.0 V, f = 1 GHz, activity α = 0.5:
**P = 0.5 × 10×10⁻¹⁵ × 1² × 10⁹ = 5 µW** per gate. A block of 10⁶ such gates burns 5 W.

steps.title: Explore
steps.body: Tap the parts in the 3-D cross-section: the n-well hosts the PMOS, the p-substrate the NMOS.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying CMOS consumes no power (it has dynamic and leakage power); forgetting V_DD² scaling is why supply voltages keep dropping.

scenes.text: A construction-site lamp flashes using a single transistor and an RC pair.

steps.title: UJT
steps.body:
One n-type bar with base contacts B1, B2 and a p-type emitter junction. **Intrinsic stand-off ratio η = R_B1/(R_B1 + R_B2)** (0.5–0.8). The emitter junction conducts when V_E reaches the **peak voltage V_P = ηV_BB + V_D** (V_D ≈ 0.7 V). Then R_B1 collapses (conductivity modulation) → negative-resistance region.

Relaxation oscillator: capacitor C charges through R toward V_BB, fires at V_P, discharges through B1; **T ≈ RC ln(1/(1 − η))**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating a UJT like a BJT; the UJT has no current gain, it is a trigger device. (Modern designs use PUTs or microcontrollers.)

steps.title: Silicon-controlled rectifier
steps.body:
Four layers PNPN, three junctions, terminals anode, cathode, gate. Off until V_AK exceeds forward-break-over voltage, or a gate pulse triggers it (cheaply). Two-transistor model (PNP + NPN) gives regenerative latching: once I_A > latching current it stays on after the gate pulse; turns off when I_A < holding current (or reverse bias).

Half-wave phase control with resistive load, firing angle α: **V_avg = (V_m/2π)(1 + cos α)**; V_rms = (V_m/2)√(1 − α/π + sin2α/2π).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Expecting the gate to turn the SCR off; ignoring dv/dt false-triggering — add an RC snubber.

lessons.title: Lab: TRIAC, DIAC, power MOSFET and IGBT

scenes.text: A factory engineer picks switches for a heater, an inverter and a lamp dimmer.
Voltage, current, speed and AC/DC decide the device.

steps.title: Devices
steps.body:
- **TRIAC**: bidirectional thyristor, triggered in both half-cycles; AC phase control (dimmers, heaters).
- **DIAC**: bidirectional trigger diode (~30 V breakover) used with TRIAC.
- **Power MOSFET**: voltage-driven, very fast (100 kHz–MHz), low R_DS(on); up to ~600–1000 V; body diode.
- **IGBT**: MOSFET input + BJT output; high voltage (600 V–6.5 kV), high current, 5–50 kHz; inverters, motor drives, EVs.
- **GTO/IGCT**: turn-off by gate for very high power.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Power MOSFET with R_DS(on) = 20 mΩ carrying 10 A: conduction loss = I²R = 100 × 0.02 = **2 W**.
IGBT with V_CE(sat) = 1.8 V at 10 A: 18 W — worse at low voltage, better at high voltage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using a SCR on AC when full-wave control is needed (use a TRIAC or back-to-back SCRs); driving MOSFET gates slowly (high switching loss).

lessons.title: Lab: Opto devices and solar cells

scenes.text: A microcontroller must switch a mains relay without any electrical connection between them.
An optocoupler passes the signal by light.

steps.title: Opto devices
steps.body:
- **LDR**: resistance falls with light (CdS).
- **Photodiode** (reverse biased) and **phototransistor** (gain, slower).
- **Optocoupler**: LED + phototransistor; **CTR = I_C/I_F × 100 %** (typ. 50–600 %); isolation voltage 3–5 kV.
- **Solar cell**: short-circuit current I_sc ∝ irradiance; V_oc ≈ 0.6 V (Si); **fill factor FF = P_max/(V_ocI_sc)** (0.7–0.85); efficiency η = P_max/(irradiance × area).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
A cell: V_oc = 0.6 V, I_sc = 3 A, FF = 0.75 → **P_max = 0.6 × 3 × 0.75 = 1.35 W**. Area 100 cm², 1000 W/m² (10 W on the cell) → η = 13.5 %.

steps.title: Process flow

steps.title: Semiconductor physics
steps.body:
- n·p = n_i²; V_T = kT/q = 25.85 mV at 300 K.
- σ = q(nμ_n + pμ_p); D = μV_T; L = √(Dτ).
- V_H = IB/(nqt); R_H = ±1/(nq).
- E_F − E_i = V_T ln(n/n_i).

steps.title: Diodes
steps.body:
- V₀ = V_T ln(N_AN_D/n_i²); W = √[(2εV₀/q)(1/N_A+1/N_D)].
- I = I_s(e^(V/ηV_T) − 1); r_d = ηV_T/I; −2 mV/°C.
- C_j = C_j0/(1+V_R/V₀)^m; C_D = τI/V_T.
- Rectifier: HW V_dc = V_m/π, γ = 1.21, η = 40.6 %; FW V_dc = 2V_m/π, γ = 0.482, η = 81.2 %.
- Filter V_r = I/(f_rC).

steps.title: Transistors
steps.body:
- β = α/(1−α); g_m = I_C/V_T; r_π = β/g_m; A_v = −g_m(R_C∥R_L).
- S = (1+β)(1+R_TH/R_E)/(1+β+R_TH/R_E).
- JFET: I_D = I_DSS(1−V_GS/V_P)². MOSFET sat: I_D = ½k′(W/L)V_OV²; g_m = 2I_D/V_OV.
- C_ox = ε_ox/t_ox; CMOS P = αCV²f.
- SCR V_avg = (V_m/2π)(1+cosα); UJT V_P = ηV_BB + V_D.

steps.title: Procedure

2. Transfer characteristic: V_DS = 10 V; vary V_GS 0 to V_P; record I_D.
3. I_DSS = I_D at V_GS = 0; V_P where I_D → 0.

activity.prompt: Typical viva questions on devices.

items.q: Why does a diode conduct only in one direction?
items.a: Forward bias lowers the junction barrier so majority carriers diffuse across; reverse bias raises it so only tiny minority-carrier drift flows.

items.q: Why is silicon preferred over germanium?
items.a: Larger band gap gives lower leakage, higher temperature capability, and a native oxide (SiO₂) for MOS devices.

items.q: Difference between Zener and avalanche breakdown?
items.a: Zener is tunnelling in thin heavily-doped junctions (V_Z < 5 V, negative TC); avalanche is impact ionisation (V_Z > 7 V, positive TC).

items.q: Why is the JFET input impedance high?
items.a: The gate junction is reverse biased, so gate current is negligible.

items.q: Why is the base of a BJT thin and lightly doped?
items.a: To minimise recombination so most injected carriers reach the collector.

lessons.title: Distributed line model and characteristic impedance

story.title: The coax that behaved like a filter

scenes.text: A technician runs 30 m of cable to a 3 GHz antenna. At 50 Hz the cable is just two wires, but at 3 GHz its length is 300 wavelengths long.
At that size every centimetre has its own inductance and capacitance, so the line must be modelled as distributed elements.

steps.title: Why lumped models fail
steps.body:
A circuit is 'lumped' when its size is much smaller than the wavelength (rule of thumb: below lambda/10). At microwave frequencies (300 MHz - 300 GHz, lambda = 1 m to 1 mm in free space) the line length is comparable to or greater than lambda, so voltage and current vary with position as well as time.

Model a small length dz by series R dz, L dz and shunt G dz, C dz, where R (ohm/m), L (H/m), G (S/m), C (F/m) are per-unit-length parameters.

steps.title: Telegrapher's equations and results
steps.body:
- dV/dz = -(R + jwL) I and dI/dz = -(G + jwC) V
- Propagation constant: gamma = alpha + j beta = sqrt[(R + jwL)(G + jwC)]
- Characteristic impedance: Z0 = sqrt[(R + jwL)/(G + jwC)]
- Lossless line (R = G = 0): Z0 = sqrt(L/C), beta = w sqrt(LC), phase velocity vp = 1/sqrt(LC) = c/sqrt(er) for a TEM line with dielectric constant er.
- Wavelength on the line: lambda = vp/f = 2 pi/beta.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A lossless line has L = 250 nH/m and C = 100 pF/m.
1. Z0 = sqrt(250e-9 / 100e-12) = sqrt(2500) = 50 ohm.
2. vp = 1/sqrt(LC) = 1/sqrt(2.5e-17) = 2 x 10^8 m/s.
3. At 2 GHz, lambda = 2e8/2e9 = 0.1 m = 10 cm.

**Example 2.** A coax filled with polyethylene (er = 2.25) carries 1 GHz. vp = 3e8/1.5 = 2e8 m/s, so lambda = 20 cm and beta = 2 pi / 0.2 = 31.4 rad/m.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the free-space wavelength inside a dielectric-filled line.
- Confusing Z0 (a property of geometry and dielectric) with the load impedance.
- Saying Z0 depends on line length: it does not, and it is not measurable with an ohmmeter.

lessons.title: Reflection coefficient, VSWR and return loss

scenes.text: A 50 ohm transmitter feeds an antenna whose impedance is 100 ohm at the operating frequency.
Part of the wave reflects, forming a standing-wave pattern whose peaks and dips an engineer can measure.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
For a load ZL on a line of impedance Z0:
- **Reflection coefficient at the load** Gamma = (ZL - Z0)/(ZL + Z0); at distance d from the load Gamma(d) = Gamma exp(-j 2 beta d), magnitude unchanged on a lossless line.
- **VSWR** S = Vmax/Vmin = (1 + |Gamma|)/(1 - |Gamma|), so |Gamma| = (S - 1)/(S + 1).
- **Return loss** RL = -20 log10 |Gamma| dB.
- **Mismatch loss** ML = -10 log10 (1 - |Gamma|^2) dB.
- Short: Gamma = -1 (S infinite); open: Gamma = +1; matched: Gamma = 0 (S = 1).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** ZL = 100 ohm, Z0 = 50 ohm.
1. Gamma = 50/150 = 1/3.
2. S = (1 + 1/3)/(1 - 1/3) = 2.
3. RL = -20 log(1/3) = 9.54 dB.
4. Reflected power = (1/3)^2 = 11.1 %; ML = -10 log(1 - 0.111) = 0.51 dB.

**Example 2.** Measured S = 3. |Gamma| = 2/4 = 0.5, so 25 % of incident power is reflected, RL = 6.02 dB.

**Example 3.** ZL = 25 - j0 on a 75 ohm line: Gamma = (25 - 75)/(100) = -0.5, S = 3.

steps.title: Interpreting numbers
steps.body: Datasheets quote VSWR 1.5:1 as good (|Gamma| = 0.2, RL = 14 dB, 4 % power reflected). VSWR 2:1 gives RL 9.5 dB. Higher return loss (a bigger positive dB number) means a better match.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing RL with a negative sign: RL as defined above is positive for a passive load.
- Using 10 log instead of 20 log for |Gamma| (it is a field ratio).
- Forgetting that reflected power is |Gamma|^2, not |Gamma|.

lessons.title: Input impedance and the quarter-wave transformer

story.title: One short piece of cable fixes a mismatch

scenes.text: A designer must connect a 200 ohm antenna to a 50 ohm feeder at a single frequency.
A line section exactly one quarter wavelength long, with a carefully chosen impedance, can do it.

steps.title: Input impedance formula
steps.body:
For a lossless line of length l terminated in ZL:

Zin = Z0 (ZL + j Z0 tan(beta l)) / (Z0 + j ZL tan(beta l)).

Special cases:
- l = lambda/2: Zin = ZL (repeats every half wavelength).
- l = lambda/4: Zin = Z0^2/ZL (impedance inverter).
- Short load: Zin = j Z0 tan(beta l) (inductive for l < lambda/4). Open load: Zin = -j Z0 cot(beta l).

**Quarter-wave transformer:** to match real ZL to real Zs, insert a lambda/4 section with Z01 = sqrt(Zs ZL). It is narrow-band; bandwidth grows if several sections are used.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Match 200 ohm load to 50 ohm line: Z01 = sqrt(50 x 200) = 100 ohm; length lambda/4 at f0.

**Example 2.** A lambda/4 section of Z0 = 50 ohm terminated in 100 ohm gives Zin = 2500/100 = 25 ohm.

**Example 3.** Open-circuited 50 ohm stub of length lambda/8: beta l = pi/4, Zin = -j 50 cot(pi/4) = -j50 ohm (capacitive).

**Example 4.** At 2 GHz with vp = 2e8 m/s, lambda/4 = 0.1/4 = 2.5 cm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying the quarter-wave transformer to a complex load without first cancelling its reactance.
- Forgetting the section length uses the wavelength inside the dielectric.
- Believing the match holds across wide bands: reflection grows away from f0.

lessons.title: Lab: Laws, dividers and series-parallel reduction

scenes.text: Asha's 20 V bench supply shows 4 A on its meter, but she expected a different value from her breadboard network.
She reduces the network step by step to find the equivalent resistance and checks the meter reading.

steps.title: Lumped elements and the two laws
steps.body:
A **lumped network** has elements small compared with the signal wavelength, so voltage and current are defined at every terminal.

- **KCL**: the algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero (charge conservation). Σ I_in = Σ I_out.
- **KVL**: the algebraic sum of voltages around any closed loop is zero (energy conservation).
- **Ohm's law**: V = IR for a linear resistor; power P = VI = I²R = V²/R (watts).

steps.title: Series, parallel and dividers
steps.body:
Series: R_eq = R1 + R2 + …, same current. Parallel: 1/R_eq = Σ 1/Rk, same voltage; for two resistors R_eq = R1R2/(R1+R2).

**Voltage divider** (series): V_k = V·R_k/ΣR.
**Current divider** (two branches): I1 = I·R2/(R1+R2) — the *other* resistor appears in the numerator.

steps.title: Worked example 1
steps.body:
A 20 V source feeds (4 Ω + 6 Ω) in parallel with 10 Ω.

1. Series branch = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω.
2. Parallel: 10 ∥ 10 = 5 Ω.
3. I = 20/5 = **4 A**.
4. Each branch carries 2 A; power = 20 × 4 = 80 W.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the divider formula with the *same* resistor in the numerator for currents.
- Adding parallel resistances directly.
- Forgetting that an ideal voltage source is a short for current when 'killed', and a current source is an open circuit.

activity.prompt: Three resistors 12 Ω, 6 Ω and 4 Ω are connected in parallel. Find the equivalent resistance.

quiz.q: KCL is a statement of conservation of:
quiz.why: Current is charge flow; no charge accumulates at a node in a lumped network.

quiz.q: Two resistors 3 Ω and 6 Ω are in parallel. Equivalent resistance?

scenes.text: A sensor board has two loops sharing a 4 Ω resistor. Ravi needs every loop current to size the traces.
He writes KVL around each mesh and solves two equations in two unknowns.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Mesh analysis applies **KVL** to each independent loop of a *planar* network.

1. Assign a clockwise current to every mesh.
2. For mesh k: (sum of resistances in the mesh)·Ik − (shared resistance)·(neighbour current) = (sum of source rises).
3. Solve; branch current in a shared element = difference of mesh currents.

Number of equations = b − n + 1 (branches − nodes + 1).

steps.title: Supermesh
steps.body: If a **current source** lies on the boundary between two meshes, its voltage is unknown. Merge the two meshes into a **supermesh**: write KVL around the outer loop (skipping the source) and add a constraint equation I2 − I1 = I_source.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Mesh 1: 12 V source, 2 Ω, shared 4 Ω. Mesh 2: 2 Ω and shared 4 Ω, no source.

- Mesh 1: (2+4)I1 − 4I2 = 12
- Mesh 2: −4I1 + (2+4)I2 = 0 → I2 = (2/3)I1
- 6I1 − (8/3)I1 = 12 → (10/3)I1 = 12 → **I1 = 3.6 A**, I2 = 2.4 A.
- Current in the shared 4 Ω = I1 − I2 = 1.2 A.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sign error on the mutual term (it is always negative when all mesh currents are clockwise).
- Ignoring the supermesh with a current source on a shared branch.
- Applying mesh analysis directly to a non-planar circuit.

activity.prompt: Using the example network (12 V, 2 Ω, shared 4 Ω, 2 Ω), find the mesh-2 current I2.

quiz.q: A circuit has 6 branches and 4 nodes. Number of independent mesh equations?
When all mesh currents are clockwise, the mutual resistance term in the mesh equation is:
quiz.why: Neighbour currents flow opposite to the loop direction in the shared branch.

quiz.q: A current source shared by two meshes is handled by:
quiz.why: Its unknown voltage is eliminated by the outer-loop KVL plus a constraint.

quiz.q: In the worked example the current through the shared 4 Ω is:

scenes.text: A technician only needs one voltage — at the node feeding a sensor — not every loop current.
Nodal analysis lets her write one KCL equation for that node.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Nodal analysis applies **KCL** with node voltages measured from a chosen *reference (ground)* node.

1. Choose reference; label the other n − 1 nodes.
2. At each node: Σ(conductance × (V_node − V_neighbour)) = Σ source currents entering.
3. Solve the (n − 1) linear equations, often written as **G·V = I**.

Good choice when there are more meshes than nodes, or many current sources.

steps.title: Supernode
steps.body: A voltage source between two non-reference nodes forms a **supernode**: write one KCL for the combined node and add V_a − V_b = V_s.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
20 V source → 5 Ω → node A; A to ground via 10 Ω; a 2 A source injects current into A.

KCL (currents leaving A = injected): (V_A − 20)/5 + V_A/10 = 2.
Multiply by 10: 2V_A − 40 + V_A = 20 → 3V_A = 60 → **V_A = 20 V**.
Check: 0 A through the 5 Ω; 2 A through the 10 Ω from the source ✓.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing the sign convention (currents leaving vs entering) within one equation.
- Forgetting to include the conductance of every branch connected to the node.

steps.title: Source transformation
steps.body:
A voltage source V in series with R is equivalent (at the external terminals) to a current source I = V/R in parallel with the same R. Example: 10 V with 5 Ω ⇔ 2 A with 5 Ω. The arrow direction of the current source follows the source's positive terminal.

Not allowed for ideal sources with R = 0 (voltage) or R = ∞ (current).

steps.title: Delta ↔ Star
steps.body:
**Δ → Y** (R_a is the star resistor at node a, Δ resistors R_ab, R_ca adjacent):
R_a = R_ab·R_ca / (R_ab + R_bc + R_ca), and cyclically.

**Y → Δ**: R_ab = (R_aR_b + R_bR_c + R_cR_a)/R_c.

Balanced case: R_Y = R_Δ/3.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:

Check: the resistance between a and b in the Y is 5 + 3.33 = 8.33 Ω; in the Δ it is 10 ∥ (20+30) = 500/60 = 8.33 Ω ✓.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body:
In a **linear bilateral** network with several independent sources, the response (current or voltage) in any element equals the **algebraic sum of the responses due to each source acting alone**, with the other independent sources replaced by their internal resistances: voltage sources → short circuit, current sources → open circuit.

Dependent sources are **never** deactivated. Superposition cannot be used directly for power (P ∝ I², non-linear).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
12 V — 4 Ω — node A; 6 Ω from A to ground; a 3 A source injects current into A.

1. 12 V alone (current source open): V_A' = 12 × 6/(4+6) = 7.2 V.
2. 3 A alone (voltage source shorted): 4 Ω ∥ 6 Ω = 2.4 Ω, V_A'' = 3 × 2.4 = 7.2 V.
3. V_A = 7.2 + 7.2 = **14.4 V**.
Check by nodal: (V_A−12)/4 + V_A/6 = 3 → 3V_A − 36 + 2V_A = 36 → V_A = 14.4 ✓.

steps.title: Statements
steps.body:

**Norton**: equivalent to a current source I_N (the short-circuit current) in parallel with R_N = R_th, with V_th = I_N·R_th.

R_th: (a) kill independent sources and look into the terminals; or (b) V_oc/I_sc; or (c) with dependent sources present, apply a test source, R_th = V_test/I_test.

steps.title: Theorem
steps.body:
A load receives **maximum power** from a source of Thevenin resistance R_th when **R_L = R_th** (DC). Then
P_max = V_th²/(4R_th).

For AC with complex source impedance Z_th = R_th + jX_th, maximum power requires **Z_L = Z_th\*** (complex conjugate). If only R_L is variable (X fixed): R_L = |Z_th + jX_L|... i.e. R_L = √(R_th² + (X_th+X_L)²).

Efficiency at matching = 50 % (equal power in R_th).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
V_th = 9 V, R_th = 3 Ω.

- R_L = 3 Ω, I = 9/6 = 1.5 A.
- P_max = 1.5² × 3 = 6.75 W = 81/12 ✓.
- Source dissipation also 6.75 W, so efficiency = 50 %.
For R_L = 6 Ω: I = 1 A, P = 6 W < 6.75 W.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking matching maximises efficiency — power stations aim for R_L ≫ R_source.
- Using R_L = Z_th instead of its conjugate in AC.

steps.title: The theorems
steps.body:
- **Reciprocity**: in a linear bilateral single-source network, swapping the source and the ammeter positions leaves the ratio V/I unchanged (transfer impedance symmetrical).
- **Millman**: parallel branches (V_k, R_k) have common voltage V = Σ(V_k/R_k)/Σ(1/R_k).
- **Substitution**: a branch with known voltage/current can be replaced by an independent source of that value.
- **Compensation**: change ΔR in a branch changes branch current by ΔI = −I·ΔR/(R_tot + ΔR) ... equivalently a source −I·ΔR in series.
- **Tellegen**: Σ v_k i_k = 0 over all branches (power absorbed = power delivered) for any lumped network with the same graph.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reciprocity fails with dependent sources, non-linear or non-bilateral elements.
- Millman with a branch that has no series resistance (ideal source).

steps.title: Charging a capacitor
steps.body:
For a series RC circuit with a step Vs applied at t = 0 and v_C(0) = 0:

**v_C(t) = Vs(1 − e^(−t/τ))**, i(t) = (Vs/R)e^(−t/τ), τ = RC (seconds).

- At t = τ the capacitor reaches 63.2 % of Vs.
- After 5τ it is within 1 % of the final value (99.3 %).
- General first-order formula: x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0⁺) − x(∞)]e^(−t/τ).

steps.title: Rise of current

At t = 0⁺ the inductor behaves like an **open circuit** (current continuity); at t → ∞ like a **short**.

Decay (source removed through a freewheel path): i(t) = I₀ e^(−t/τ).

steps.title: Rules at a switching instant
steps.body:
- Capacitor voltage is continuous: v_C(0⁺) = v_C(0⁻).
- Inductor current is continuous: i_L(0⁺) = i_L(0⁻).
- Everything else (resistor currents, inductor voltage, capacitor current) may jump.

Procedure: (1) steady state before switching → initial values; (2) replace C by a voltage source / L by a current source of those values at 0⁺; (3) find x(∞); (4) find τ with the sources off; (5) x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0⁺) − x(∞)]e^(−t/τ).

steps.title: Characteristic equation
steps.body:
Series RLC (source-free): s² + (R/L)s + 1/(LC) = 0.

Define **α = R/2L** (neper frequency) and **ω₀ = 1/√(LC)** (resonant frequency).

- **α > ω₀ overdamped**: two real roots, no oscillation.
- **α = ω₀ critically damped**: R = 2√(L/C); fastest non-oscillatory decay.
- **α < ω₀ underdamped**: s = −α ± jω_d, **ω_d = √(ω₀² − α²)**; response e^(−αt)(A cos ω_d t + B sin ω_d t).

Damping ratio ζ = α/ω₀; Q = ω₀L/R.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using α = R/L for the series circuit (that's 2α); for parallel RLC α = 1/2RC.
- Calling ω_d the resonant frequency.

steps.title: Phasor basics
steps.body:
A sinusoid v = V_m cos(ωt + φ) is represented by the phasor V = V_rms∠φ. Impedances: Z_R = R, Z_L = jωL = jX_L, Z_C = 1/(jωC) = −jX_C.

Z = R + jX; |Z| = √(R² + X²); φ = tan⁻¹(X/R). For R-L: current lags voltage by φ. Admittance Y = 1/Z = G + jB.

KVL, KCL, mesh, nodal, Thevenin all work unchanged with complex numbers.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
R = 30 Ω in series with X_L = 40 Ω on 230 V.

- Z = 30 + j40 = 50∠53.13° Ω.
- I = 230/50 = **4.6 A**, lagging by 53.13°.
- Power factor = cos φ = 30/50 = **0.6 lag**.
- V_R = 138 V, V_L = 184 V (arithmetically greater than 230 V total? √(138²+184²) = 230 ✓ — they add as phasors).

steps.title: Power triangle

- Real power P = VI cos φ (W).
- Reactive power Q = VI sin φ (VAr), positive for inductive loads.
- Apparent power S = VI (VA); S² = P² + Q²; pf = P/S.

**Correction**: Q_C = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂); C = Q_C/(ωV²).

courses.summary: Z, Y, ABCD and h parameters of two-port networks, conversions, termination and cascading, plus graph theory: trees, cutsets, tie-sets and incidence matrices.
outcomes: Derive and compute Z, Y, ABCD and h parameters

scenes.text: A lab gets a sealed attenuator with four terminals. Only port measurements are allowed.
Open-circuiting each port in turn gives the Z parameters.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
With port-1 (V₁, I₁) and port-2 (V₂, I₂) both currents entering:

V₁ = z₁₁I₁ + z₁₂I₂, V₂ = z₂₁I₁ + z₂₂I₂.

- z₁₁ = V₁/I₁ (I₂ = 0), z₂₂ = V₂/I₂ (I₁ = 0): open-circuit driving-point impedances.
- z₁₂ = V₁/I₂ (I₁ = 0), z₂₁ = V₂/I₁ (I₂ = 0): open-circuit transfer impedances.

Reciprocal network: z₁₂ = z₂₁. Symmetrical: also z₁₁ = z₂₂.

steps.title: Worked example (T-network)
steps.body:
T: series arm R_a = 10 Ω at port 1, series arm R_b = 20 Ω at port 2, shunt R_c = 5 Ω common.

- z₁₁ = R_a + R_c = **15 Ω**
- z₂₂ = R_b + R_c = **25 Ω**
- z₁₂ = z₂₁ = R_c = **5 Ω**
Δz = 15×25 − 5×5 = 350 Ω².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Short-circuiting instead of open-circuiting for Z parameters; using the outgoing-current convention for I₂ (the standard has I₂ *into* the port).

activity.prompt: For the T-network (R_a = 10 Ω, R_b = 20 Ω, R_c = 5 Ω) find z₂₂.

quiz.q: Z parameters are measured with ports:
Z parameters of a single series impedance Z between the ports (no shunt): do they exist?
options: No — the open-circuit parameters are infinite/undefined (use ABCD or Y)
quiz.why: With a port open no current flows, so voltage is undefined: Z matrix does not exist for a pure series element.

scenes.text: A transistor datasheet lists h-parameters, not Z. Why?
Short-circuit and open-circuit tests are easy to do on a transistor at its operating point.

steps.title: Y and h definitions
steps.body:
**Y**: I₁ = y₁₁V₁ + y₁₂V₂, I₂ = y₂₁V₁ + y₂₂V₂ (short-circuit parameters). [Y] = [Z]⁻¹: y₁₁ = z₂₂/Δz, y₁₂ = −z₁₂/Δz, y₂₁ = −z₂₁/Δz, y₂₂ = z₁₁/Δz.

**h (hybrid)**: V₁ = h₁₁I₁ + h₁₂V₂, I₂ = h₂₁I₁ + h₂₂V₂, with h₁₁ = input impedance (V₂ = 0), h₁₂ = reverse voltage ratio (I₁ = 0), h₂₁ = forward current gain (V₂ = 0), h₂₂ = output admittance (I₁ = 0).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
From Z = [[15, 5],[5, 25]], Δz = 350.

- y₁₁ = 25/350 = **0.0714 S**
- y₁₂ = y₂₁ = −5/350 = −0.01429 S
- y₂₂ = 15/350 = 0.0429 S

Forward current gain with the output shorted: h₂₁ = y₂₁/y₁₁ = −0.01429/0.0714 = **−0.2**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the minus signs in matrix inversion; mixing up which test (short vs open) defines each hybrid parameter.

activity.prompt: From Z = [[15, 5],[5, 25]] Ω, compute y₁₁.

quiz.q: Y parameters are found with ports:
Why do transistor datasheets use h-parameters?
options: Easy to measure at low frequency with open/short terminations
quiz.why: Input short and output open conditions are practical.

scenes.text: A transmission chain cascades three two-port sections.

steps.title: ABCD (transmission) parameters
steps.body:
V₁ = A V₂ − B I₂, I₁ = C V₂ − D I₂ (I₂ leaving port 2).

A = V₁/V₂ (I₂ = 0), B = −V₁/I₂ (V₂ = 0), C = I₁/V₂ (I₂ = 0), D = −I₁/I₂ (V₂ = 0).
Reciprocal: AD − BC = 1. Symmetrical: A = D.
**Cascade**: [T] = [T₁][T₂].

From Z: A = z₁₁/z₂₁, B = Δz/z₂₁, C = 1/z₂₁, D = z₂₂/z₂₁.
Input impedance with load Z_L: Z_in = (A Z_L + B)/(C Z_L + D).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using +I₂ instead of −I₂; multiplying cascade matrices in the wrong order.

quiz.why: Output of the first is input of the second.

lessons.title: Lab: Graph theory — trees, cutsets, tie-sets

story.title: How many equations do I really need?

scenes.text: A large PCB network has 9 branches and 6 nodes. Writing every KCL is wasteful.
Graph theory counts the independent equations before solving.

steps.title: Terms
steps.body:
A **graph** replaces each element by a branch (line) between nodes. A **tree** connects all n nodes with no loop: it has **n − 1 twigs**. Remaining branches are **links**: l = b − n + 1.

- **Incidence matrix A** (n × b): a_jk = +1 leaving, −1 entering, 0 otherwise; rank n − 1; KCL: A i = 0.
- **Fundamental cutset** (one twig + links): n − 1 independent KCL equations; matrix Q.
- **Fundamental tie-set** (one link + twigs): b − n + 1 independent KVL equations; matrix B. B Qᵀ relations: B_t = −Q_lᵀ.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
b = 9, n = 6.

- Twigs = 5. Links = 9 − 6 + 1 = **4**.
- Independent KCL equations = 5; independent KVL = 4.
- Total trees of a complete graph on n nodes = n^(n−2) (Cayley): K₄ has 16 trees.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting that the incidence matrix has one dependent row; counting a tree that contains a loop.

activity.prompt: A connected graph has 9 branches and 6 nodes. How many links does a tree leave?

steps.title: Why ABCD

lessons.title: Lab: Network functions, poles and zeros

story.title: Reading a transfer function like a map

scenes.text: A filter's transfer function is given only as a ratio of polynomials.
Its pole and zero positions tell you stability, speed and gain.

steps.title: Types of network function
steps.body:
With zero initial conditions, N(s) = ratio of Laplace transforms. **Driving-point**: Z(s) = V₁/I₁, Y(s) = I₁/V₁. **Transfer**: voltage gain G₂₁ = V₂/V₁, current gain, transfer impedance Z₂₁ = V₂/I₁, transfer admittance Y₂₁.

H(s) = K(s − z₁)…/(s − p₁)…. Poles = roots of the denominator; zeros = roots of the numerator. The impulse response is a sum of terms e^(p_k t); stability requires all poles in the open left half plane (LHP).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Reading the sign of poles backwards; forgetting that a pole at the origin gives marginal stability, not instability.

activity.prompt: For H(s) = 10(s+2)/((s+1)(s+5)) find the DC gain H(0).

lessons.title: Lab: Hurwitz polynomials and the Routh test

scenes.text: A feedback amplifier's characteristic equation is s³ + 2s² + 3s + 8 = 0.
The Routh array tells her, without finding the roots, whether it is stable.

steps.title: Hurwitz and Routh
steps.body:
A polynomial is **Hurwitz** if all roots lie in the open LHP (zeros on the jω axis are allowed only for the 'strictly Hurwitz' relaxation in synthesis, as simple roots). Necessary: all coefficients positive, none missing.

Routh array for a₃s³ + a₂s² + a₁s + a₀: row s³: a₃, a₁; row s²: a₂, a₀; row s¹: b₁ = (a₂a₁ − a₃a₀)/a₂; row s⁰: a₀. The number of sign changes in the first column = number of RHP roots. Cubic condition: a₂a₁ > a₃a₀.

steps.title: Worked example 2
steps.body: s³ + 2s² + 3s + 8: b₁ = (2×3 − 8)/2 = **−1**. First column: 1, 2, −1, 8 → two sign changes → **2 RHP roots**, unstable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Concluding stability from positive coefficients alone (necessary but not sufficient above second order).

activity.prompt: For s³ + 2s² + 3s + 8, compute the s¹-row element b₁ of the Routh array.

lessons.title: Lab: Positive-real functions and Foster synthesis

scenes.text: A designer has a target driving-point impedance and needs a physical network from coils and capacitors.
Foster's forms turn a partial-fraction expansion directly into a ladder of series and parallel blocks.

steps.title: Realizability
steps.body:
A driving-point function F(s) is **positive real (PR)** if Re F(s) ≥ 0 for Re s ≥ 0 and F real for real s. PR functions are realizable by passive R, L, C (and no active elements).

**LC immittances**: odd ratio of polynomials; poles and zeros simple, on the jω axis, interlacing; residues positive. **Foster I**: expand Z(s) in partial fractions → series connection of L (term ks), C (k/s) and parallel LC tanks (k s/(s²+ω²)). **Foster II**: expand Y(s) → parallel connection of blocks. Cauer forms: continued-fraction ladders.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the term at infinity (ks) after polynomial division; giving negative element values (a sign the function is not PR).

steps.title: Filter basics
steps.body:
First-order RC low-pass: H = 1/(1 + jωRC), cut-off f_c = 1/(2πRC), roll-off −20 dB/decade.

**Butterworth** (maximally flat): |H(jω)|² = 1/(1 + (ω/ω_c)^(2n)), roll-off −20n dB/decade. Order for passband loss A_p (dB) at ω_p and stopband loss A_s at ω_s:
n ≥ log[(10^(A_s/10) − 1)/(10^(A_p/10) − 1)] / (2 log(ω_s/ω_p)).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Not rounding the order up; confusing −3 dB cut-off with the passband edge when A_p ≠ 3 dB.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
Normalised 3rd-order Butterworth (1 Ω, 1 rad/s): g₁ = 1, g₂ = 2, g₃ = 1.

Scaling: shunt C = g/(R₀ω_c), series L = g R₀/ω_c, where ω_c = 2πf_c.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
R₀ = 50 Ω, f_c = 1 MHz, ω_c = 6.283×10⁶ rad/s.

- C₁ = 1/(50 × 6.283×10⁶) = **3.183 nF**.
- L₂ = 2 × 50/6.283×10⁶ = **15.92 µH**.
- C₃ = 3.183 nF.
Topology: shunt C₁, series L₂, shunt C₃ (π-filter). Attenuation at 2 MHz = 10 log(1 + 2⁶) = 18.1 dB.

steps.title: Real parts
steps.body: Pick the nearest standard values (3.3 nF, 15 µH) and re-check cut-off; tolerance of ±5 % shifts f_c by a similar amount.

courses.title: Unit 7 · Revision, practicals and exam
courses.summary: Formula and key-point sheet, standard network-theory laboratory experiments (theorems, transients, resonance) with procedure, observation tables and viva questions, previous-year-style problems and a 20-question exam.
outcomes: Recall the key formulas of all network theory units

Answer viva questions on theorems and resonance
Attempt exam-style problems under time pressure

scenes.text: Kabir has one hour to revise the whole subject.
He builds a one-page sheet of formulas he must be able to write from memory.

steps.title: Laws and theorems
steps.body:
- KCL: ΣI = 0; KVL: ΣV = 0. Divider: V_k = V·R_k/ΣR; I₁ = I·R₂/(R₁+R₂).
- Δ→Y: R_a = R_abR_ca/ΣR; balanced R_Y = R_Δ/3.
- Thevenin: V_th = V_oc, R_th = V_oc/I_sc. P_max = V_th²/(4R_th) at R_L = R_th (conjugate in AC).
- Millman: V = Σ(V/R)/Σ(1/R). Tellegen: Σvi = 0.
- Mesh equations b−n+1; nodal n−1.

steps.title: Transients and AC
steps.body:
- RC: τ = RC; RL: τ = L/R; x(t) = x(∞) + [x(0⁺) − x(∞)]e^(−t/τ).
- Series RLC: α = R/2L, ω₀ = 1/√LC; ω_d = √(ω₀² − α²); R_crit = 2√(L/C).
- Z_L = jωL, Z_C = 1/jωC; S = P + jQ; Q_C = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂); C = Q_C/ωV².
- Resonance: f₀ = 1/2π√LC; Q = ω₀L/R; BW = f₀/Q.
- 3φ: P = √3V_LI_L cos φ.

steps.title: Two-ports and synthesis
steps.body:
- Z: open-circuit; Y: short-circuit; AD − BC = 1 for reciprocal.
- Z_in = (AZ_L + B)/(CZ_L + D); cascade = matrix product.
- Tree: n−1 twigs, b−n+1 links.
- Hurwitz: all poles in LHP; Routh sign changes = RHP roots.
- Butterworth: |H|² = 1/(1+(ω/ω_c)^(2n)).

steps.title: Exam technique
steps.body: Write the formula, substitute with units, box the answer; for theorems state the conditions (linear, bilateral) before using them.

steps.title: Aim and procedure
steps.body:

2. Use a DSO; set the time base to 100 ms/div.
3. Note the time at which v_C reaches 63.2 % of 5 V = 3.16 V.
4. Repeat for 2τ and 3τ; tabulate v_C versus t.

lessons.title: Lab: Series resonance and viva questions

scenes.text: You will sweep the frequency of a series RLC circuit and find the peak current.
The examiner then asks viva questions.

steps.title: Aim and procedure
steps.body:
Aim: find f₀, Q and bandwidth of a series RLC circuit.

1. L = 1 mH, C = 0.1 µF, R = 10 Ω; AC source 1 V.
2. Vary frequency from 5 to 30 kHz; record the voltage across R (∝ current).
3. f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) = 1/(2π × 10⁻⁵) = **15.92 kHz**.
4. Find f₁, f₂ where the current is 0.707 of maximum; BW = f₂ − f₁ = R/2πL = **1.59 kHz**; Q = f₀/BW = 10.
5. Plot current vs frequency on semilog paper.

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body: Keep the source amplitude constant while sweeping; use a low-ESR capacitor; note that the generator's output impedance adds to R.

steps.title: Before you start
steps.body: Read the task once fully. Note what 'done' looks like, then work step by step. If you get stuck, use the hint — then try again without it.

activity.prompt: Common viva questions — read each answer.

items.q: What happens to impedance at series resonance?
items.a: X_L = X_C so Z = R, which is the minimum; current is maximum.

items.q: How is Q related to bandwidth?
items.a: BW = f₀/Q; higher Q gives narrower bandwidth and better selectivity.

items.q: Why can the voltage across L or C exceed the supply voltage?
items.a: At resonance each reactive voltage equals Q times the source voltage, though they cancel each other.

items.q: Why is Thevenin's theorem not valid for a diode circuit?
items.a: The diode is non-linear; the theorem requires linear elements.

items.q: State the condition for maximum power transfer in AC.
items.a: The load impedance must be the complex conjugate of the source impedance.

scenes.text: A biomedical engineer records a heartbeat. The voltage varies continuously with time, but the monitor stores one number every 4 ms.
The same heartbeat is now two signals: a continuous-time x(t) and a discrete-time x[n] = x(nT). Signals and Systems gives one language for both.

steps.title: What is a signal?
steps.body:
A **signal** is a function carrying information, usually of time. **Continuous-time (CT)** signals x(t) are defined for every real t; **discrete-time (DT)** signals x[n] only for integer n. Amplitude can also be continuous or quantised: an *analog* signal is CT with continuous amplitude, a *digital* signal is DT with quantised amplitude.

A **system** transforms an input signal into an output signal: y(t) = T{x(t)}.

steps.title: Standard signals
steps.body:
- **Unit step** u(t) = 1 for t ≥ 0, 0 for t < 0 (u[n] likewise for n ≥ 0).
- **Unit ramp** r(t) = t·u(t) = ∫u(τ)dτ.
- **Unit impulse** δ(t): zero for t ≠ 0, with ∫δ(t)dt = 1. In DT, δ[n] = 1 only at n = 0.
- **Real exponential** e^{at}; **complex exponential** e^{jωt} = cos ωt + j sin ωt.
- **Rectangular pulse** rect(t/τ), **sinc** sinc(t) = sin(πt)/(πt).

Relations: δ(t) = du/dt; u(t) = ∫_{-∞}^{t} δ(τ)dτ; in DT δ[n] = u[n] − u[n−1].

steps.title: Properties of the impulse
steps.body:
- **Sampling (sifting):** ∫ x(t)δ(t − t0)dt = x(t0).
- **Scaling:** δ(at) = δ(t)/|a|.
- **Product:** x(t)δ(t − t0) = x(t0)δ(t − t0).
- **Even:** δ(−t) = δ(t).

steps.title: Solved example 1
steps.body:
Evaluate I = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (t² + 3) δ(t − 2) dt.

Step 1: sifting property with t0 = 2.
Step 2: I = (2² + 3) = **7**.

Now I2 = ∫ cos(πt) δ(2t − 1) dt. Write δ(2t − 1) = δ(2(t − 0.5)) = ½ δ(t − 0.5). I2 = ½ cos(0.5π) = **0**.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body:
Express the rectangular pulse of height 5 lasting from t = 1 to t = 4 using steps.

x(t) = 5[u(t − 1) − u(t − 4)]. Check: at t = 2, 5(1 − 0) = 5; at t = 5, 5(1 − 1) = 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating δ(t) as a function with value ∞ — it is a distribution defined by its integral.
- Forgetting the 1/|a| factor in δ(at).
- Confusing u(0): the value at 0 is ½ in some texts; in DT u[0] = 1.
