scenes.text: A lab technician must decide whether a signal has finite energy (a pulse such as a lightning strike) or finite power (a mains sine wave), because the measurement method differs.
She uses two integrals: total energy and average power.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
For a CT signal: **E = ∫|x(t)|²dt** over (−∞, ∞), **P = lim_{T→∞} (1/2T) ∫_{−T}^{T} |x(t)|² dt**.

For DT: **E = Σ|x[n]|²**, **P = lim (1/(2N+1)) Σ_{−N}^{N}|x[n]|²**.

- **Energy signal:** 0 < E < ∞ (then P = 0).
- **Power signal:** 0 < P < ∞ (then E = ∞).
- Some signals (e.g. e^{t}, ramp) are neither.

steps.title: Periodicity
steps.body:
x(t) is periodic if x(t + T) = x(t) for all t; the smallest T > 0 is the **fundamental period** T0 and ω0 = 2π/T0.

Sum of two periodic signals with periods T1, T2 is periodic iff T1/T2 is rational; then T0 = LCM(T1, T2).

DT: e^{jΩ0 n} is periodic iff Ω0/2π = m/N is rational; N is the smallest integer with N·Ω0 = 2πm. **Unlike CT, a DT sinusoid is not always periodic.**

steps.title: Solved example 2 — power
steps.body: x(t) = 4cos(10t + 30°). Power of A cos(ωt+φ) is A²/2 = 16/2 = **8**. Average over one period: (1/T)∫16cos² = 16·½ = 8. Since E = ∞ it is a power signal.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — DT period
steps.body: x[n] = cos(3πn/8). Ω0 = 3π/8, Ω0/2π = 3/16 → m/N = 3/16 in lowest terms so **N = 16**. For cos(n/5), Ω0/2π = 1/(10π) is irrational → **not periodic**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reducing m/N is essential: cos(πn/4): 1/8 → N = 8, not 4m.
- Using A² instead of A²/2 for the power of a sinusoid.
- Calling a periodic signal an energy signal — periodic signals have infinite energy.

lessons.title: System properties: linearity, time-invariance, causality, stability

scenes.text: An audio amplifier with y = 3x sounds fine. Another with y = x² adds harsh distortion.
A test engineer feeds scaled and delayed inputs to see how the output behaves.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Linear:** T{a x1 + b x2} = a T{x1} + b T{x2} (additivity + homogeneity).
- **Time-invariant:** if x(t) → y(t) then x(t − t0) → y(t − t0).
- **Causal:** output at t depends only on inputs at ≤ t.
- **Memoryless (static):** output at t depends only on input at the same t.
- **BIBO stable:** every bounded input gives bounded output.
- **Invertible:** distinct inputs give distinct outputs.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — y(t) = t x(t)
steps.body:
Linearity: T{a x1 + b x2} = t(a x1 + b x2) = a·t x1 + b·t x2 ✓ **linear**.
Time invariance: delayed input x(t − t0) gives t x(t − t0); delayed output is y(t − t0) = (t − t0)x(t − t0). Not equal → **time-varying**. Memoryless, causal, not BIBO stable (t grows unbounded for x = 1).

steps.title: Solved example 2 — y[n] = x[n] + 2 (a bias)
steps.body: Zero input gives y = 2 ≠ 0 → violates homogeneity → **non-linear** (an *incremental* linear system). Time-invariant, causal, memoryless, stable.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — y(t) = x(−t)
steps.body: Linear. Time-varying: x(t − t0) gives x(−t − t0), but y(t − t0) = x(−t + t0). **Non-causal** (y(−1) needs x(1)). Stable.

steps.title: Quick checks
steps.body:
- Terms like x², |x|, constants, sin x → non-linear.
- Explicit t multiplying x, or x(at) with a ≠ 1, → time-varying.
- Argument like t + 1 or n + 1 → non-causal.
- Integral/sum of the past → memory.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Concluding 'non-linear' for y = 2x + 1 only from the +1 — correct, but the reason is non-zero output for zero input.
- Testing time invariance by shifting the output *before* substituting the shifted input into the rule.

activity.prompt: Sort each system as Linear or Non-linear.

quiz.why: Scaling the argument breaks time invariance.

scenes.text: In a design review, you must justify in writing why a sensor-conditioning block is safe to use in a feedback loop.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: For any given system you answer, in order: memory? causality? linearity? time-invariance? stability? Each answer needs a one-line proof or counterexample.

steps.title: Worked case
steps.body: y[n] = x[n] − x[n−1] (first difference). Memory: yes (uses n−1). Causal: yes. Linear: yes. Time-invariant: yes. BIBO: |y| ≤ 2·max|x| → stable. Impulse response h[n] = δ[n] − δ[n−1].

steps.title: Reminder
steps.body: A single counterexample is enough to disprove a property; a proof must cover all inputs.

lessons.title: Impulse response and the convolution sum

scenes.text: Clap once in an empty hall and record the echo. That recording is the room's impulse response.
Any speech in that hall is just many scaled, delayed claps — so the output is a sum of scaled, delayed echoes.

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body:
Any DT signal: x[n] = Σ_k x[k] δ[n − k]. For an LTI system with h[n] = T{δ[n]}, linearity and shift-invariance give

**y[n] = Σ_{k=−∞}^{∞} x[k] h[n − k] = x[n] * h[n]**.

CT: **y(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t − τ) dτ**.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
- Commutative: x*h = h*x. Associative: (x*h1)*h2 = x*(h1*h2) → cascade multiplies in frequency.
- Distributive: x*(h1+h2) → parallel.
- Identity: x*δ = x. Shift: x[n]*δ[n−n0] = x[n−n0].
- Length: if x has N1 samples and h has N2, y has **N1 + N2 − 1** samples.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to flip h.
- Wrong output length / origin: starting index of y = start(x) + start(h).
- Adding instead of multiplying within terms.

steps.title: Graphical method
steps.body: 1) Sketch x(τ) and h(τ). 2) Flip h to h(−τ). 3) Shift by t → h(t − τ). 4) Multiply and integrate over overlap; the integral changes form in each overlap region, so find the breakpoints.

steps.title: Solved example 1 — u(t) * u(t)
steps.body: y(t) = ∫u(τ)u(t − τ)dτ = ∫_0^t dτ = t for t ≥ 0. **y(t) = t u(t) = ramp**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — rect * rect
steps.body: Two unit-height rectangles of width 2 (from 0 to 2) convolve to a triangle from 0 to 4, peak = 2 at t = 2 (area of overlap = width × height² = 2).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Wrong limits when regions change (before overlap, partial, full, leaving).
- Not including u(t) in the final answer: y(t) = 0 for t < 0.

scenes.text: A guitar pedal with feedback can ring forever and blow the speakers. A designer inspects its impulse response to decide.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Conditions
steps.body:
- **Memoryless** iff h[n] = Kδ[n].
- **Causal** iff h[n] = 0 for n < 0 (h(t) = 0 for t < 0).
- **BIBO stable** iff Σ|h[n]| < ∞ (∫|h(t)|dt < ∞).
- **Invertible** if a g exists with h*g = δ.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: h[n] = (0.5)^n u[n]. Σ|h| = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2 < ∞ → stable, causal. h[n] = 2^n u[n]: Σ diverges → unstable. h[n] = (0.5)^{|n|}: Σ = 1 + 2·(0.5/(1−0.5)) = 3 → stable but non-causal.

steps.title: Example 2 (CT)
steps.body: h(t) = e^{−3t}u(t): ∫ = 1/3, stable. h(t) = e^{t}u(t): diverges, unstable. h(t) = u(t) (integrator): ∫ diverges → unstable although bounded (marginally stable); a bounded input u(t) gives the ramp.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using |h| bounded as the stability test — it must be absolutely summable.
- Forgetting the |n| in two-sided sequences.

- Forgetting initial rest — otherwise the system is not LTI.
- Calling recursion automatically unstable: only if the pole is outside the unit circle.

story.title: Why a guitar string sounds like a guitar

scenes.text: A plucked string is periodic, so it is a sum of a fundamental and harmonics. The mix of harmonic strengths is its timbre.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
For periodic x(t) with period T0 and ω0 = 2π/T0 (Dirichlet conditions hold):

**x(t) = Σ_k c_k e^{jkω0t}, c_k = (1/T0) ∫_{T0} x(t) e^{−jkω0t} dt**.

c_0 is the DC average. For real x, c_{−k} = c_k*. Trigonometric form: x = a0 + Σ(a_k cos kω0t + b_k sin kω0t) with a_k = 2Re c_k, b_k = −2Im c_k.

steps.title: Symmetry and Parseval
steps.body:
Even x → only cosines (c_k real); odd x → only sines (c_k imaginary); half-wave symmetry → only odd harmonics.

**Parseval:** (1/T0)∫|x|² dt = Σ|c_k|².

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 1/T0 factor.
- Mixing two-sided |c_k|² with one-sided amplitude²/2.
- Gibbs phenomenon: ≈9 % overshoot at jumps never disappears with more terms.

lessons.title: Lab: Fourier transform and its pairs

scenes.text: Let the period T0 → ∞: the discrete harmonics merge into a continuum, giving the Fourier transform.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
**X(ω) = ∫ x(t) e^{−jωt} dt**, **x(t) = (1/2π)∫ X(ω) e^{jωt} dω**. Exists if x is absolutely integrable (sufficient). In terms of f: X(f) = ∫x e^{−j2πft}dt.

Standard pairs:
- δ(t) ↔ 1; 1 ↔ 2πδ(ω)
- e^{−at}u(t) ↔ 1/(a + jω), a>0
- e^{−a|t|} ↔ 2a/(a² + ω²)
- rect(t/τ) ↔ τ sinc(ωτ/2π) = τ sin(ωτ/2)/(ωτ/2)
- cos ω0t ↔ π[δ(ω−ω0)+δ(ω+ω0)]
- u(t) ↔ πδ(ω) + 1/jω

steps.title: Properties
steps.body: Linearity; time shift x(t−t0) ↔ X e^{−jωt0}; frequency shift e^{jω0t}x ↔ X(ω−ω0); scaling x(at) ↔ X(ω/a)/|a|; differentiation ↔ jωX; integration ↔ X/jω + πX(0)δ; convolution ↔ product; multiplication ↔ (1/2π) convolution; duality; Parseval E = (1/2π)∫|X|²dω.

steps.title: Solved example 2
steps.body: Rectangle of height 1, width 2 ms: X(0) = area = 2×10⁻³. First null where ωτ/2 = π → ω = 2π/τ → f = 1/τ = 500 Hz.

steps.title: Solved example 3 — modulation
steps.body: x(t) = m(t)cos(ω_c t) ↔ ½[M(ω−ω_c)+M(ω+ω_c)]. If M occupies |ω| ≤ W, the product occupies ω_c ± W: bandwidth 2W.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dropping the 1/|a| in the scaling property.
- Mixing f and ω conventions (2π factors).
- Forgetting the πδ term in the transform of u(t).

scenes.text: A tone control passes low frequencies and cuts high ones. Its H(ω) is the ratio of output to input spectrum.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: H(ω)
steps.body: For LTI system with stable h: **H(ω) = F{h}**, Y(ω) = H(ω)X(ω). For input e^{jω0t}, the output is H(ω0)e^{jω0t}; for A cos(ω0t+φ): |H|A cos(ω0t + φ + ∠H). Ideal distortionless transmission: H = K e^{−jωt_d} (constant magnitude, linear phase).

steps.title: Filters
steps.body: Ideal LPF/HPF/BPF/BSF are non-causal (sinc impulse response). 3-dB bandwidth: where |H|² falls to half. RC low-pass: H = 1/(1 + jωRC), ω_c = 1/RC.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Non-linear phase causes dispersion even if the magnitude is flat.

activity.prompt: Amplitude of the output for 10cos(1000t) through H=1/(1+jω/1000).

lessons.title: Energy spectral density, bandwidth and uncertainty

scenes.text: A radar engineer wants a short pulse for resolution, but short pulses mean wide bandwidth — a trade-off baked into Fourier theory.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Rayleigh and trade-off
steps.body: Energy: E = (1/2π)∫|X(ω)|²dω; ESD = |X|². Power-signal: PSD S(ω) from the autocorrelation R(τ) ↔ S(ω) (Wiener–Khinchin). Compressing in time by a expands the spectrum by a (**time–bandwidth product** is roughly constant).

steps.title: Example
steps.body: A pulse of width τ has main-lobe null bandwidth ≈ 1/τ. τ = 1 µs → ≈ 1 MHz; τ = 10 ns → 100 MHz.

steps.title: Example 2 — Parseval
steps.body: x = e^{−t}u(t): E = ½. Fraction of energy within |ω| ≤ 1 rad/s: (1/2π)∫_{−1}^{1} dω/(1+ω²) = (1/2π)(2·π/4) = 0.25 → 50 % of total.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Believing a signal can be both strictly time-limited and band-limited — it cannot.

courses.summary: Bilateral and unilateral Laplace transforms, region of convergence, properties, inverse by partial fractions, transfer function, poles, stability and circuit analysis.

scenes.text: e^{t}u(t) has no Fourier transform because it grows. Multiply by e^{−σt} and it does — that is the Laplace idea.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
**X(s) = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} x(t)e^{−st}dt**, s = σ + jω. Unilateral: lower limit 0⁻. The **ROC** is the set of σ for which the integral converges; the transform is incomplete without it.

Pairs (unilateral, causal):
- δ(t) ↔ 1 (all s)
- u(t) ↔ 1/s, Re s > 0
- t u(t) ↔ 1/s²
- e^{−at}u(t) ↔ 1/(s + a), Re s > −a
- cos ω0t u ↔ s/(s²+ω0²); sin ω0t u ↔ ω0/(s²+ω0²)
- e^{−at}cos ω0t ↔ (s+a)/((s+a)²+ω0²)
- t^n u ↔ n!/s^{n+1}

steps.title: ROC rules
steps.body: Right-sided → ROC is a right half-plane; left-sided → left half-plane; two-sided → a strip; finite-duration → whole plane. ROC contains no poles. Stable system ⇔ ROC includes jω axis. Causal + rational ⇒ ROC right of the rightmost pole.

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: x(t) = e^{−2t}u(t) + e^{3t}u(−t). First term: 1/(s+2), Re s > −2. Second: −1/(s−3), Re s < 3. Sum: 1/(s+2) − 1/(s−3) = −5/((s+2)(s−3)), ROC −2 < Re s < 3 (strip; contains jω axis so FT exists).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing X(s) without ROC (e^{−at}u(t) and −e^{−at}u(−t) have the same algebra, different ROC).
- Using the unilateral transform for non-causal analysis.

activity.prompt: Complete: the Laplace transform of e^{−3t}u(t) is 1/(s + ___).

scenes.text: A thermostat engineer wants the final temperature of a heater without solving the full response.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Properties
steps.body:
Linearity; time shift x(t−t0)u(t−t0) ↔ e^{−st0}X(s); s-shift e^{−at}x ↔ X(s+a); scaling x(at) ↔ X(s/a)/a; differentiation dx/dt ↔ sX(s) − x(0⁻); d²x/dt² ↔ s²X − s x(0⁻) − x'(0⁻); integration ↔ X/s; t x(t) ↔ −dX/ds; convolution ↔ product.

**Initial value:** x(0⁺) = lim_{s→∞} sX(s). **Final value:** x(∞) = lim_{s→0} sX(s) — valid only if all poles of sX lie in the open left half-plane.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Applying the final-value theorem to X = 1/(s²+1) (poles on jω axis, no limit exists).

lessons.title: Lab: Inverse Laplace by partial fractions

story.title: From algebra back to a waveform

scenes.text: After solving a circuit in the s-domain you must convert back to a time waveform. Partial fractions break X(s) into pairs you know.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: 1) Ensure degree(num) < degree(den) (else divide). 2) Factor denominator. 3) Residues: for simple pole p_i, A_i = (s − p_i)X(s)|_{s=p_i}. Repeated pole of order 2: A/(s−p)² + B/(s−p). Complex poles: complete the square. 4) Use ROC to choose causal/anti-causal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not dividing out an improper fraction (leaves δ terms).
- Wrong sign for left-sided ROC: −e^{−at}u(−t).

activity.prompt: For X(s)=(3s+5)/((s+1)(s+2)), find x(1) in decimals (x=2e^{−t}+e^{−2t}).

lessons.title: Transfer function, poles, zeros and stability

scenes.text: A badly compensated amplifier rings and oscillates. Its transfer function has poles too close to the jω axis.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: H(s)
steps.body: **H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) = L{h(t)}** for zero initial conditions. Poles: roots of the denominator; zeros: roots of the numerator. For a causal system, BIBO stable ⇔ all poles in the open left half-plane. Frequency response H(jω) is H(s) evaluated on the jω axis (if stable).

steps.title: Second-order
steps.body: H(s) = ω_n²/(s² + 2ζω_n s + ω_n²). ζ<1: underdamped, poles −ζω_n ± jω_n√(1−ζ²); overshoot e^{−πζ/√(1−ζ²)}; ζ=1 critical; ζ>1 over-damped.

steps.title: Example 1 — ODE to H
steps.body: y'' + 5y' + 6y = 2x'+ 4x → H = (2s+4)/(s²+5s+6) = 2(s+2)/((s+2)(s+3)) = 2/(s+3) (pole-zero cancellation). Stable.

steps.title: Example 3 — RC
steps.body: Series RC with output across C: H = 1/(1 + sRC). R=1 kΩ, C=1 µF: pole at −1000 rad/s, ω_c = 1000 rad/s (159 Hz).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Cancelling a right-half-plane pole-zero pair hides an unstable internal mode.
- Assuming stability from poles of the *numerator*.

activity.prompt: Percent overshoot for ζ = 0.5 (second-order system).

scenes.text: A series RLC with R=20 Ω, L=0.1 H, C=10 µF is driven by a 10 V step. You want the current.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Checks
steps.body: Initial current = 0 ✓; final current 0 (capacitor blocks DC) ✓; ringing period ≈ 2π/995 = 6.3 ms; envelope time constant 10 ms.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting that the capacitor impedance is 1/(sC), not sC.

lessons.title: Lab: DTFT and DT Fourier analysis

scenes.text: Whatever you sample, the spectrum repeats every 2π in digital frequency. That periodicity is the signature of discrete time.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: DTFT
steps.body: **X(e^{jΩ}) = Σ x[n]e^{−jΩn}**, **x[n] = (1/2π)∫_{−π}^{π}X e^{jΩn}dΩ**. Always periodic with 2π. Exists if Σ|x| < ∞. Properties mirror the CTFT: shift ↔ e^{−jΩn0}, convolution ↔ product, Parseval Σ|x|² = (1/2π)∫|X|²dΩ. Relation: Ω = ωT_s = 2πf/f_s.

steps.title: Pairs
steps.body: δ[n] ↔ 1; a^n u[n] ↔ 1/(1 − ae^{−jΩ}), |a|<1; rectangular {1 for |n| ≤ N} ↔ sin((N+½)Ω)/sin(Ω/2); e^{jΩ0n} ↔ 2πΣδ(Ω−Ω0−2πk).

steps.title: Example 2
steps.body: 3-point moving average h = {1/3,1/3,1/3} centred (n=−1,0,1): H = (1/3)(1 + 2cosΩ). H(0) = 1; H(2π/3) = 0 — a null at f = f_s/3.

steps.title: Example 3 — digital frequency
steps.body: f = 1 kHz, f_s = 8 kHz → Ω = 2π/8 = π/4 rad/sample.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Reading frequency beyond π (f_s/2) — it is just an alias of a lower one.

activity.prompt: |X| at Ω=π for x[n]=(0.5)^n u[n] (3 decimals).

scenes.text: Differential equations became algebra with Laplace; difference equations become algebra with the Z-transform.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
**X(z) = Σ x[n]z^{−n}**. ROC: values of z where the sum converges. Pairs:
- δ[n] ↔ 1 (all z)
- u[n] ↔ 1/(1 − z⁻¹) = z/(z−1), |z|>1
- a^n u[n] ↔ z/(z − a), |z|>|a|
- −a^n u[−n−1] ↔ z/(z − a), |z|<|a|
- n a^n u[n] ↔ a z⁻¹/(1−az⁻¹)²
- cos Ω0n u[n] ↔ (1 − z⁻¹cosΩ0)/(1 − 2z⁻¹cosΩ0 + z⁻²)

Properties: delay x[n−k] ↔ z^{−k}X; scaling a^n x ↔ X(z/a); differentiation n x ↔ −z dX/dz; convolution ↔ product; initial value x[0] = lim_{z→∞}X; final value x[∞] = lim_{z→1}(1−z⁻¹)X (if valid).

steps.title: ROC
steps.body: Right-sided: |z| > r (outside outermost pole); left-sided: |z| < r; two-sided: ring; finite: whole plane except possibly 0/∞. A causal system is stable iff all poles lie **inside** the unit circle (ROC includes |z| = 1).

steps.title: Example 1
steps.body: x[n] = {1,2,3} starting at n=0: X(z) = 1 + 2z⁻¹ + 3z⁻²; ROC all z except 0.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Same X(z), different ROC → different signals.
- Right-half-plane stability thinking (that is s-domain); in z the unit circle is the boundary.

activity.prompt: Z-transform of a^n u[n] is z/(z − ___) with ROC |z| > ___.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — design a notch filter

scenes.text: An ECG sampled at 500 Hz is polluted by 50 Hz mains. You place zeros on the unit circle at the hum frequency.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Design
steps.body: Ω0 = 2π·50/500 = 0.2π rad. Zeros at e^{±jΩ0}: numerator 1 − 2cos(Ω0)z⁻¹ + z⁻². cos(0.2π)=0.8090 → b = {1, −1.618, 1}. Poles at r e^{±jΩ0} with r = 0.95: denominator 1 − 2r cosΩ0 z⁻¹ + r²z⁻² = 1 − 1.5371z⁻¹ + 0.9025z⁻². Stable (r<1). The pole pair near the zeros keeps the rest of the spectrum nearly flat.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Choosing r too close to 1 makes ringing long and sensitivity to quantisation high.

activity.prompt: Notch frequency in rad/sample for 50 Hz at f_s = 500 Hz, in units of π.

courses.title: Unit 6 · Revision, practicals & exam
courses.summary: Formula sheet, standard Signals & Systems lab experiments (MATLAB/Python style), viva questions, original exam-style problems and a 20-question exam.
outcomes: Recall all key formulas and transform pairs
Plan and record standard SS lab experiments
Answer viva questions
Attempt exam-style problems under time

scenes.text: You have one hour to revise the whole subject. The sheet below is the page you want in your head.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Signals
steps.body:
- E = ∫|x|²dt, P = (1/T)∫_T|x|²dt; sinusoid A cos: P = A²/2.
- δ(at) = δ(t)/|a|; ∫xδ(t−t0) = x(t0); u = ∫δ, r = ∫u.
- x(at−b): shift by b then scale by a.
- DT cos(Ω0n) periodic iff Ω0/2π = m/N (lowest terms).

steps.title: LTI
steps.body:
- y = x*h; length N1+N2−1; Σy = ΣxΣh.
- Causal: h=0 for n<0. Stable: Σ|h|<∞.
- Cascade → h1*h2; parallel → h1+h2.

steps.title: Fourier
steps.body:
- c_k = (1/T0)∫x e^{−jkω0t}; Parseval Σ|c_k|² = average power.
- Pairs: δ↔1; e^{−at}u↔1/(a+jω); rect(τ)↔τ sinc; cos↔π[δ+δ].
- x(t−t0)↔Xe^{−jωt0}; x(at)↔X(ω/a)/|a|; x*h↔XH; xm↔(1/2π)X*M.

steps.title: Laplace / Z / sampling
steps.body:
- L: u↔1/s; e^{−at}↔1/(s+a); cos↔s/(s²+ω0²); IVT lim sX, FVT lim sX (LHP poles).
- Z: a^n u ↔ z/(z−a), |z|>|a|; delay z⁻¹; stable causal ⇔ poles inside |z|=1.
- Nyquist f_s > 2f_m; alias f_a = |f − k f_s|; Ω = 2πf/f_s.

steps.title: Top 6 slips
steps.body: 1) ROC missing. 2) Forgetting flip in convolution. 3) A² vs A²/2. 4) 2π factors in FT. 5) Shift-scale order. 6) Final-value theorem with jω poles.

activity.prompt: Match the transform pair.

lessons.title: Lab: Generation of signals and basic operations

scenes.text: The lab asks you to generate unit step, ramp, impulse, exponential and sinusoid in MATLAB/Python/Scilab and apply shifting, scaling, folding.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Aim and apparatus
steps.body: Aim: generate standard CT and DT signals and perform operations. Software: MATLAB/Octave/Python (NumPy, Matplotlib). Time vector t = -5:0.01:5 (CT approximation); n = -10:10 (DT, use stem plot).

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Define t or n. 2) Step: u = (t>=0). 3) Impulse DT: d = (n==0). 4) Exponential: x = exp(-0.5*t).*(t>=0). 5) Sinusoid: x = sin(2*pi*5*t). 6) Shift: x(t−2) by evaluating function at t−2. 7) Fold: fliplr. 8) Plot and label.

steps.title: Observation table
steps.body: For x[n]=n for 0≤n≤4: x[n−2] begins at n=2 with values 0,1,2,3,4 at n = 2..6; x[−n] occupies n = −4..0.

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body: Label axes, use stem for DT, keep sample interval small for CT plots, and avoid aliasing in the plotted sinusoid (more than 20 points per cycle).

activity.prompt: Order the lab procedure for plotting a shifted DT signal.
items: Define the index vector n
Define x[n] on that vector
Create shifted index n+2 for x[n−2]
Plot with stem and label axes
Compare with original and note the delay

quiz.q: Points per cycle for a decent plot

lessons.title: Lab: Convolution and LTI response (with viva)

scenes.text: Compute linear convolution without conv(), verify with conv(), then find the response of a difference equation.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Procedure
steps.body: 1) Enter x and h. 2) Allocate y of length N1+N2−1. 3) Double loop y[n+k] += x[n]h[k]. 4) Compare with conv. 5) For y[n]=0.8y[n−1]+x[n] use filter(1,[1 −0.8],x).

steps.title: Precautions
steps.body: Zero-pad correctly for circular vs linear convolution; keep track of the time-origin index.
